My mind was telling me many things: Fool, why do you go to where your arrival will mean your punishment? Idiot, are you dallying again? If Creon learns it from another, must you not suffer for it?
1.230: So debating, I made my way unhurriedly, slow, and thus a short road was made long. At last, however, the view prevailed that I should come here—to you. Even if my report brings no good, still will I tell you,
1.235: since I come with a good grip on one hope, that I can suffer nothing except what is my fate.
1.237:
**Creon**
And what is it that so disheartens you?
1.238:
**Guard**
I want to tell you first about myself—I did not do the deed, nor did I see the doer,
1.240: so it would be wrong that I should come to any harm.
1.241:
**Creon**
Like a bowman you aim well at your target from a distance, and all around you hedge yourself off well from the deed. It is clear that you have some unheard-of thing to tell.
1.243:
**Guard**
That I do, for terrible news imposes great hesitation.
1.244:
**Creon**
Then tell it, will you, and so unburdened go away?
1.245:
**Guard**
Well, here it is. The corpse—some one has just given it burial and disappeared after sprinkling thirsty dust on the flesh and performing the other rites that piety demands.
1.248:
**Creon**
What are you saying? What man dared do this?
1.249:
**Guard**
I do not know. For there was no scar of a pickax to be seen there,
1.250: no earth thrown up by a mattock. The ground was hard and dry, unbroken, not rolled over by wheels. The doer was someone who left no trace. When the first day-watchman showed it to us, a discomforting amazement fell on us all.

1.757:
**Haemon**
Do you want to have your say and then have done without a reply?
1.758:
**Creon**
Is that so? By Olympus above—know this well—you will have no joy for taunting me over and above your censures.
1.760: Bring out that hated thing, so that with him looking on she may die right now in her bridegroom’s presence and at his side!
1.762:
**Haemon**
No, not at my side will she die—do not ever imagine it. Nor shall you ever look at me and set eyes on my face again.
1.765:
Indulge in your madness now with whomever of your friends can endure it.
*Exit Haemon.*
1.766:
**Chorus**
The man is gone, King Creon, in anger and haste. A young mind is fierce when stung.
1.768:
**Creon**
Let him do—no!—let him plan something more immense than befits a man. Farewell to him! Still he will not save these two girls from death.
1.770:
**Chorus**
Then the pair of them, you really intend to kill them both?
1.771:
**Creon**
Not the one who did not put her hands to the burial. You are right.
1.772:
**Chorus**
And by what mode of death do you mean to kill the other?
1.773:
**Creon**
I will take her where the path is deserted, unvisited by men, and entomb her alive in a rocky vault,
1.775: setting out a ration of food, but only as much as piety requires so that all the city may escape defilement. And praying there to Hades, the only god she worships, perhaps she will obtain immunity from death, or else will learn, at last, even this late,
1.780:
that it is fruitless labor to revere the dead.
*Exit Creon.*
1.781:
**Chorus**
Love, the unconquered in battle, Love, you who descend upon riches, and watch the night through on a girl’s soft cheek,
1.785: you roam over the sea and among the homes of men in the wilds. Neither can any immortal escape you,
1.790: nor any man whose life lasts for a day. He who has known you is driven to madness.
1.791:
**Chorus**
You seize the minds of just men and drag them to injustice, to their ruin. You it is who have incited this conflict of men whose flesh and blood are one.
1.795: But victory belongs to radiant Desire swelling from the eyes of the sweet-bedded bride. Desire sits enthroned in power beside the mighty laws.
1.800:
For in all this divine Aphrodite plays her irresistible game.
*Enter Antigone under guard from the palace.*
1.801:
**Chorus**
But now, witnessing this, I too am carried beyond the bounds of loyalty. The power fails me to keep back my streaming tears any longer, when I see Antigone making her way to the chamber where all are laid to rest,
1.806:
**Antigone**
Citizens of my fatherland, see me setting out on my last journey, looking at my last sunlight,
1.810: and never again. No, Hades who lays all to rest leads me living to Acheron’s shore, though I have not had my due portion of the chant that brings the bride, nor has any hymn been mine
1.815: for the crowning of marriage. Instead the lord of Acheron will be my groom.
1.817:
**Chorus**
Then in glory and with praise you depart to that deep place of the dead, neither struck by wasting sickness,
1.820: nor having won the wages of the sword. No, guided by your own laws and still alive, unlike any mortal before, you will descend to Hades.
1.823:
**Antigone**
I have heard with my own ears how our Phrygian guest, the daughter of Tantalus, perished
1.825: in so much suffering on steep Sipylus—how, like clinging ivy, the sprouting stone subdued her. And the rains, as men tell, do not leave her melting form, nor does the snow,
1.830: but beneath her weeping lids she dampens her collar. Most like hers is the god-sent fate that leads me to my rest.
1.834:
**Chorus**
Yet she was a goddess, as you know, and the offspring of gods,
1.835: while we are mortals and mortal-born. Still it is a great thing for a woman who has died to have it said of her that she shared the lot of the godlike in her life, and afterwards, in death.
1.839:
**Antigone**
Ah, you mock me! In the name of our fathers’ gods,
1.840: why do you not wait to abuse me until after I have gone, and not to my face, O my city, and you, her wealthy citizens? Ah, spring of Dirce, and you holy ground of Thebes whose chariots are many,
1.845: you, at least, will bear me witness how unwept by loved ones, and by what laws I go to the rock-closed prison of my unheard-of tomb! Ah, misery!
1.850: I have no home among men or with the shades, no home with the living or with the dead.
1.853:
**Chorus**
You have rushed headlong to the far limits of daring, and against the high throne of Justice
1.855: you have fallen, my daughter, fallen heavily. But in this ordeal you are paying for some paternal crime.
1.858:
**Antigone**
You have touched on my most bitter thought
1.860: and moved my ever-renewed pity for my father and for the entire doom ordained for us, the famed house of Labdacus. Oh, the horrors of our mother’s bed! Oh, the slumbers of the wretched mother at the side
1.865: of her own son, my own father! What manner of parents gave me my miserable being! It is to them that I go like this, accursed and unwed, to share their home.
1.870: Ah, my brother, the marriage you made was doomed, and by dying you killed me still alive!
1.872:
**Chorus**
Your pious action shows a certain reverence, but an offence against power can no way be tolerated by him who has power in his keeping.
1.875: Your self-willed disposition is what has destroyed you.
1.876:
**Antigone**
Unwept, unfriended, without marriage-song, I am led in misery on this journey that cannot be put off. No longer is it permitted me, unhappy girl,
1.880:
to look up at this sacred eye of the burning sun. But for my fate no tear is shed, no friend moans in sorrow.
*Enter Creon.*
1.883:
**Creon**
Do you not know that dirges and wailing before death would never be given up, if it were allowed to make them freely?
1.885: Take her away—now! And when you have enshrouded her, as I proclaimed, in her covered tomb, leave her alone, deserted—let her decide whether she wishes to die or to live entombed in such a home. It makes no difference, since our hands are clean so far as regards this girl.
1.890: But no matter what, she will be stripped of her home here above.
1.891:
**Antigone**
Tomb, bridal-chamber, deep-dug eternal prison where I go to find my own, whom in the greatest numbers destruction has seized and Persephone has welcomed among the dead!
1.895: Last of them all and in by far the most shameful circumstances, I will descend, even before the fated term of my life is spent. But I cherish strong hopes that I will arrive welcome to my father, and pleasant to you, Mother, and welcome, dear brother, to you.
1.900: For, when each of you died, with my own hands I washed and dressed you and poured drink-offerings at your graves. But now, Polyneices, it is for tending your corpse that I win such reward as this.
1.920: What law of the gods have I transgressed? Why should I look to the gods anymore? What ally should I call out to, when by my reverence I have earned a name for irreverence?
1.925: Well, then, if these events please the gods, once I have suffered my doom I will come to know my guilt. But if the guilt lies with my judges, I could wish for them no greater evils than they inflict unjustly on me.
1.929:
**Chorus**
Still the same tempest of the soul
1.930: grips this girl with the same fierce gusts.
1.931:
**Creon**
Then because of this her guards will have reason to lament their slowness.
1.933:
**Antigone**
Ah, no! That command verges close on death.
1.935:
**Creon**
I cannot console you with any hope that your doom is not to be fulfilled in that way.
1.937:
**Antigone**
O city of my fathers, land of Thebes, and you gods, our ancestors! I am led away now; there is no more delay!
1.940:
Look at me, you who are Thebes’ lords—look at the only remaining daughter of the house of your kings. See what I suffer, and at whose hands, because I revered reverence!
*Antigone is led away by the guards.*
1.944:
**Chorus**
So too endured Danae in her beauty to change
1.945: the light of the sky for brass-bound walls, and in that chamber, both burial and bridal, she was held in strict confinement. And yet was she of esteemed lineage, my daughter,
1.950: and guarded a deposit of the seed of Zeus that had fallen in a golden rain. But dreadful is the mysterious power of fate—there is no deliverance from it by wealth or by war, by towered city, or dark, sea-beaten ships.
1.955:
**Chorus**
And Dryas’s son, the Edonian king swift to rage, was tamed in recompense for his frenzied insults, when, by the will of Dionysus, he was shut in a rocky prison. There the fierce and swelling force of his madness trickled away.
1.960: That man came to know the god whom in his frenzy he had provoked with mockeries. For he had sought to quell the god-inspired women and the Bacchanalian fire,
1.965: and he angered the Muses who love the flute.
1.966:
**Chorus**
And by the waters of the Dark Rocks, the waters of the twofold sea, are the shores of Bosporus and the Thracian city Salmydessus,
1.970: where Ares, neighbor of that city, saw the accursed, blinding wound inflicted on the two sons of Phineus by his savage wife. It was a wound that brought darkness to the hollows, making them crave vengeance
1.975: for the eyes she crushed with her bloody hands and with her shuttle for a dagger.
1.977:
**Chorus**
Wasting away in their misery, they bewailed their miserable suffering
1.980: and their birth from their mother stripped of her marriage. But she traced her descent from the ancient line of the Erechtheids, and in far-distant caves she was raised amidst her father’s gusts. She was the child of Boreas,
1.985:
running swift as horses over the steep hills, a daughter of gods. Yet she, too, was assailed by the long-lived Fates, my child.
*Enter Teiresias, led by a boy, on the spectators’ right.*
1.988:
**Teiresias**
Princes of Thebes, we have come on a shared journey, two scouting the way by the eyes of one.
1.990: For this is the method of travel for the blind, using a guide.
1.991:
**Creon**
What is it, old Teiresias? What is your news?
1.992:
**Teiresias**
I will tell you. You, obey the seer.
1.993:
**Creon**
It was not my habit before, at any rate, to stand apart from your will.
1.994:
**Teiresias**
Therefore you captained this city on an upright course.
1.995:
**Creon**
I have felt and can attest your benefits.
1.996:
**Teiresias**
Realize that once more now you are poised on fortune’s razor-edge.
1.997:
**Creon**
What do you mean? I shudder to hear you!
1.998:
**Teiresias**
You will understand, when you hear the signs revealed by my art. As I took my place on my old seat of augury
1.1000: where all birds regularly gather for me, I heard an unintelligible voice among them: they were screaming in dire frenzy that made their language foreign to me. I realized that they were ripping each other with their talons, murderously—the rush of their wings did not lack meaning.
1.1005: Quickly, in fear, I tried burnt-sacrifice on a duly-kindled altar, but from my offerings Hephaestus did not blaze. Instead juice that had sweated from the thigh-flesh trickled out onto the embers and smoked and sputtered;
1.1010: the gall was scattered high up in the air; and the streaming thighs lay bared of the fat that had been wrapped around them. Such was the failure of the rites that yielded no sign, as I learned from this boy. For he is my guide, as I am guide to others.
1.1015: And it is your will that is the source of the sickness now afflicting the city. For the altars of our city and our hearths have one and all been tainted by the birds and dogs with the carrion taken from the sadly fallen son of Oedipus. And so the gods no more accept prayer and sacrifice at our hands,
1.1020: or the burning of thigh-meat, nor does any bird sound out clear signs in its shrill cries, for they have tasted the fatness of a slain man’s blood. Think, therefore, on these things, my son. All men are liable to err.
1.1025: But when an error is made, that man is no longer unwise or unblessed who heals the evil into which he has fallen and does not remain stubborn. Self-will, we know, invites the charge of foolishness. Concede the claim of the dead. Do not kick at the fallen.
1.1030: What prowess is it to kill the dead all over again? I have considered for your good, and what I advise is good. The sweetest thing is to learn from a good advisor when his advice is to your profit.
1.1033:
**Creon**
Old man, you all shoot your arrows at me, like archers at their mark, and I am not safe
1.1035: even from the plottings of the seer’s divine art, but by their tribe I have long been bought and sold and made their merchandise. Turn your profits, make your deals for the white gold of Sardis and the gold of India, if it pleases you, but you shall not cover that man with a grave,
1.1040: not even if the eagles of Zeus wish to snatch and carry him to be devoured at the god’s throne. No, not even then, for fear of that defilement will I permit his burial, since I know with certainty that no mortal has the power to defile the gods.
1.1045: But even the exceedingly clever, old Teiresias, falls with a shameful fall, when they couch shameful thoughts in fine phrasing for profit’s sake.
1.1048:
**Teiresias**
Alas! Does any man know, does any consider—
1.1049:
**Creon**
What is this? What universal truth are you announcing?
1.1050:
**Teiresias**
—by how much the most precious of our possessions is the power to reason wisely?
1.1051:
**Creon**
By as much, I think, as senselessness is the greatest affliction.
1.1052:
**Teiresias**
Yet you came into being full of that disease.
1.1053:
**Creon**
I have no desire to trade insults with the seer.
1.1054:
**Teiresias**
Yet that is what you do in saying that I prophesy falsely.
1.1055:
**Creon**
Yes, for the prophet-clan was ever fond of money.
1.1056:
**Teiresias**
And the race sprung from tyrants loves shameful gain.
1.1057:
**Creon**
Do you know that you ramble so about your king?
1.1058:
**Teiresias**
I am aware, since through me you have saved this city.
1.1059:
**Creon**
You are a wise seer, but fond of doing injustice.
1.1060:
**Teiresias**
You will stir me to utter the dire secret in my soul.
1.1061:
**Creon**
Out with it! But only if it is not for gain that you speak it.
1.1062:
**Teiresias**
Indeed, I think I speak without mention of gain—where you are concerned.
1.1063:
**Creon**
Be certain that you will not trade in my will.
1.1064:
**Teiresias**
Then know, yes, know it well! You will not live through many more
1.1065: courses of the sun’s swift chariot, before you will give in return one sprung from your own loins, a corpse in requital for corpses. For you have thrust below one of those of the upper air and irreverently lodged a living soul in the grave,
1.1070: while you detain in this world that which belongs to the infernal gods, a corpse unburied, unmourned, unholy. In the dead you have no part, nor do the gods above, but in this you do them violence. For these crimes the avenging destroyers,
1.1075: the Furies of Hades and of the gods, lie in ambush for you, waiting to seize you in these same sufferings. And look closely if I tell you this with a silvered palm. A time not long to be delayed will reveal in your house wailing over men and over women.
1.1080: All the cities are stirred up in hostility, whose mangled corpses the dogs, or the wild beasts or some winged bird buried, carrying an unholy stench to the city that held each man’s hearth. There, now, are arrows for your heart, since you provoke me,
1.1085: launched at you, archer-like, in my anger. They fly true—you cannot run from their burning sting. Boy, lead me home, so that he may launch his rage against younger men, and learn to keep a quieter tongue
1.1090:
and a better mind within his breast than he now bears.
*Exit Teiresias.*
1.1091:
**Chorus**
The man is gone, my king, leaving dire prophecies behind. And for all the time that I have had this hair on my head, now white, once dark, I know that he has never been a false prophet to our city.
1.1095:
**Creon**
I, too, know it well, and my mind is troubled. To yield is terrible, but, to resist, to strike my pride with ruin—this, too, inspires terror.
1.1098:
**Chorus**
The moment, Creon, requires that you reason wisely.
1.1099:
**Creon**
What should I do, then? Speak, and I will obey.
1.1100:
**Chorus**
Go and free the girl from her hollowed chamber. Then raise a tomb for the unburied dead.
1.1102:
**Creon**
And you recommend this? You think that I should yield?
1.1103:
**Chorus**
Yes, my king, and with all possible speed. For harms sent from the gods swiftly cut short the follies of men.
1.1105:
**Creon**
Ah, it is a struggle, but I depart from my heart’s resolve and obey. We must not wage vain wars with necessity.
1.1107:
**Chorus**
Go, do these things and do not leave their performance to others.
1.1108:
**Creon**
Right away I will go. Go, go, my servants, each and all of you! Take axes in your hands,
1.1110: and hurry to that place there in view! But since my judgment has taken this turn, I will be there to set her free, as I myself confined her. I am held by the fear that it is best to keep the established laws to life’s very end.
1.1115:
**Chorus**
God of many names, glory of the Cadmeian bride and offspring of loud-thundering Zeus, you who watch over far-famed Italy and reign
1.1120: in the valleys of Eleusinian Deo where all find welcome! O Bacchus, denizen of Thebes, the mother-city of your Bacchants, dweller by the wet stream of Ismenus on the soil
1.1125: of the sowing of the savage dragon’s teeth!
1.1126:
**Chorus**
The smoky glare of torches sees you above the cliffs of the twin peaks, where the Corycian nymphs move inspired by your godhead,
1.1130: and Castalia’s stream sees you, too. The ivy-mantled slopes of Nysa’s hills and the shore green with many-clustered vines send you, when accompanied by the cries of your divine words,
1.1135: you visit the avenues of Thebes.
1.1137:
**Chorus**
Thebes of all cities you hold foremost in honor, together with your lightning-struck mother.
1.1140: And now when the whole city is held subject to a violent plague, come, we ask, with purifying feet over steep Parnassus,
1.1146:
**Chorus**
O Leader of the chorus of the stars whose breath is fire, overseer of the chants in the night, son begotten of Zeus,
1.1150:
appear, my king, with your attendant Thyiads, who in night-long frenzy dance and sing you as Iacchus the Giver!
*Enter Messenger, on the spectators’ left.*
1.1155:
**Messenger**
Neighbors of the house of Cadmus and of Amphion, there is no station of human life that I would ever praise or blame as being settled. Fortune sets upright and Fortune sinks the lucky and unlucky from day to day,
1.1160: and no one can prophesy to men concerning the order that has just been established. For Creon, as I saw it, was once blest: he had saved this land of Cadmus from its enemies; and having won sole and total dominion in the land, he guided it on a straight course and flourished in his noble crop of children.
1.1165: And now all this has been lost. When a man has forfeited his pleasures, I do not reckon his existence as life, but consider him just a breathing corpse. Heap up riches in your house, if you wish! Live with a tyrant’s pomp! But if there is no joy
1.1170: along with all of that, I would not pay even the shadow of smoke for all the rest, compared with joy.
1.1172:
**Chorus**
What is this new grief for our princes that you have come to report?
1.1173:
**Messenger**
They are dead, and the living are guilty of the deaths.
1.1174:
**Chorus**
Who is the murderer? Who the murdered? Tell us.
1.1175:
**Messenger**
Haemon is dead—his blood was shed by no strange hand.
1.1176:
**Chorus**
Was it his father’s, or his own?
1.1177:
**Messenger**
He did it by his own, enraged with his father for the murder.
1.1178:
**Chorus**
Ah, prophet, how true, then, you have proved your word!
1.1179:
**Messenger**
Knowing that these things are so, you must consider the rest.
1.1180:
**Chorus**
Wait, I see the unhappy Eurydice, Creon’s wife, nearby. She comes from the house either knowing of her son, or merely by chance.
*Enter Eurydice.*
1.1183:
**Eurydice**
People of Thebes, I heard your words as I was on my way to the gates to address divine Pallas with my prayers.
1.1185: At one and the same time I was loosening the bolts of the gate to open it, and the sound of a blow to our house struck my ear. In terror I sank back into the arms of my handmaids, and my senses fled.
1.1190: But repeat what your news was, for I shall hear it with ears that are no strangers to sorrow.
1.1192:
**Messenger**
Dear mistress, I will tell what I witnessed and leave no word of the truth unspoken. For what good would it do that should I soothe you with words in which I must later be found false?
1.1195: The truth is always best. I attended your husband as his guide to the furthest part of the plain, where unpitied the body of Polyneices, torn by dogs, still lay. After we had prayed to the goddess of the roads
1.1200: and to Pluto to restrain their anger in mercy, we washed him with pure washing, and with freshly-plucked boughs we burned what remains there were. Lastly we heaped a high-mounded tomb of his native earth. Afterwards we turned away to enter the maiden’s stoney-bedded
1.1205: bridal chamber, the caverned mansion of Hades’ bride. From a distance, one of us servants heard a voice of loud wailing near that bride’s unwept bed and came to tell our master Creon. And as the King moved closer and closer, obscure signs rising from a bitter cry surrounded him—
1.1210: he groaned and said in bitter lament, Ah, misery, am I now the prophet of evil? Am I going on the path most lined with grief of all that I have walked before? My son’s voice greets me. Go, my servants,
1.1215: hurry closer, and when you have reached the tomb, enter the opening where the stones of the mound have been torn away, up to the cell’s very mouth. See if it is Haemon’s voice that I recognize, or if I am cheated by the gods.
1.1219: This search, at our desperate master’s word,
1.1220: we went to make, and in the furthest part of the tomb we saw her hanging by the neck, fastened by a halter of fine linen threads, while he was embracing her with arms thrown around her waist, bewailing the loss of his bride to the spirits below, as well as his father’s deeds, and his grief-filled marriage.
1.1225: But his father, when he saw him, cried aloud with a dreadful cry and went in and called to him with a voice of wailing: Ah, unhappy boy, what have you done! What plan have you seized on? By what misfortune have you lost your reason?
1.1230: Come out, my son, I pray you, I beg you! But the boy glared at him with savage eyes, spat in his face, and without a word in response drew his twin-edged sword. As his father rushed out in flight, he missed his aim. Then the ill-fated boy was enraged with himself
1.1235: and straightway stretched himself over his sword and drove it, half its length, into his side. Still conscious, he clasped the maiden in his faint embrace, and, as he gasped, he shot onto her pale cheek a swift stream of oozing blood.
1.1240:
Corpse enfolding corpse he lay, having won his marriage rites, poor boy, not here, but in Hades’ palace, and having shown to mankind by how much the failure to reason wisely is the most severe of all afflictions assigned to man.
*Eurydice departs into the house.*
1.1244:
**Chorus**
What would you infer from this? The lady
1.1245: has turned back and gone without a word, either for good or for evil.
1.1246:
**Messenger**
I, too, am startled. Still I am nourished by the hope that at the grave news of her son she thinks it unworthy to make her laments before the city, but in the shelter of her home will set her handmaids to mourn the house’s grief.
1.1250: For she is not unhabituated to discretion, that she should err.
1.1251:
**Chorus**
I do not know. But to me, in any case, a silence too strict seems to promise trouble just as much as a fruitless abundance of weeping.
1.1253:
**Messenger**
I will find out whether she is not, in fact, hiding some repressed plan in the darkness of her passionate heart.
1.1255:
I will go in, since you are right—in an excess of silence, too, there may be trouble.
*Exit Messenger.*
*Enter Creon, attended and carrying the shrouded body of Haemon, on the spectators’ left.*
1.1257:
**Chorus**
Look, here is the King himself approaching, his hands grasping a monument plainly signing that his—if we may say it—and no one else’s,
1.1260: was the madness of this error.
1.1261:
**Creon**
Ah, the blunders of an unthinking mind, blunders of rigidity, yielding death! Oh, you witnesses of the killers and the killed, both of one family!
1.1265: What misery arises from my reasonings! Haemon, you have died after a young life, youngest and last of my sons! O God! You have departed not by your foolishness, but by my own!
1.1270:
**Chorus**
Ah, how late you seem to see the right!
1.1271:
**Creon**
God, I have mastered the bitter lesson! But then, then, I think, some god struck me on my head with a crushing weight, and drove me into savage paths,
1.1275:
—ah!—and overthrew my joy to be trampled on! Ah, the labors men must toil through!
*Enter the Messenger from the house.*
1.1278:
**Messenger**
My master, you have come, I think, like one whose hands are not empty, but who has a ready store: first, you carry that burden visible in your arms;
1.1280: second, you will soon look upon further sufferings inside your house.
1.1281:
**Creon**
What worse suffering is still to follow upon these sufferings?
1.1282:
**Messenger**
Your wife is dead, true mother of that corpse, poor lady, by wounds newly cut.
1.1284:
**Creon**
O harbor of Hades, hard to purify!
1.1285: Why, why do you ruin me? Herald of evil, of grief, what word do you say? Ah, you have done in a dead man anew! What are you saying, boy? What is this you report to me
1.1290:
God no!—what new slaughter, my wife’s doom, is heaped upon this ruin?
*The doors of the palace are opened, and the corpse of Eurydice is disclosed.*
1.1293:
**Chorus**
The sight is at hand. It is no longer hidden inside.
1.1295: There I see a new, a second evil! What destiny, ah, what, can still await me? I have just now taken my son in my arms, and now I see another corpse before me!
1.1300: Oh, tormented mother! Oh, my son!
1.1301:
**Messenger**
By the altar, with a sharp-whetted sword, she struck until her eyes went slack and dark. Before that she bewailed the noble fate of Megareus who died earlier, and then the fate of this boy, and also, with her last breath,
1.1305: she called down evil fortune upon you, the slayer of her sons.
1.1306:
**Creon**
Ah, no! I tremble with fear. Why does no one strike me full on my chest with a two-edged sword?
1.1310: I am miserable—ah—and bathed in miserable anguish!
1.1312:
**Messenger**
Yes, because you were accused of responsibility for both this son’s death, and the other’s, by her whose corpse you see.
1.1314:
**Creon**
What was the manner of the violent deed by which she departed?
1.1315:
**Messenger**
Her own hand struck her to the heart upon learning her son’s sharply-lamented fate.
1.1317:
**Creon**
Ah this guilt can never be fastened onto any other mortal so as to remove my own! It was I, yes, I, who killed you, I the wretch.
1.1320: I admit the truth. Lead me away, my servants, lead me from here with all haste, who am no more than a dead man!
1.1325:
**Chorus**
The course you recommend is to your gain, if there can be gain amidst evil. What is briefest is best, when trouble lies at your feet.
1.1328:
**Creon**
Let it come, let it appear, that fairest of fates for me, that brings my final day,
1.1330: the fate supreme! Oh, let it come, so that I may never see tomorrow’s light!
1.1334:
**Chorus**
These things are in the future. We must see to present affairs.
1.1335: Fulfillment of these things rests in the hands where it should rest.
1.1336:
**Creon**
All that I crave was summed in that prayer.
1.1337:
**Chorus**
Then pray no more; for mortals have no release from destined misfortune.
1.1339:
**Creon**
Lead me away, I beg you, a rash, useless man.
1.1340: I have murdered you, son, unwittingly, and you, too, my wife—the misery! I do not know which way I should look, or where I should seek support. All is
1.1345:
amiss that is in my hands, and, again, a crushing fate has leapt upon my head.
*As Creon is being conducted into the house, the Chorus Leader speaks the closing verses.*
1.1347:
**Chorus**
Wisdom is provided as the chief part of happiness, and our dealings with the gods must be in no way unholy. The great words of arrogant men have to make repayment with great blows, and in old age teach wisdom.

1.1:
**Athena**
Always, son of Laertes, have I observed you on the prowl to snatch some means of attack against your enemies. So now at the tent of Ajax by the ships where he has his post at the camp’s outer edge, I watch you
1.5: for a long time as you hunt and scan his newly pressed tracks, in order to see whether he is inside or away. Your course leads you well to your goal, like that of a keen-scenting Laconian hound. For the man has just now gone in,
1.10: with sweat dripping from his head and from his hands that have killed with the sword. There is no further need for you to peer inside these doors. Rather tell me what your goal is that you have shown such eagerness for, so that you may learn from her who holds the knowledge.
1.14:
**Odysseus**
Voice of Athena, dearest to me of the gods,
1.15: how clearly, though you are unseen, do I hear your call and snatch its meaning in my mind, just as I would the bronze tongue of the Tyrrhenian trumpet! And now you have discerned correctly that I am circling my path on the track of a man who hates me, Ajax the shield-bearer.
1.20: It is he and no other that I have been tracking so long. For tonight he has done us a deed beyond comprehension—if he is indeed the doer. We know nothing for certain, but drift in doubt. And so I of my of accord took up the burden of this search.
1.25: For we recently found all the cattle, our plunder, dead—yes, slaughtered by human hand—and with them the guardians of the flocks. Now, all men lay responsibility for this crime to him. And further, a scout who had seen him
1.30: bounding alone over the plain with a newly-wet sword reported to me and declared what he saw. Then immediately I rush upon his track, and sometimes I follow his signs, but sometimes I am bewildered, and cannot read whose they are. Your arrival is timely, for truly in all matters, both those of the past
1.35: and those of the future, it is your hand that steers me.
1.36:
**Athena**
I know it, Odysseus, and some time ago I came on the path as a lookout friendly to your hunt.
1.38:
**Odysseus**
And so, dear mistress, do I toil to good effect?
1.39:
**Athena**
Know that that man is the doer of these deeds.
1.40:
**Odysseus**
Then to what end did he thrust his hand so senselessly?
1.41:
**Athena**
He was mad with anger over the arms of Achilles.
1.42:
**Odysseus**
Why, then, his onslaught upon the flocks?
1.43:
**Athena**
It was in your blood, he thought, that he was staining his hand.
1.44:
**Odysseus**
Then was this a plot aimed against the Greeks?
1.45:
**Athena**
Yes, and he would have accomplished it, too, had I not been attentive.
1.46:
**Odysseus**
And what reckless boldness was in his mind that he dared this?
1.47:
**Athena**
Under night’s cover he set out against you, by stealth and alone.
1.48:
**Odysseus**
And did he get near us? Did he reach his goal?
1.49:
**Athena**
He was already at the double doors of the two generals.
1.50:
**Odysseus**
How, then, did he restrain his hand when it was eager for murder?
1.51:
**Athena**
It was I who prevented him, by casting over his eyes oppressive notions of his fatal joy, and I who turned his fury aside on the flocks of sheep and the confused droves guarded by herdsmen, the spoil which you had not yet divided.
1.55: Then he fell upon them and kept cutting out a slaughter of many horned beasts as he split their spines in a circle around him. At one time he thought that he was killing the two Atreidae, holding them in his very hand; at another time it was this commander, and at another that one which he attacked. And I, while the man ran about in diseased frenzy,
1.60: I kept urging him on, kept hurling him into the snares of doom. Soon, when he rested from this toil, he bound together the living oxen along with with all the sheep and brought them home, as though his quarry were men, not well-horned cattle. And now he abuses them, bound together, in the house. But to you also will I show this madness openly, so that when you have seen it you may proclaim it to all the Argives. Be of good courage and stand your ground, and do not regard the man as a cause of disaster for you. I will turn away the beams of his eyes
1.70:
and keep them from landing on your face.
*To Ajax.*
1.71: You there, you who bind back your captive’s arms, I am calling you, come here! I am calling Ajax! Come out in front of the house!
1.74:
**Odysseus**
What are you doing, Athena? Do not call him out.
1.75:
**Athena**
Hold your peace! Do not earn a reputation for cowardice!
1.76:
**Odysseus**
No, by the gods, let it content you that he stay inside.
1.77:
**Athena**
What is the danger? Was he not a man before?
1.78:
**Odysseus**
Yes, a man hostile to me in the past, and especially now.
1.79:
**Athena**
And is not the sweetest mockery the mockery of enemies?
1.80:
**Odysseus**
I am content that he stay within his tent.
1.81:
**Athena**
Do you fear to see a madman right before your eyes?
1.82:
**Odysseus**
I would not shrink from him in fear, if he were sane.
1.83:
**Athena**
But he will not see you now, even though you stand nearby.
1.84:
**Odysseus**
How could that be, if he still sees with the same eyes?
1.85:
**Athena**
I shall darken them, though their sight is keen.
1.86:
**Odysseus**
It is true: all is possible when a god contrives.
1.87:
**Athena**
Stand silent, then, and stay where you are.
1.88:
**Odysseus**
I must stay. But I would prefer to be far from here!
1.89:
**Athena**
You there, Ajax, once again I call you! Why do you show so little regard for your ally?
*Enter Ajax, holding a blood-stained whip in his hand.*
1.91:
**Ajax**
Welcome, Athena! Welcome, daughter sprung from Zeus! How well have you stood by me! I will crown you with trophies of pure gold in gratitude for this quarry!
1.94:
**Athena**
A fine pledge. But tell me this—have you dyed your sword well in the Greek army?
1.96:
**Ajax**
I can make that boast. I do not deny it.
1.97:
**Athena**
And have you launched your armed hand against the Atreidae?
1.98:
**Ajax**
Yes, so that never again will they dishonor Ajax.
1.99:
**Athena**
The men are dead, as I interpret your words.
1.100:
**Ajax**
Dead they are. Now let them rob me of my arms!
1.101:
**Athena**
I see. And the son of Laertes, how does his fortune with respect to you? Has he escaped you?
1.103:
**Ajax**
That blasted fox! You ask me where he is?
1.104:
**Athena**
Yes, I do. I mean Odysseus, your adversary.
1.105:
**Ajax**
My most pleasing prisoner, mistress, he sits inside. I do not wish him to die just yet.
1.107:
**Athena**
Until you do what? Or win what greater advantage?
1.108:
**Ajax**
Until he be bound to a pillar beneath my roof—
1.109:
**Athena**
What evil, then, will you inflict on the poor man?
1.110:
**Ajax**
—and have his back crimsoned by the lash, before he dies.
1.111:
**Athena**
Do not abuse the poor man so cruelly!
1.112:
**Ajax**
In all else, Athena, I bid you take your pleasure, but he will pay this penalty and no other.
1.114:
**Athena**
Well, then, since it delights you to do so, put your arm to use; spare no portion of your plan.
1.116:
**Ajax**
I go to my work. And I give you this commission: be always for me the close-standing ally that you have been for me today!
*Exit Ajax.*
1.118:
**Athena**
Do you see, Odysseus, how great is the strength of the gods? Whom could you have found more prudent than this man,
1.120: or better able to do what the situation demanded?
1.121:
**Odysseus**
I know of no one, but in his misery I pity him all the same, even though he hates me, because he is yoked beneath a ruinous delusion—I think of my own lot no less than his.
1.125: For I see that all we who live are nothing more than phantoms or fleeting shadow.
1.127:
**Athena**
Therefore since you witness his fate, see that you yourself never utter an arrogant word against the gods, nor assume any swelling pride, if in the scales of fate you are weightier
1.130:
than another in strength of hand or in depth of ample wealth. For a day can press down all human things, and a day can raise them up. But the gods embrace men of sense and abhor the evil.
*Exit Odysseus and Athena.*
*Enter the Chorus of Salaminian Sailors, followers of Ajax.*
1.134:
**Chorus**
Son of Telamon, you who hold
1.135: your throne on wave-washed Salamis near the open sea, when your fortune is fair, I rejoice with you. But whenever the stroke of Zeus, or the raging rumor of the Danaans with the clamor of their evil tongues attacks you, then I shrink with great fear and shudder in terror,
1.140: like the fluttering eye of the winged dove. Just so with the passing of the night loud tumults oppressed us to our dishonor, telling how you visited the meadow wild with horses and destroyed
1.145: the cattle of the Greeks, their spoil, prizes of the spear which had not yet been shared, how you killed them with flashing iron. Such are the whispered slanders that Odysseus moulds and breathes into the ears of all,
1.150: and he wins much belief. For now he tells tales concerning you that easily win belief, and each hearer rejoices with spiteful scorn at your burdens more than he who told. Point your shaft at a noble spirit,
1.155: and you could not miss; but if a man were to speak such things against me, he would win no belief. It is on the powerful that envy creeps. Yet the small without the great are a teetering tower of defence.
1.160: For the lowly stand most upright and prosperous when allied with the great, and the great when served by less. But foolish men cannot learn good precepts in these matters beforehand. It is men of this sort that subject you to tumult, and
1.165: we lack the power to repel these charges without you, O King. For when they have escaped your eye, they chatter like flocking birds. But, terrified by a mighty vulture,
1.170: perhaps, if you should appear, they would quickly cower without voice in silence.
1.172:
**Chorus**
Was it Artemis ruler of bulls, Zeus’s daughter, that drove you, O powerful Rumor, O mother of my shame,
1.175: drove you against the herds of all our people? Was she exacting retribution, perhaps, for a victory that had paid her no tribute, whether it was because she had been cheated of the glory of captured arms, or because a stag had been slain without gifts for recompense? Or can the bronze-cuirassed Lord of War
1.180: have had some cause for anger arising out of an alliance of spears, and taken vengeance for the outrage by contrivance shrouded in night?
1.182:
**Chorus**
For never of your own heart alone, son of Telamon, would you have gone so far down the sinister path
1.185: as to fall upon the flocks. When the gods send madness, it cannot but reach its target, but may Zeus and Phoebus avert the evil rumor of the Greeks! And if it is the great kings who slander you with their furtive stories,
1.190: or if it is he born of the abject line of Sisyphus, do not, my king, do not win me an evil name by keeping your face still hidden in the tent by the sea.
1.193:
**Chorus**
Come now, up from your seat, wherever you are settled in this long-lived pause from battle
1.195: and are making the flame of disaster blaze up to the sky! The violent insolence of your enemies rushes fearlessly about in the breezy glens, while the tongues of all the army cackle out a load of grief.
1.200:
For me, sorrow stands firmly planted.
*Enter Tecmessa.*
1.201:
**Tecmessa**
Mates of the ship of Ajax, offspring of the race that springs from the Erechtheids, the soil’s sons, cries of grief are the portion of us who care from afar for the house of Telamon.
1.205: Ajax, our terrible, mighty lord of untamed power, now lies plagued by a turbid storm of disease.
1.208:
**Chorus**
And what is the heavy change from the fortune of yesterday which this night has produced?
1.210: Daughter of Teleutas the Phrygian, speak, since for you his spear-won mate bold Ajax maintains his love, so that with some knowledge you could suggest an explanation.
1.214:
**Tecmessa**
Oh, how am I to tell a tale too terrible for words?
1.215: Grave as death is the suffering which you will hear. By madness our glorious Ajax was seized in the night, and he has been subjected to utter disgrace. All this you may see inside his dwelling—butchered victims bathed in blood,
1.220: sacrifices of no hand but his.
1.221:
**Chorus**
What report of the fiery warrior have you revealed to us, unbearable, nor yet escapable—
1.225: a report which the great Danaans propound, which their powerful storytelling spreads! Ah, me, I shudder at the future’s advancing step. In public view the man will die
1.230: because the dark sword in his frenzied hand massacred the herds and the horse-guiding herdsmen.
1.231:
**Tecmessa**
Ah! Then it was from there, from there that he came to me with his captive flock!
1.235: Of part, he cut the throats on the floor inside; some, striking their sides, he tore asunder. Then he caught up two white-footed rams and sheared off the head of one and its tongue-tip, and flung them away;
1.240: the other he bound upright to a pillar, and seizing a heavy strap from a horse’s harness he flogged it with a whistling, doubled lash, while he cursed it with awful imprecations which a god, and no mortal, had taught him.
1.245:
**Chorus**
The time has come for each of us to veil his head and steal away on foot, or to sit and take on the swift yoke of rowing,
1.250: giving her way to the sea-faring ship. So angry are the threats which the brother-kings, the sons of Atreus, speed against us! I fear to share in bitter death beneath an onslaught of stones,
1.255: crushed at this man’s side, whom an untouchable fate holds in its grasp.
1.257:
**Tecmessa**
It grips him no longer. For like a southerly wind after it has started up sharply without bright lightning he grows calm. And now in his right mind he has new pain.
1.260: To look on self-made suffering, when no other has had a hand in it—this induces sharp pains.
1.263:
**Chorus**
But if he has stopped his madness, I have good hope that all may yet be well, since the trouble is of less account once it has passed.
1.265:
**Tecmessa**
And which, if the choice were given you, would you choose—to distress your friends, and have joy yourself, or to share the grief of friends who grieve?
1.268:
**Chorus**
The twofold sorrow, lady, is certainly the greater evil.
1.269:
**Tecmessa**
Then we are ruined now, although the plague is past.
1.270:
**Chorus**
What do you mean? I do not understand what you say.
1.271:
**Tecmessa**
That man, while afflicted, found joy for himself in the dire fantasies that held him, though his presence distressed us who were sane. But now, since he has had pause and rest from the plague,
1.275: he has been utterly subjected to lowly anguish, and we similarly grieve no less than before. Surely, then, these are two sorrows, instead of one?
1.278:
**Chorus**
Indeed, I agree, and so I fear that a blow sent by a god has hit him. How could it be otherwise, if his spirit is no lighter
1.280: than when he was plagued, now that he is released?
1.281:
**Tecmessa**
This, you must know, is how matters stand.
1.282:
**Chorus**
In what way did the plague first swoop down on him? Tell us who share your pain how it happened.
1.284:
**Tecmessa**
You will hear all that took place, since you are involved.
1.285: In the dead of night when the evening lamps were no longer aflame, he seized a two-edged sword and wanted to leave on an aimless foray. Then I admonished him and said, What are you doing, Ajax? Why do you set out unsummoned on this expedition,
1.290: neither called by messenger, nor warned by trumpet? In fact the whole army is sleeping now. But he answered me curtly with that trite jingle: Woman, silence graces woman. And I, taking his meaning, desisted, but he rushed out alone.
1.295: What happened out there, I cannot tell. But he came in with his captives hobbled together—bulls, herding dogs, and his fleecy quarry. Some he beheaded; of some he cut the twisted throat or broke the spine; others
1.300: he abused in their bonds as though they were men, though falling only upon cattle. At last he darted out through the door, and dragged up words to speak to some shadow—now against the Atreidae, now about Odysseus—with many a mocking boast of all the abuse that in vengeance he had fully repaid them during his raid.
1.305: After that he rushed back again into the house, and somehow by slow, painful steps he regained his reason. And as he scanned the room full of his disastrous madness, he struck his head and howled; he fell down, a wreck amid the wrecked corpses of the slaughtered sheep, and there he sat
1.310: with clenched nails tightly clutching his hair. At first, and for a long while, he sat without a sound. But then he threatened me with those dreadful threats, if I did not declare all that had happened, and he demanded to know what on earth was the business he found himself in.
1.315: And in my fear, friends, I told him all that had been done, as far as I knew it for certain. But he immediately groaned mournful groans, such as I had never heard from him before. For he had always taught that such wailing
1.320: was for cowardly and low-hearted men. He used to grieve quietly without the sound of loud weeping, but instead moaned low like a bull. And now, prostrate in such miserable fortune, tasting no food, no drink,
1.325: the man sits idly where he has fallen in the middle of the iron-slain cattle. And plainly he plans to do something terrible. Somehow his words and his laments say as much. Ah, my friends—for it was my errand to ask you this—come in and help him, if in any way you can.
1.330: Men of his kind can be won over by the words of friends.
1.331:
**Chorus**
Tecmessa, daughter of Teleutas, terrible is your news that our lord has been possessed by his sorrows.
*Within.*
1.334:
**Tecmessa**
Soon there will be more sorrow, it seems. Did you not hear
1.335: Ajax, did you not hear his resounding howl?
1.337:
**Chorus**
The man seems to be sick, or else to be still pained by the disease which was recently with him, since he sees its traces.
1.340:
**Tecmessa**
Ah, miserable me! Eurysaces, it is for you he calls! What can his purpose be? Where are you? I am miserable!
1.342:
**Ajax**
Teucer! Where is Teucer? Will his raid last for ever? While I perish?
1.344:
**Chorus**
He seems to be sane—open the door!
1.345: Perhaps merely at the sight of me he will come to a more respectable mood.
1.346:
**Tecmessa**
There, it is open. Now you can look on this man’s deeds, and his true condition.
*Ajax is discovered sitting amidst the slaughtered cattle.*
1.348:
**Ajax**
Ah, good sailors, you alone of my friends
1.350: who alone still abide by the true bond of friendship, see how great a wave has just now crested over and broken around me, set on by a murderous storm!
1.354:
**Chorus**
Ah, lady, too true, it seems, was your testimony!
1.355: The fact proves that he is not sane.
1.356:
**Ajax**
Ah, you clan staunch in maritime skill, who embarked and stroked the oar-blade upon the brine, in you, in you alone
1.360: I see a defense against suffering. Come, slay me on top of these!
1.362:
**Chorus**
Hush! Speak words of better omen! Do not cure evil by prescribing evil; do not increase the anguish of your mad disaster.
1.364:
**Ajax**
Do you see the bold, the strong of heart,
1.365: the dauntless in battles with the enemy—do you see me now, terrible in the force of my hands against beasts unformidable? Oh, the mockery! How I have been violated!
1.368:
**Tecmessa**
Ajax, my lord, I beg you, do not talk this way!
1.369:
**Ajax**
Away with you! Will you not take yourself outside!
1.371:
**Chorus**
By the gods I plead, give way and acquire good sense!
1.372:
**Ajax**
My rotten fortune!—I let slip from my grasp those men who were begging for punishment,
1.375: and fell instead on cattle with twisted horns and fine goats, making their dark blood flow!
1.377:
**Chorus**
Why grieve when the deed is past recall? These things can never be but as they are.
1.379:
**Ajax**
Ah, you who spy out all things,
1.380: you ready tool of every crime, ah, son of Laertes, you filthiest sneak in all the army, I am sure you laugh loud and long for joy!
1.383:
**Chorus**
It is at the god’s dispensation that every man both laughs and mourns.
1.384:
**Ajax**
Yet if only I could see him, even shattered as I am!
1.386:
**Chorus**
Make no big threats! Do you not see the trouble you are in?
1.387:
**Ajax**
O Zeus, forefather of my forebears, if only I might destroy that deep dissembler, that hateful sneak, and
1.390: the two brother-kings, and finally die myself, also!
1.392:
**Tecmessa**
When you make that prayer, pray at the same time for me that I, too, may die. What reason is there for me to live when you are dead?
1.395: O Gloom of the underworld, to my eyes brightest-shining, take me, take me to dwell with you—yes, take me. I am no longer worthy to look for help to the race of the gods,
1.400: or for any good from men, creatures of a day. No, the daughter of Zeus, the valiant goddess, abuses me to my destruction. Where, then, can a man flee? Where can I go to find rest?
1.405: If my past achievements go to ruin, my friends, along with such victims as these near me, and if I am inclined to foolish plunderings, then with sword driven by both hands all the army would murder me!
1.410:
**Tecmessa**
Ah, what misery for me that a valuable man should speak words of a sort which he would never before now have endured to speak!
1.412:
**Ajax**
Ah! You paths of the sounding sea, you tidal caves and wooded pastures by the shore, long, long, too long indeed
1.415: have you detained me here at Troy. But no more will you hold me, no more so long as I have the breath of life. Of that much let sane men be sure. O neighboring streams of Scamander,
1.420: kindly to the Greeks, no more shall you look on Ajax, whose equal in the army—here I will boast—
1.425: Troy has never seen come from the land of Hellas. But now deprived of honor I lie low here in the dust!
1.428:
**Chorus**
In truth I do not know how to restrain you, nor how to let you speak further, when you have fallen on such harsh troubles.
1.430:
**Ajax**
Aiai! Who would ever have thought that my name would so descriptively suit my troubles? For well now may Ajax cry Aiai—yes, twice and three times. Such are the harsh troubles with which I have met. Look, I am one whose father’s
1.435: prowess won him the fairest prize of all the army, whose father brought every glory home from this same land of Ida; but I, his son, who came after him to this same ground of Troy with no less might and proved the service of my hand in no meaner deeds,
1.440: I am ruined as you see by dishonor from the Greeks. And yet of this much I feel sure: if Achilles lived, and had been called to award the first place in valor to any claimant of his arms, no one would have grasped them before me.
1.445: But now the Atreidae have made away with them to a man without scruples and thrust away the triumphs of Ajax. And if these eyes and this warped mind had not swerved from the purpose that was mine, they would have never in this way procured votes in judgment against another man.
1.450: As it was, the daughter of Zeus, the grim-eyed, unconquerable goddess, tripped me up at the instant when I was readying my hand against them, and shot me with a plague of frenzy so that I might bloody my hands in these grazers. And those men exult to have escaped me—
1.455: not that I wanted their escape. But if a god sends harm, it is true that even the base man can elude the worthier. And now what shall I do, when I am plainly hated by the gods, abhorred by the Greek forces and detested by all Troy and all these plains?
1.460: Shall I leave my station at the ships and the Atreidae to their own devices in order to go home across the Aegean? And how shall I face my father Telamon, when I arrive? How will he bear to look on me, when I stand before him stripped, without that supreme prize of valor
1.465: for which he himself won a great crown of fame? No, I could not bear to do it! But then shall I go against the bulwark of the Trojans, attacking alone in single combats and doing some valuable service, and finally die? But, in so doing I might, I think, gladden the Atreidae.
1.470: That must not happen. Some enterprise must be sought whereby I may prove to my aged father that in nature, at least, his son is not gutless. It is a stain upon a man to crave the full term of life, when he finds no variation from his ignominious troubles.
1.475: What joy is there in day following day, now advancing us towards, now drawing us back from the verge of death? I would not buy at any price the man who feels the glow of empty hopes.
1.480: The options for a noble man are only two: either live with honor, or make a quick and honorable death. You have heard all.
1.481:
**Chorus**
No man shall say that you have spoken a bastard word, Ajax, or one not bred of your own heart. Yet at least pause; dismiss these thoughts, and grant friends the power to rule your purpose.
1.485:
**Tecmessa**
Ajax, my lord, the fortune that humans are compelled to endure is their gravest evil. I was the daughter of a free-born father mighty in wealth, if any Phrygian was. Now I am a slave, for somehow the gods so ordained,
1.490: and even more so did your strong hand. Therefore, since I have come into your bed, I wish you well, and I do beg you, by the Zeus of our hearth, by your marriage-bed in which you coupled with me, do not condemn me to the cruel talk
1.495: of your enemies, do not leave me to the hand of a stranger! On whatever day you die and widow me by your death, on that same day, be sure, I shall also be seized forcibly by the Greeks and, with your son, shall obtain a slave’s portion.
1.500: Then one of my masters will name me bitterly, shooting me with taunts: See the concubine of Ajax, who was the mightiest man in the army. See what menial tasks she tends to, in place of such an enviable existence! Such things will men say, and so will destiny afflict me
1.505: while the shame of these words will stain you and your family. Show respect to your father, whom you abandon in miserable old age, and respect your mother with her share of many years, who often prays to the gods that you may come home alive.
1.510: Pity, too, my king, your son. Pity him the great sorrow which at your death you will bequeath both to him and to me, if robbed of nurturing care he must spend his days apart from you, an orphan tended by guardians who are neither family nor friends. I have nothing left to which I can look,
1.515: save you, and you are the reason. Your spear ravaged my country to nothingness, and another fate has brought down my mother and father, giving them a home in Hades in their death. What homeland, then, could I have without you? What wealth? My welfare is entirely in your hands.
1.520: So remember me, too. A true man should cherish remembrance, if anywhere he takes some pleasure. It is kindness that always begets kindness. But whoever lets the memory of benefits seep from him, he can no longer be a noble man.
1.525:
**Chorus**
Ajax, I wish that pity touched your heart as it does mine. Then you would approve her words.
1.527:
**Ajax**
She will have approval as far as I am concerned, if only she takes heart and graciously does my bidding.
1.529:
**Tecmessa**
Dear Ajax, I will obey you in everything.
1.530:
**Ajax**
Then bring me my son, so that I may see him.
1.531:
**Tecmessa**
But in my fear I released him from my keeping.
1.532:
**Ajax**
Because of these troubles of mine? Or what do you mean?
1.533:
**Tecmessa**
Yes, for fear that somehow the poor child would get in your way, and die.
1.534:
**Ajax**
Yes, that would have been truly worthy of my destiny.
1.535:
**Tecmessa**
Well, at least I took care to avert that disaster.
1.536:
**Ajax**
I approve of your action and of your foresight.
1.537:
**Tecmessa**
How, then, can I serve you, as things stand now?
1.538:
**Ajax**
Let me speak to him and see him face to face.
1.539:
**Tecmessa**
Oh, yes—he is close by, watched by our servants.
1.540:
**Ajax**
Then why is his presence delayed?
1.541:
**Tecmessa**
My child, your father calls you. Bring him here, servant, whichever of you is guiding his steps.
1.543:
**Ajax**
Is the man coming? Or has he missed your call?
1.544:
**Tecmessa**
Here now one of the servants approaches with him.
*Enter the Servant and Eurysaces.*
1.545:
**Ajax**
Lift him; lift him up here. Doubtless he will not shrink to look on this newly-shed blood, if he is indeed my true-born son and heir to his father’s manners. But he must at once be broken into his father’s harsh ways and moulded to the likeness of my nature.
1.550: Ah, son, may you prove luckier than your father, but in all else like him. Then you would not prove base. Yet even now I may well envy you on this account, that you have no perception of these evils about us. Yes, life is sweetest when one lacks sense,
1.555: that is, until one learns to know joy or pain. But when you come to that knowledge, then you must be sure to prove among your father’s enemies of what mettle and of what lineage you are. Meanwhile feed on light breezes, and nurse your tender life for your mother’s joy.
1.560: There is no Greek—I know it for certain—who will do violence to you with hard outrages, even when you are without me. So trusty is the guard, Teucer himself, whom I will leave at your gates. He will not falter in his care for you, although now he walks a far path, busied with the hunt of enemies.
1.565: O my warriors, my seafaring comrades! On you as on him, I lay this shared task of love: give my command to Teucer! Let him take this child to my home and set him before the face of Telamon, and of my mother, Eriboea,
1.570: so that he may become the comfort of their age into eternity. And order him that no commissioners of games, nor he who is my destroyer, should make my arms a prize for the Greeks. No, you take this for my sake, Son, my broad shield from which you have your name.
1.575:
Hold it and wield it by the sturdy thong, this sevenfold, spear-proof shield! But the rest of my arms shall be my gravemates.
*To Tecmessa.*
1.578: Come, take the child right away, shut tight the doors and make no laments before the house.
1.580: God, what a weepy thing is woman. Quick, close the house! It is not for a skilful doctor to moan incantations over a wound that craves the knife.
1.583:
**Chorus**
I am afraid when I hear this eager haste. Your tongue’s sharp edge does not please me.
1.585:
**Tecmessa**
Ajax, my lord, what can you have in mind?
1.586:
**Ajax**
Do not keep asking me, do not keep questioning. Self-restraint is a virtue.
1.587:
**Tecmessa**
Ah, how I despair! Now, by your child, by the gods, I implore you, do not betray us!
1.589:
**Ajax**
You annoy me too much. Do you not know
1.590: that I no longer owe any service to the gods?
1.591:
**Tecmessa**
Hush, no impiety!
**Ajax**
Speak to those who hear.
1.592:
**Tecmessa**
You will not listen?
**Ajax**
Already your words have been too many.
1.593:
**Tecmessa**
Yes, because I am afraid, my king!
**Ajax**
*To the Attendants.*
Close the doors this instant!
1.594:
**Tecmessa**
In the name of the gods, be softened!
**Ajax**
You have foolish hope, I think,
1.595:
if you plan so late to begin schooling my temper.
*Ajax is shut into the tent. Exit Tecmessa with Eurysaces.*
1.596:
**Chorus**
O famous Salamis, you, I know, have your happy seat among the waves that beat your shore, eternally conspicuous in the eyes of all men.
1.600: But I, miserable, have long been delayed here, still making my bed through countless months in the camp on the fields of Ida.
1.605: I am worn by time and with anxious expectation still of a journey to Hades the abhorred, the unseen.
1.609:
**Chorus**
And now a new struggle awaits me, ah, me!—a match with
1.610: Ajax, hard to cure, sharing his tent with a madness of divine origin. It is he whom mighty in bold war you dispatched from you once far in the past. But now he is changed; he grazes his thoughts in isolated places
1.615: and has been found a heavy sorrow for his friends. His hands’ former achievements, deeds of prowess supreme,
1.620: have fallen without friends, without friends, before the unfriendly, miserable Atreidae.
1.622:
**Chorus**
Surely his mother, companion of antiquity and
1.625: grey with age, when she hears that he has been afflicted with the ruin of his mind will raise a loud cry of wailing. It is not the nightingale’s piteous lament
1.630: that she, unhappy, will sing. Rather in shrill-toned odes the dirge will rise, while the hollow sound of beating hands and the shredding of grey hair will fall upon her breast.
1.635:
**Chorus**
Yes, better hid in Hades is the man plagued by foolishness, who by the lineage from where he springs is noblest of the enduring Achaeans, yet now is
1.640: constant no more in his inbred temperament, but wanders outside himself. O Telamon, unhappy father, how heavy a curse upon your son awaits your hearing, a curse which never yet has
1.645:
any life-portion of the heirs of Aeacus nourished but his!
*Enter Ajax, sword in hand, followed by Tecmessa.*
1.646:
**Ajax**
All things the long and countless years first draw from darkness, and then bury from light; and there is nothing which man should not expect: the dread power of oath is conquered, as is unyielding will.
1.650: For even I, who used to be so tremendously strong—yes, like tempered iron—felt my tongue’s sharp edge emasculated by this woman’s words, and I feel the pity of leaving her a widow and the boy an orphan among my enemies. But I will go to the bathing-place and
1.655: the meadows by the shore so that by purging my defilements I may escape the heavy anger of the goddess. Then I will find some isolated spot, and bury this sword of mine, most hateful weapon, digging down in the earth where none can see.
1.660: Let Night and Hades keep it underground! For ever since I took into my hand this gift from Hector, my greatest enemy, I have gotten no good from the Greeks. Yes, men’s proverb is true:
1.665: the gifts of enemies are no gifts and bring no good. And so hereafter I shall, first, know how to yield to the gods, and, second, learn to revere the Atreidae. They are rulers, so we must submit. How could it be otherwise? Things of awe and might
1.670: submit to authority. So it is that winter with its snow-covered paths gives place to fruitful summer; night’s dark orbit makes room for day with her white horses to kindle her radiance; the blast of dreadful winds
1.675: allows the groaning sea to rest; and among them all, almighty Sleep releases the fettered sleeper, and does not hold him in a perpetual grasp. And we men—must we not learn self-restraint? I, at least, will learn it, since I am newly aware that an enemy is to be hated only as far as
1.680: suits one who will in turn become a friend. Similarly to a friend I would wish to give only so much help and service as suits him who will not forever remain friendly. For the masses regard the haven of comradeship as treacherous. But concerning these things it will be well. You, wife,
1.685:
go inside and pray to the gods that the desires of my heart be completed to the very end.
*Exit Tecmessa.*
You also, my comrades, honor my wishes just as she does, and command Teucer, when he comes, to take care of us, and to be kind to you at the same time.
1.690:
I am going to where my journey inexorably leads. But you do as I say, and before long, perhaps, though I now suffer, you will hear that I have found rest and peace.
*Exit Ajax.*
1.693:
**Chorus**
I shiver with rapture; I soar on the wings of sudden joy!
1.695: O Pan, O Pan, appear to us, sea-rover, from the stony ridge of snow-beaten Cyllene. King, dancemaker for the gods, come, so that joining with us you may set on the Nysian and the Cnosian steps,
1.700: your self-taught dances. Now I want to dance. And may Apollo, lord of Delos, step over the Icarian sea
1.705: and join me in his divine form, in eternal benevolence!
1.707:
**Chorus**
Ares has dispelled the cloud of fierce trouble from our eyes. Joy, joy! Now, Zeus, now can the white radiance of prosperous days approach
1.710: our swift, sea-speeding ships, since Ajax forgets his pain anew, and has instead fully performed all prescribed sacrifices to the gods with worship and strict observance. The strong years make all things fade.
1.715:
And so I would not say that anything was beyond belief, when beyond our hopes, Ajax has been converted from his fury and mighty struggles against the Atreidae.
*Enter the Messenger, from the Greek camp.*
1.719:
**Messenger**
Friends, my first news is this:
1.720: Teucer has just now returned from the Mysian heights. He has come to the generals’ quarters mid-camp, and is being shouted at by all the Greeks at once. Recognizing him from a distance as he approached, they gathered around him
1.725: and then pelted him with jeers from every side—no one held back—calling him the brother of the maniac, of the plotter against the army, and saying that he would not be able to avoid entirely losing flesh and life before their flying stones. In this way they had come to the point where swords
1.730: had been plucked from sheaths and were drawn in their hands. But then the conflict, when it had nearly run its full course, was halted by the conciliatory words of the elders. But where shall I find Ajax, to tell him this? To our lord I must tell all.
1.735:
**Chorus**
He is not inside, but is recently departed. He has yoked a new purpose to his new mood.
1.737:
**Messenger**
No! Oh, no! Too late, then, was he who sent me on this errand, or I myself came too slowly.
1.740:
**Chorus**
What is this urgent matter? What part of it has been neglected?
1.741:
**Messenger**
Teucer declared that Ajax should not slip out of the house, until he himself arrives.
1.743:
**Chorus**
Well, he is departed, I repeat, bent on the purpose that is best for him—to be rid of his anger at the gods.
1.745:
**Messenger**
These words betray great foolishness, if there is any wisdom in the prophecies of Calchas.
1.747:
**Chorus**
What does he prophesy? What knowledge of this affair do you bring?
1.748:
**Messenger**
This much I know and witnessed on the spot. Leaving the royal circle of the chiefs who sat in council,
1.750: Calchas separated himself from the Atreidae and put his right hand with all kindness into the hand of Teucer. The prophet then addressed him and strictly commanded him to use every possible resource to keep Ajax inside his tent for the duration of this day that now shines on us, and to prevent him from moving about
1.755: if he wished ever to look on him alive. For this day alone will the anger of divine Athena lash at him. That was the prophet’s warning. Yes, the seer went on to explain, lives that have grown too proud and no longer yield good fall on grave difficulties sent from the gods,
1.760: especially when someone born to man’s estate forgets that fact by thinking thoughts too high for man. And Ajax, even at the time he first set out from home, showed himself foolish, when his father advised him well. For Telamon told him, My son, seek victory in arms, but always seek it with the help of god. Then with a tall boast and foolishly he replied, Father, with the help of the gods even a worthless man might achieve victory; but I, even without that help, fully trust to bring that glory within my grasp.
1.770: So much he boasted. Then once again in answer to divine Athena—at a time when she was urging him forward and telling him to turn a deadly hand against the enemy—he answered her with words terrible and blasphemous, Queen, stand beside the other Greeks; where Ajax stands, battle will never break our line. It was by such words, you must know, that he won for himself the intolerable anger of the goddess since his thoughts were too high for man. But if he survives this day, perhaps with the god’s help we may find means to save him.
1.780: With those words the seer finished, and at once Teucer rose from his seat and sent me with these orders for you to follow. But if I have been cheated of success, Ajax does not live. Otherwise Calchas has no skill.
1.785:
come out and see this man and his news. The razor lies close at our throat, poised to cut off all joy.
*Enter Tecmessa, with Eurysaces.*
1.787:
**Tecmessa**
Why do you stir me from my place of rest, when I have just found peace from those relentless troubles?
1.790: hear the news of Ajax that he has brought us—news at which I felt sudden grief.
1.791:
**Tecmessa**
Oh, no, what is your news, man? Surely we are not ruined?
1.792:
**Messenger**
I have no clue of your condition, but know only that, if Ajax is away, I have little hope for him.
1.794:
**Tecmessa**
But he is away, so I am in agony to know what you mean.
1.795:
**Messenger**
Teucer strictly commands that you keep Ajax under shelter of his tent and not allow him to go out alone.
1.797:
**Tecmessa**
But where is Teucer? And why these orders?
1.798:
**Messenger**
He has just now returned, and he suspects that such a departure carries death for Ajax.
1.800:
**Tecmessa**
Oh, misery! From whom can he have learned this?
1.801:
**Messenger**
From Thestor’s son, the prophet. His prophecy applies to today, when the issue is one of life or death for Ajax.
1.803:
**Tecmessa**
Ah, me! My friends, protect me from the doom threatened by fate! Hurry, some of you, to speed Teucer’s coming;
1.805: let others go to the westward bays, and others to the eastward, and there seek the man’s disastrous path. I see now that I have been deceived by my husband and cast out of the favor that I once had with him. Ah, my child, what shall I do? I must not sit idle.
1.810: I too will go as far as my strength will carry me. Move, let us be quick, this is no time to sit still, if we wish to save a man who is eager for death.
1.813:
**Chorus**
I am ready to help, and I will show it in more than word. Speed of action and speed of foot will follow together.
*Exeunt Tecmessa and the Chorus. A Servant takes Eurysaces into the tent. The scene changes to a lonely place on the shore. Enter Ajax, still with sword.*
1.815:
**Ajax**
The sacrificial killer stands planted in the way that will cut most deeply—if I have the leisure for even this much reflection. First, it is the gift of Hector, that enemy-friend who was most hateful to me and most hostile to my sight; next, it is fixed in enemy soil, the land of Troy,
1.820: newly-whetted on the iron-devouring stone; and finally I have planted it with scrupulous care, so that it should prove most kind to me by a speedy death. Yes, we are well equipped. And so, O Zeus, be the first to aid me, as is proper.
1.825: It is no large prize that I ask you to award me. Send on my behalf some messenger with news of my downfall to Teucer, so that he may be the first to raise me once I have fallen on this sword and made it newly-wet, and so that I am not first spotted by some enemy
1.830: and cast out and exposed as prey to the dogs and birds. For this much, Zeus, I appeal to you. I call also on Hermes, guide to the underworld, to lay me softly to sleep with one quick, struggle-free leap, when I have broken open my side on this sword.
1.835: And I call for help to the eternal maidens who eternally attend to all sufferings among mortals, the dread, far-striding Erinyes, asking them to learn how my miserable life is destroyed by the Atreidae.
1.840: And may they seize those wicked men with most wicked destruction, just as they see me. Come, you swift and punishing Erinyes, devour all the assembled army and spare nothing!
1.845: And you, Helios, whose chariot-wheels climb the steep sky, when you see the land of my fathers, draw in your rein spread with gold and tell my disasters and my fate to my aged father and to the unhappy woman who nursed me.
1.850: Poor mother! Indeed, I think, when she hears this news, she will sing a song of loud wailing throughout the entire city. But it is not for me to weep in vain like this. No, the deed must quickly have its beginning. O Death, Death, come now and lay your eyes on me!
1.855: And yet I will meet you also in that other world and there address you. But you, beam of the present bright day, I salute you and the Sun in his chariot for the last time and never again. O light! O sacred soil
1.860: of my own Salamis, firm seat of my father’s hearth! O famous Athens, and your race kindred to mine! And you, springs and rivers of this land—and you plains of Troy I salute you also—farewell, you who have nurtured me! This is the last word that Ajax speaks to you.
1.865:
The rest he will tell to the shades in Hades.
*Ajax falls upon his sword.*
*The Chorus reenters in two bands.*
1.866:
**First Semichorus**
Toil follows toil yielding toil! Where, where have I not trudged? And still no place can say that I have shared its secret.
1.872:
**Second Semichorus**
We made it, we shipmates of your voyage.
1.874:
**Semichorus 2**
All the westward flank of the ships has been scoured for tracks.
1.876:
**Semichorus 2**
Only an abundance of toil. There was nothing more to see.
1.877:
**Semichorus 1**
Neither, as a matter of fact, has the man been seen along the path that faces the shafts of the morning sun.
1.879:
**Chorus**
Who, then, can guide me? What toiling
1.880: fisherman, busy about his sleepless hunt, what nymph of the Olympian heights or of the streams that flow toward
1.885: Bosporus, can say whether she has anywhere seen the wanderings of fierce-hearted Ajax? It is cruel that I, who have roamed with such great toil, cannot come near him with a fair course,
1.890:
but fail to see where the enfeebled man is.
*Enter Tecmessa near the corpse of Ajax.*
1.892:
**Chorus**
Whose cry broke from that nearby grove?
1.894:
**Chorus**
There, I see his unfortunate young bride, who was the prize of his spear,
1.895: Tecmessa, dissolved in that pitiful wailing.
1.896:
**Tecmessa**
I am lost, destroyed, razed to the ground, my friends!
1.898:
**Tecmessa**
Here is our Ajax—his blood newly shed, he lies folded around the sword, burying it.
1.900:
**Chorus**
Ah, no! Our homecoming is lost! Ah, my king, you have killed me, the comrade of your voyage! Unhappy man—broken-hearted woman!
1.904:
**Tecmessa**
His condition demands that we cry aiai.
1.905:
**Chorus**
But by whose hand can the ill-fated man have contrived this end?
1.906:
**Tecmessa**
He did it with his own hand; it is obvious. This sword which he planted in the ground and on which he fell convicts him.
1.908:
**Chorus**
Ah, what blind folly I have displayed! All alone, then, you bled, unguarded by your friends! And I took no care, so entirely dull was I, so totally stupid. Where, where lies inflexible Ajax, whose name means anguish?
1.915:
**Tecmessa**
No, he is not to be looked at! I will cover him over entirely with this enfolding shroud, since no one—no one, that is, who loves him—could bear to see him spurt the darkened gore of his self-inflicted slaughter up his nostrils and out of the bloody gash.
1.920: Ah, what shall I do? What loved one is there to lift you in his arms? Where is Teucer? How timely would be his arrival, if he would but come to compose the corpse of his brother here! Ah, unlucky Ajax, from so great a height you are fallen so low!
1.924: Even among your enemies you are worthy of mourning!
1.925:
**Chorus**
You were bound, poor man, with that unbending heart you were bound, it seems, to fulfill a harsh destiny of limitless toils! So wild to my ears
1.930: were the words of hatred which in your fierce mood you moaned against the Atreidae with such deadly passion. True it is that that moment was a potent source of sorrows,
1.935: when the arms were made the prize for a contest in the skills of warfare!
1.938:
**Chorus**
True anguish, I know, pierces your heart.
1.940:
**Chorus**
I do not wonder, lady, that you wail and wail again, when you have just lost one so loved.
1.942:
**Tecmessa**
It is for you to analyze my troubles, but for me to feel them too fully.
1.944:
**Tecmessa**
Oh, my son, to what a heavy yoke of slavery
1.945: we advance! What cruel task-masters stand over us!
1.946:
**Chorus**
Ah, the deeds of the two ruthless Atreidae which you name in our present grief would be unthinkable! May the gods hold them back!
1.950:
**Tecmessa**
These events that you see would not have happened as they have without the will of the gods.
1.951:
**Chorus**
Yes, they have brought upon us a burden too heavy to bear.
1.952:
**Tecmessa**
Yet what suffering the divine daughter of Zeus, fierce Pallas, engenders for Odysseus’ sake!
1.955:
**Chorus**
No doubt the much-enduring hero exults in his dark soul and mocks in loud laughter at these frenzied sorrows—what shame!—
1.960: and with him, when they hear the news, will laugh the royal brothers, the Atreidae.
1.961:
**Tecmessa**
Then let them mock and rejoice at this man’s misery. Perhaps, even though they did not cherish him while he lived, they will lament his death, when they meet with the difficulties of war. Men of crooked judgment do not know what good
1.965: they have in their hands until they have thrown it away. His death is more bitter to me than it is sweet to the Greeks; but in any case to Ajax himself it is a joy, since he has accomplished all that he desired to get—his longed-for death. So why should they exult over him?
