1.970: He died before the gods, not at all before them—no! And so let Odysseus toss his insults in empty glee. For them Ajax is no more; for me he is gone, abandoning me to anguish and mourning.
1.975:
**Chorus**
Quiet—I think I hear the voice of Teucer striking a note that points to this disaster.
*Enter Teucer.*
1.977:
**Teucer**
Beloved Ajax, brother whose face was so dear to me, have you truly fared as the mighty rumor says?
1.979:
**Chorus**
He is dead, Teucer. Take it as fact.
1.980:
**Teucer**
Then I am destroyed by my heavy fortune!
1.981:
**Chorus**
When things stand as they do—
**Teucer**
Ah, misery, misery!
1.982:
**Chorus**
—you have cause to mourn.
**Teucer**
O rash passion!
1.983:
**Chorus**
Yes, Teucer, far too rash.
**Teucer**
Ah, misery—what about the man’s child? Where in all of Troy can I find him?
1.985:
**Chorus**
He is alone near the tent.
**Teucer**
*To Tecmessa.*
Then bring him here right away, so that we may prevent some enemy from snatching him away, as a hunter snatches a cub from a lioness and leaves her barren! Go quickly; give me your help! It is the habit of men everywhere to laugh in triumph over the dead when they are mere corpses on the ground.
*Exit Tecmessa.*
1.990:
**Chorus**
Yes, while still alive, Teucer, Ajax ordered you to care for the child, just as you are in fact doing.
1.992:
**Teucer**
This sight is truly most painful to me of all that my eyes have seen.
1.995: And the journey truly loathsome to my heart above all other journeys is this one that I have just now made while pursuing and scouting out your footsteps, dearest Ajax, once I learned of your fate! For a swift rumor about you, as if sent from some god, passed throughout all the Greek army, telling that you were dead and gone.
1.1000:
I heard the rumor while still far away from you, and I groaned quietly in sadness. But now that I see its truth, my heart is utterly shattered! Oh, god! Come, uncover him; let me see the worst.
*The corpse of Ajax is uncovered.*
O face painful to look upon and full of cruel boldness,
1.1005: what a full crop of sorrows you have sown for me in your death! Where can I go? What people will receive me, when I have failed to help you in your troubles? No doubt Telamon, your father and mine, will likely greet me with a smile and kind words,
1.1010: when I return without you. Yes, of course he will—a man who, even when enjoying good fortune, tends not to smile more brightly than before! What will a man like him leave unsaid? What insult will he forego against the bastard offspring of his spear’s war-prize, against your cowardly, unmanly betrayer, dear Ajax,
1.1015: or better yet, your treacherous betrayer with designs to govern your domain and your house after your death? So will he insult me; he is a man quick to anger, severe in old age, and his rage seeks quarrels without cause. And in the end I shall be thrust out of our land, and cast off,
1.1020: branded by his taunts as a slave instead of a freeman. These are my prospects at home. At Troy, on the other hand, my enemies are many, while I have few things to help me. All this have I gained from your death! Ah, me, what shall I do? How shall I draw your poor corpse
1.1025: off the sharp tooth of this gleaming sword, the murderer who, it seems, made you breathe your last? Now do you see how in time Hector, though dead, was to destroy you? By the gods, note the fortune of this mortal pair.
1.1030: First Hector with the very warrior’s belt given to him by Ajax was lashed to the chariot-rail and shredded without end, until his life fled with his breath. Now Ajax here had this gift from Hector, and by this he has perished in his deadly fall. Was it not the Fury who forged this blade,
1.1035: was not that belt the product of Hades, the grim artificer? I, for my part, would affirm that these happenings and all happenings ever are designed by the gods for men. But if there is anyone in whose judgment my words are unacceptable, let him cherish his own thoughts, as I do mine.
1.1040:
**Chorus**
Do not go on at length, but consider how you will bury him and what you will next say. For I see our enemy approaching, and chances are that he comes to mock at our sorrows, like one who would do us harm.
1.1044:
**Teucer**
What man of the army do you see?
1.1045:
**Chorus**
Menelaus, the beneficiary of this expedition.
1.1046:
**Teucer**
I see him; he is not hard to recognize when near.
*Enter Menelaus.*
1.1047:
**Menelaus**
You there, I tell you not to lift that corpse for burial, but leave it where it lies.
1.1049:
**Teucer**
Why do you waste your breath on this arrogant command?
1.1050:
**Menelaus**
It conveys my decree, and the decree of the army’s supreme ruler.
1.1051:
**Teucer**
Would you mind, then, telling me what reason you pretend?
1.1052:
**Menelaus**
This—that when we had hoped we were bringing Ajax from home to be an ally and a friend for the Greeks, we found him on closer examination to be an enemy worse than the Phrygians,
1.1055: since he plotted the murder of the entire army and marched by night against us in order to take us with his spear. And if some god had not smothered this attempt, we would have been allotted the fate which he now has, and we would be dead and lie prostrate by an ignoble doom,
1.1060: while he would be living. But now a god has turned his outrage aside, so that it fell on the sheep and cattle. For this reason there is no man so powerful that he will be able to entomb the corpse of Ajax. Instead he shall be cast forth somewhere on the yellow sand
1.1065: to become forage for the birds of the seashore. So then do not inflame the terrible force of your spirit. If we were unable to master him while he lived, in any case in death, at least, we shall rule him despite your opposition and control him by force of our hands. For while he lived, there never was a time
1.1070: when he would obey my commands. Now it is, in truth, the mark of a base nature when a commoner does not think it right to obey those who stand over him. Never can the laws maintain a prosperous course in a city where fear has no fixed place,
1.1075: nor can a camp be ruled any more with moderation, if it lacks the guarding force of fear and reverence. A man, though he grow his body great and mighty, must expect to fall, even from a light blow. Whoever knows fear and shame both,
1.1080: you can be certain that he has found his salvation; but where there is license to attack others and act at will, do not doubt that such a State, though she has run before a favoring wind, will eventually sink with time into the depths. No, let me see fear, too, established, where fear is fitting;
1.1085: let us not think that we can act on our desires without paying the price in pain. These things come by turns. He was once the hot attacker, now it is my hour to glory. And so I warn you not to bury him,
1.1090: so that you can avoid falling into your own grave.
1.1091:
**Chorus**
Menelaus, after laying down wise precepts, do not then violate the dead.
1.1093:
**Teucer**
Never again, my fellow Salaminians, will I be amazed if some nobody by birth does wrong,
1.1095: when those who are reputed to be born of noble blood employ such wrongful sentiments in their arguments. Come, tell me from the first once more—do you really say that you brought Ajax here to the Greeks as an ally personally recruited by you? Did he not sail of his own accord? As his own master?
1.1100: On what grounds are you his commander? On what grounds have you a right to kingship over the men whom he brought from home? It was as Sparta’s king that you came, not as master over us. Nowhere was it established among your lawful powers that you should order him any more than he you.
1.1105: You sailed here under the command of others, not as a supreme commander who might at any time exercise authority over Ajax. No, rule the troops you rule, and use your reverend words to punish them! But this man, whether you or the other general forbid it, I will lay
1.1110: in the grave as justice demands, and I will not fear your tongue. It was not at all for your wife’s sake that Ajax made this expedition, as did those toil-worn drudges. No, it was for the sake of the oath by which he had sworn, and not at all for you, since it was not his habit to value nobodies.
1.1115: And so when you come here again, bring more heralds, and the leader of the expedition, too. Your bluster could not make me turn to notice you, so long as you are what you are.
1.1118:
**Chorus**
Again, I say, in these troubles I cannot approve of such a tone. Harsh words sting, however just they are.
1.1120:
**Menelaus**
The bowman seems to feel no little grandeur.
1.1121:
**Teucer**
I do, since it is no lowly skill that I possess.
1.1122:
**Menelaus**
How you would boast, if you had a shield!
1.1123:
**Teucer**
Even without a shield I would be a match for you fully armed.
1.1124:
**Menelaus**
What a tongue you have! What dreadful anger it feeds!
1.1125:
**Teucer**
When right is with him, a man’s thoughts may be grand.
1.1126:
**Menelaus**
What, is it right that the man who murdered me should prosper?
1.1127:
**Teucer**
Murdered you? It is truly a strange happening, if in fact you live after being killed.
1.1128:
**Menelaus**
A god rescued me. So far as that corpse is concerned, I am in Hades.
1.1129:
**Teucer**
Then since it was the gods who saved you, do not dishonor the gods.
1.1130:
**Menelaus**
What, would I find fault with divine law?
1.1131:
**Teucer**
Yes, if by your presence here you prevent burial of the dead.
1.1132:
**Menelaus**
Prevent it I do, since he was at war with me and I with him. Burial in such a case would not be right.
1.1133:
**Teucer**
What do you mean? Did Ajax ever stand forth publicly to war with you?
1.1134:
**Menelaus**
He hated me as I hated him, and you knew it, too.
1.1135:
**Teucer**
Yes, he hated you because you had been caught fixing the votes in order to rob him.
1.1136:
**Menelaus**
At the hands of the jurymen, not mine, he suffered that loss.
1.1137:
**Teucer**
You could make a thousand stealthy crimes look pretty.
1.1138:
**Menelaus**
That sentiment leads to pain for someone I know.
1.1139:
**Teucer**
The pain will be no greater, I think, than that which we will inflict.
1.1140:
**Menelaus**
I will tell you once and for all—there is to be no burial for him.
1.1141:
**Teucer**
And hear my reply—he shall be buried immediately.
1.1142:
**Menelaus**
Once I saw a bold-tongued man who had urged sailors to set sail during wintertime. Yet in him you could have found no voice
1.1145: when the worst of the storm was upon him. No, hidden beneath his cloak he allowed the crew to trample on him at will. And so it is with you and your raging speech—perhaps a great storm, even if its blast comes from a small cloud, will extinguish your shouting.
1.1150:
**Teucer**
Yes, and I have seen a man stuffed with foolishness who exulted in his neighbor’s misfortunes. It turned out that a man like me and of similar temperament stared at him and said, Man, do not wrong the dead; for, if you do, rest assured that you will come to harm. So he warned the misguided man before him. Take note—I see him now, and I think that he is no one but you. Have I spoken in riddles?
1.1159:
**Menelaus**
I will go—it would be a disgrace to have it known
1.1160: that I argue when I have the power to use force.
1.1161:
**Teucer**
Leave then! The worst disgrace for me is that I should listen to a fool’s empty chatter.
*Exit Menelaus.*
1.1163:
**Chorus**
A trial of this great discord will soon come about. But you, Teucer, with all the speed you can muster,
1.1165:
be quick to seek a hollow grave for Ajax, where he shall establish his dank tomb, a constant memorial for mortals.
*Enter Tecmessa and Eurysaces.*
1.1168:
**Teucer**
And now just in time his son and his wife approach
1.1170: to arrange the burial of the pitiable corpse. Come here, nephew. Take your place near him, and grasp in supplication your father, your begetter. Kneel and pray for help, with locks of hair in your hand from me, her, and thirdly you;
1.1175: they are the suppliant’s only resource. But if any soldier from the army should tear you by violence from this body, then for his wickedness may he be wickedly cast out of his country and get no burial, but be severed at the root with all his race, just as I shear this lock.
1.1180:
Take it, Nephew, and keep it safe. Let no one move you, but kneel there and cling to the dead. And you there, do not stand idly by like women, not men. Help defend us until I return, when I have seen to a grave for him, though all the world forbids it.
*Exit Teucer.*
1.1185:
**Chorus**
Which will be the last year? When will the sum of the years of our many wanderings stop bringing upon me the unending doom of toilful spear-battles
1.1190: throughout broad Troy, the cause of sorrow and of shame for Greece?
1.1192:
**Chorus**
If only that man had first passed into the depths of the sky or into Hades, the common home of all,
1.1195: before he taught the Greeks the shared plague of Ares’ detested arms! Ah, those toils of his invention, which produced so many more toils! Look how that man has ravaged humanity!
1.1200: or deep wine-cups did that man provide me, no sweet din of flutes, that miserable man, or pleasing rest in the night.
1.1205: And from love—god!—from love he has totally barred me. Here I lie uncared for, while heavy dews constantly wet my hair,
1.1211:
**Chorus**
In the past bold Ajax was always my bulwark against night’s terrors and flying missiles. But now he has become an offering consecrated
1.1215: to a malignant divinity. What joy, then, what delight awaits me anymore? O to be where the wooded wave-washed cape fences off the deep sea,
1.1220:
to be beneath Sunium’s jutting plateau, so that we might salute sacred Athens!
*Enter Teucer.*
1.1223:
**Teucer**
Here I am! I hurried back when I saw the supreme commander, Agamemnon, rapidly approaching.
1.1225:
It is plain to me that he will let his clumsy tongue fly.
*Enter Agamemnon.*
1.1226:
**Agamemnon**
So it is you, they tell me, who dared open your mouth wide to make fierce threats against us—and are you still unpunished? Yes, I mean you—you, the captive slave’s son. No doubt if you were born from a noble mother,
1.1230: your talk would reach the sky and you would proudly strut about, when now it is the case that, though you are a nobody and a nothing, you have stood up for this other nothing lying here, and have vowed that we came out with no authority either as admirals or as generals to rule the Greeks or you. No, as an autonomous ruler, you say, Ajax set sail.
1.1235: Does it not shame me that I hear these proud words from slavish mouths? What was the man whom you shout about with such arrogance? Where did he advance, or where did he stand his ground, where I did not do the same? Have the Greeks, then, no other men but him? To our own harm, it seems, we announced
1.1240: to the Greeks the contests for the arms of Achilles, if on all sides we are accounted corrupt because of Teucer, and if it will never satisfy you Salaminians, even when you are defeated, to accept the verdict which satisfied the majority of the judges. But instead you will always no doubt aim your slanderous arrows at us,
1.1245: or treacherously lash at our backs when you fall behind us in the race. Yet in a place where such ways prevail, there could be no settled order for any law, if we are to thrust the rightful winners aside and bring those in the rear up to the front ranks.
1.1250: These tendencies must be checked. It is not the stout, broad-shouldered men that are the steadiest allies. No, it is the wise who prevail in every engagement. A broad-backed ox is kept straight on the road all the same when only a small whip directs him.
1.1255: And a dose of this very medicine, I foresee, will find you before long, unless you gain a little good sense. He no longer exists, but is already a shade, yet still you boldly insult us and give your tongue too much freedom. Restrain yourself, I say. Recall your birth, your nature.
1.1260: Bring someone else here—a man who is freeborn—who can plead your cause before me in your place. For when you speak, I no longer understand— I do not know your barbarian language.
1.1264:
**Chorus**
If only you both had the sense to exercise self-restraint!
1.1265: There is no better advice that I could give you two.
1.1266:
**Teucer**
My, how quickly gratitude to the dead seeps away from men and is found to have turned to betrayal, since this man no longer offers even the slightest praise in remembrance of you, Ajax, even though it was for his sake
1.1270: you toiled so often in battle, offering your own life to the spear! No, your assistance is dead and gone, all flung aside! Full and foolish talker, do you no longer remember anything of the time when you were trapped inside your defenses,
1.1275: when you were all but destroyed in the turn of the battle and he, he alone came and saved you at the moment when the flames were already blazing around the decks at your ships’ sterns and Hector was leaping high over the trench towards the vessels?
1.1280: Who averted that? Was it not Ajax who did it, the one who, you say, nowhere set foot where you were not? Well, do you grant that he did his duty to you there? And what about when another time, all alone, he confronted Hector in single combat according to the fall of the lots, and not at anyone’s command?
1.1285: The lot which he cast in was not the kind to flee the challenge; it was no lump of moist earth, but one which would be the first to leap lightly from the crested helmet! It was this man who did those deeds, and I, the slave, the son of the barbarian mother, was at his side.
1.1290: Pitiful creature, how can you be so blind as to argue the way you do? Are you not aware of the fact that your father’s father Pelops long ago was a barbarian, a Phrygian? That Atreus, your own begetter, set before his brother a most unholy feast made from the flesh of his brother’s children?
1.1295: And you yourself were born from a Cretan mother, whose father found a stranger straddling her and who was consigned by him to be prey for the mute fish. So being of such a kind, can you reproach a man like me for my lineage? I am the son of Telamon,
1.1300: who won my mother for his consort as prize for valor supreme in the army. And she was the daughter of Laomedon, of royal blood, and it was as the flower of the spoil that Alcmena’s son gave her to Telamon. Thus nobly born as I am from two noble parents,
1.1305: could I disgrace my own flesh and blood, whom even as he lies here subdued by such massive troubles, you, making your pronouncements without a blush of shame, would thrust out without burial? Now consider this well: wherever you cast him away, with him you will also cast our three corpses.
1.1310: It is right for me to die before all men’s eyes while I am toiling in his cause, rather than for your wife—or should I say your brother’s? With this in mind, then, look not to my safety, but to yours instead, since if you cause me any grief at all, you will soon wish
1.1315:
that you had been more timid than bold when confronting me.
*Enter Odysseus.*
1.1316:
**Chorus**
Lord Odysseus, you arrive at the right time, if mediation, not division, is your purpose in coming.
1.1318:
**Odysseus**
What is the trouble, friends? From far off I heard shouting from the Atreidae over this brave man’s corpse.
1.1320:
**Agamemnon**
Is it not because we, Lord Odysseus, have long had to hear the worst, most shameful language from this man?
1.1322:
**Odysseus**
How so? I can pardon a man a retaliatory barrage of abuse if another has insulted him.
1.1324:
**Agamemnon**
I insulted him, since his conduct toward me was of the same stripe.
1.1325:
**Odysseus**
And what did he do that harmed you?
1.1326:
**Agamemnon**
He declares that he will not leave this corpse without due burial, but will entomb it in spite of me.
1.1328:
**Odysseus**
Then may a friend speak the truth, and still remain your helpmate no less than before?
1.1330:
**Agamemnon**
Speak. Otherwise I would be less than sane, since I count you my greatest friend among all the Greeks.
1.1332:
**Odysseus**
Listen, then. In the name of the gods, do not let yourself so ruthlessly cast this man out unburied. Do not in any way let the violence of your hatred overcome you
1.1335: so much that you trample justice under foot. To me, too, this man was once the most hostile enemy in the army from the day on which I beat him for possession of Achilles’ arms. Yet for all that he was hostile towards me, I would not dishonor him in return or refuse to admit
1.1340: that in all our Greek force at Troy he was, in my view, the best and bravest, excepting Achilles. It would not be just, then, that he should be dishonored by you. It is not he, but the laws given by the gods that you would damage. When a good man is dead, there is no justice
1.1345: in doing him harm, not even if you hate him.
1.1346:
**Agamemnon**
You, Odysseus—do you champion him against me in this battle?
1.1347:
**Odysseus**
I do, though I did hate him, when it was honorable for me to hate.
1.1348:
**Agamemnon**
But should you not also trample him now that he is dead?
1.1349:
**Odysseus**
Do not take delight, son of Atreus, in that superiority which brings no honor.
1.1350:
**Agamemnon**
Reverence, I tell you, is not easily practiced by the autocrat.
1.1351:
**Odysseus**
But it is easy to grant dispensations to friends when they advise well.
1.1352:
**Agamemnon**
A good man should listen to those in charge.
1.1353:
**Odysseus**
Stop! Your power is victorious when you surrender to your friends.
1.1354:
**Agamemnon**
Remember to what sort of man you show this kindness!
1.1355:
**Odysseus**
The man was once my enemy, yes, but he was also noble.
1.1356:
**Agamemnon**
Why do you do this? Why do you so respect an enemy’s corpse?
1.1357:
**Odysseus**
I yield to his excellence much more than his hostility.
1.1358:
**Agamemnon**
Men who act as you do are the unstable sort in humankind.
1.1359:
**Odysseus**
Quite the majority of men, I assure you, are friendly at one time, and bitter at another.
1.1360:
**Agamemnon**
So then, are these the type of friends that you recommend we make?
1.1361:
**Odysseus**
It is not my habit to recommend an inflexible spirit.
1.1362:
**Agamemnon**
You will make us appear to be cowards today.
1.1363:
**Odysseus**
On the contrary, we will be men of justice in the eyes of all the Greeks.
1.1364:
**Agamemnon**
Then do you truly urge me to allow the burying of the dead?
1.1365:
**Odysseus**
Yes, for I too shall come to that necessity.
1.1366:
**Agamemnon**
How true it is that in all things alike each man works for himself!
1.1367:
**Odysseus**
And for whom should I work more than for myself?
1.1368:
**Agamemnon**
It must be called your doing then, not mine.
1.1369:
**Odysseus**
However you do it, in all respects you will at least prove beneficent.
1.1370:
**Agamemnon**
In any case, be quite certain that to you I would grant a larger favor than this. To that man, however, as on earth, so below I give my hatred. But you can do what you will.
*Exit Agamemnon.*
1.1374:
**Chorus**
Whoever denies, Odysseus, that you were born wise in judgment
1.1375: is a total fool since you have shown it just now.
1.1376:
**Odysseus**
And now I announce that from this point on I am ready to be Teucer’s friend as much as I was once his enemy. And I would like to join in the burying of your dead and share your labors, omitting no service
1.1380: which mortals should render to their best and bravest warriors.
1.1381:
**Teucer**
Good Odysseus, I have only praise for your words. You have greatly belied my fears. Of all the Greeks you were his deadliest enemy, and yet you alone have stood by him with helping hand and did not come here and allow yourself in life
1.1385: to violate the dead Ajax ruthlessly, as did the crazed general who came, since he and his brother wanted to cast out the outraged corpse without burial. Therefore may the Father supreme on Olympus above us,
1.1390: and the unforgetting Fury and Justice the Fulfiller destroy them for their wickedness with wicked deaths, just as they sought to cast this man out with unmerited, outrageous mistreatment. But you, progeny of aged Laertes, I hesitate to permit you to touch the corpse in burial,
1.1395: lest I so offend the dead. In all other tasks do indeed be our partner. And if you wish to bring any soldier of the army with you, he shall be welcome. For the rest, I will make all things ready. But you, Odysseus, know that to us you have been a good and noble friend.
1.1400:
**Odysseus**
It was my wish to help, but if it is not pleasing to you that I should assist here, I accept your decision and depart.
*Exit Odysseus.*
1.1402:
**Teucer**
Enough. Already the interval has been long drawn out. Come, hurry some of you to dig the hollow grave; others erect the
1.1405: cauldron wrapped in fire on its high stand for prompt preparation of the ritual cleansing. Let another company bring from the tent the finery which he wore in battle beneath his shield. And you, too, child, with such strength as you have
1.1410: lay a loving hand upon your father and help me to lighten his body; for his channels are still warm and spray upwards the dark force of his spirit. Come, come everyone who claims to be our friend, start forward and move on,
1.1415: laboring in service to this man of perfect excellence. To a nobler man such service has never yet been rendered.
1.1418:
**Chorus**
Many things, I tell you, can be known through mortal eyes; but before he sees it happening, no one can foretell
1.1420: the future, or what his fate will be.

1.1:
*Before the palace of Oedipus in Thebes. Suppliants of all ages are seated on the steps of the altars. Oedipus enters, in the robes of a king: for a moment he gazes silently on the groups at the altars, then speaks.*
**Oedipus**
My children, latest-born wards of old Cadmus, why do you sit before me like this with wreathed branches of suppliants, while the city reeks with incense,
1.5: rings with prayers for health and cries of woe? I thought it unbefitting, my children, to hear these things from the mouths of others, and have come here myself, I, Oedipus renowned by all. Tell me, then, venerable old man—since it is proper that you
1.10: speak for these—in what mood you sit here, one of fear or of desire? Be sure that I will gladly give you all my help. I would be hard-hearted indeed if I did not pity such suppliants as these.
1.14:
**Priest of Zeus**
Oedipus, ruler of my land, you see the age of those who sit
1.15: on your altars—some, nestlings still too tender for flight, others, bowed with age, priests, like me of Zeus, and some, these here, the chosen youth. The rest of the folk sit
1.20: with wreathed branches in the market-place, and before the shrines of Pallas, and where Ismenus gives answer by fire. For the city, as you yourself see, is now sorely vexed, and can no longer lift her head from beneath the angry waves of death.
1.25: A blight has fallen on the fruitful blossoms of the land, the herds among the pastures, the barren pangs of women. And the flaming god, the malign plague, has swooped upon us, and ravages the town: he lays waste to the house of Cadmus, but enriches Hades with
1.30: groans and tears. It is not because we rank you with the gods that I and these children are suppliants at your hearth, but because we deem you the first among men in life’s common fortunes and in dealings with the divinities:
1.35: when you came to the city of the Cadmeans, you freed us from the tax that we rendered to the hard songstress, and that when you knew no more than anyone else, nor had you been taught, but rather by the assistance of a god, as the story goes, you uplifted our life.
1.40: Now, Oedipus, king glorious in our eyes, we, your suppliants, beseech you to find some defence for us, whether you hear it from some divine omen, or learn of it from some mortal. For I see that the outcome of the councils of experienced men
1.45: most often have effect. On, best of mortals, uplift our state! On, guard your fame, since now this land calls you savior on account of your former zeal. Let us not remember of your reign that
1.50: we were first restored and then cast down: lift this state so that it falls no more! With good omen you provided us that past happiness: show yourself the same now too, since if you are to rule this land just as you do now, it is better to be lord of men than of a wasteland.
1.55: Neither walled town nor ship is anything, if it is empty and no men dwell within.
1.58:
**Oedipus**
My piteous children, I know quite well the desires with which you have come: I know well that
1.60: you all are sick, and though you are sick I know well that there is not one of you who is as sick as I. Your pain comes on each of you for himself alone, and for no other, but my soul is in pain at once for the city, for myself, and for you.
1.65: Thus you are not awakening me from sleep: no, be sure that I have wept many tears, wandered far and wide in my thought. I have made use of the only remedy which I could find after close consideration: I sent my relative
1.70: Creon, Menoeceus’ son, to Apollo’s Pythian residence to learn what we might do or say to protect this city. And now, when the lapse of days is reckoned, I am troubled about what he is doing, for he has been away an unreasonably long time
1.75: beyond what is fitting. But when he arrives, I would be no true man if did not perform all that the god reveals.
1.78:
**Priest**
You have spoken opportunely, since at this time these people here indicate that Creon is drawing near.
1.80:
**Oedipus**
Lord Apollo, may he come to us in the brightness of saving fortune, even as his face is bright!
1.82:
**Priest**
He seems to bring comfort, since otherwise he would not be coming crowned so thickly with berry-laden bay.
1.84:
**Oedipus**
We will soon know: he is within hearing-range.
*To Creon.*
1.85: Prince, my kinsman, child of Menoeceus, what news have you brought us from the god?
1.87:
**Creon**
Good news. I tell you that even troubles hard to bear will end in perfect peace if they find the right issue.
1.89:
**Oedipus**
But what is the oracle? So far, your words
1.91:
**Creon**
If you want to hear in the presence of these people, I am ready to speak: otherwise we can go inside.
1.93:
**Oedipus**
Speak to all. The sorrow that I bear for these is more than for my own life.
1.95:
**Creon**
I will tell you what I heard from the god. Phoebus our lord clearly commands us to drive out the defilement which he said was harbored in this land, and not to nourish it so that it cannot be healed.
1.99:
**Oedipus**
With what sort of purification? What is the manner of the misfortune?
1.100:
**Creon**
By banishing the man, or by paying back bloodshed with bloodshed, since it is this blood which brings the tempest on our city.
1.102:
**Oedipus**
And who is the man whose fate he thus reveals?
1.103:
**Creon**
Laius, my lord, was the leader of our land before you assumed control of this state.
1.105:
**Oedipus**
I know it well—by hearsay, for I never saw him.
1.106:
**Creon**
He was slain, and the god now bids us to take vengeance on his murderers, whoever they are.
1.108:
**Oedipus**
Where on earth are they? Where shall the dim track of this old crime be found?
1.110:
**Creon**
In this land, the god said. What is sought for can be caught; only that which is not watched escapes.
1.112:
**Oedipus**
Was it in the house, or in the field, or on foreign soil that Laius met his bloody end?
1.114:
**Creon**
He left our land, as he said, on a mission to Delphi.
1.115: And once he had set forth, he never again returned.
1.116:
**Oedipus**
And was there none to tell? Was there no travelling companion who saw the deed, from whom tidings might have been gained, and used?
1.118:
**Creon**
All perished, save one who fled in fear, and he could tell with assurance only one thing of all that he saw.
1.120:
**Oedipus**
And what was that? One thing might hold the clue to many, if we could only get a small beginning for hope.
1.122:
**Creon**
He said that robbers fell upon them, not one man alone, but with a great force.
1.124:
**Oedipus**
How then, unless some intrigue had been worked with bribes
1.125: from here in Thebes, would the robbers have been so bold?
1.126:
**Creon**
Such things were surmised. But once Laius was slain no avenger arose in the midst of our troubles.
1.128:
**Oedipus**
But when royalty had fallen in this way, what trouble prevented a full search?
1.130:
**Creon**
The riddling Sphinx had forced us to let things that were obscure go, and to investigate the pressing trouble.
1.132:
**Oedipus**
I will start afresh, and once more make dark things plain. Worthily has Phoebus Apollo—and worthily have you—bestowed this care on behalf of the dead. And so, as is fitting, you will find me allied with you
1.135: in seeking vengeance for this land, and for the god as well. I will dispel this taint not on behalf of far-off friends, but for my own benefit. For whoever killed Laius
1.140: might wish to take vengeance on me also with a hand as fierce. Avenging Laius, therefore, I serve myself. Come, my children, as quickly as possible rise from the altar-steps, and lift these suppliant boughs. Let someone summon here Cadmus’ people, warning them that I will leave nothing untried.
1.145: For with the god’s help our good fortune—or our ruin—will be made certain.
1.147:
**Priest**
My children, let us rise. What we came to seek, this man promises of his own accord. And may Phoebus, who sent these oracles,
1.150:
come to us as savior and deliverer from the pestilence.
*The chorus of Theban elders enters.*
1.151:
**Chorus**
O sweetly-speaking message of Zeus, in what spirit have you come to glorious Thebes from golden Pytho? I am on the rack, terror shakes my soul, O Delian healer to whom wild cries rise,
1.155: in holy fear of you, wondering what debt you will extract from me, perhaps unknown before, perhaps renewed with the revolving years. Tell me, immortal Voice, child of golden Hope.
1.159:
**Chorus**
First I call on you, daughter of Zeus, immortal Athena,
1.160: and on your sister, Artemis, guardian of our earth, who sits on her glorious throne above the circle of our market-place, and on far-shooting Apollo: oh shine forth for me, my three-fold help against death!
1.165: If ever before you drove a fiery pest from our borders to stop ruin rushing upon our city, come now also!
1.169:
**Chorus**
Alas, countless are the sorrows I bear.
1.170: A plague is on all our people, and thought can find no weapon for defense. The fruits of the glorious earth do not grow; by no birth of offspring do women surmount the pangs in which they shriek.
1.175: You can see life after life speed away, like a bird on the wing, swifter than irresistible fire, to the shore of the western god.
1.179:
**Chorus**
With such deaths, past numbering, the city perishes.
1.180: Unpitied, her children lie on the ground, spreading pestilence, with no one to mourn them. Meanwhile young wives and grey-haired mothers raise a wail at the steps of the altars, some here, some there,
1.185: and groan in supplication for their terrible woes. The prayers to the Healer ring clear, and with them the voice of lamentation. For which things, golden daughter of Zeus, send us the bright face of comfort.
1.190:
**Chorus**
Grant that the fierce god of death, who now without the bronze of shields, though among cries like those of battle, wraps me in the flames of his onset, may turn his back in speedy flight from our land, borne by a favorable wind to the great chamber of Amphitrite,
1.195: or to the Thracian waves, those waters where none find haven. For if night leaves anything undone in the working of destruction, day follows to accomplish it. You who wield the
1.200: powers of fiery lightning, Zeus our father, slay him beneath your thunder-bolt.
1.203:
**Chorus**
Lycean Lord, would that the shafts from your bent bow’s string of woven gold might
1.205: go forth in their might, our champions in the face of the foe, and the flashing fires of Artemis too, with which she darts through the Lycian hills. I call him whose locks are bound with gold,
1.210: who is named with the name of this land, ruddy Bacchus to whom Bacchants cry, to draw near with the blaze of his shining torch,
1.215: our ally against the god unhonored among the gods.
1.216:
**Oedipus**
You pray. And in answer to your prayer, if you will give a loyal reception to my words and minister to your own disease, you may hope to find help and relief from woes. These words I will speak publicly, as one who was a stranger to the report,
1.220: a stranger to the deed. I would not go far on the trail if I were tracing it alone, without a clue. But as it is—since it was only after the event that I was counted a Theban among Thebans—to you, Cadmeans all, I do thus proclaim: Whoever knows
1.225: by whom Laius son of Labdacus was slain, I order him to declare all to me. And if he is afraid, I order him to remove the danger of indictment from his path by denouncing himself: he will suffer no other punishment, but will only leave this land, unhurt.
1.230: If anyone knows the assassin to be an alien, from another land, let him not keep silent. I will reward him, and my thanks shall rest with him besides. But if he keeps silent, if anyone, through fear, seeks to screen himself or a friend from my orders,
1.235: then hear what I shall do: I charge you that no resident of this land, which I rule, give shelter to or address that murderer, whoever he is, or make him a partner in prayer or sacrifice,
1.240: or give him a share of the lustral rite. Ban him from your houses, all of you, knowing that this is the defilement, as the oracle of the Pythian god has recently shown to me. In this way
1.245: I am an ally both to the god and to the dead man. And I pray solemnly that the slayer, whoever he is, whether he alone is guilty or he has partners, may, in the horrible way he deserves, wear out his unblest life. And for myself I pray that if he should,
1.250: with my knowledge, become a resident of my house, I may suffer the same things which I have just called down on others. And I order you to make all these words good, for my sake, for the sake of the god, and for the sake of our land, thus rendered unfruitful and ungodly.
1.255: For even if the matter had not been urged upon us by a god, it still would not have been fit that you should leave the guilt unpunished as it is, when one so noble—and he your king—had perished. You should have searched it out. But now, since I hold the powers which he once held,
1.260: possessing his bed and the wife who bore his children, and since, had his hope of offspring not been unsuccessful, children born of one mother would have tied us with a common bond—as it was, fate swooped upon his head—I will uphold this cause, as though it were that of my own father,
1.265: and will leave no stone unturned in my search for the one who shed the blood, for the honor of the son of Labdacus and of Polydorus and the elder Cadmus and Agenor of old. And for those who do not obey me, I pray that the gods
1.270: send them neither harvest of the earth nor fruit of the womb, but that they perish with the present fate, or one still worse. But to all you, the loyal Cadmeans who are satisfied by these things, may justice, our ally,
1.275: and all the gods be gracious always.
1.276:
**Chorus**
As you have put me under oath, on my oath, my king, I will speak. I am not the slayer, nor can I reveal him. As for the investigation, it was for Phoebus, who enjoined it, to tell us who did the deed.
1.280:
**Oedipus**
Justly said. But no man on earth can force the gods to do what they do not want.
1.282:
**Chorus**
I would like to say what seems to me the next best course.
1.283:
**Oedipus**
And if there is a third course, do not hesitate to reveal it too.
1.284:
**Chorus**
I know that our lord Teiresias is the seer most like our
1.285: lord Apollo: from him, my king, an investigator might learn most clearly about these affairs.
1.287:
**Oedipus**
Not even this have I neglected. On Creon’s suggestion, I sent a man twice to bring him. And I have been wondering for some time why he is not here.
1.290:
**Chorus**
Indeed—his skill apart—the rumors are but faint and old.
1.291:
**Oedipus**
What are the rumors? I am investigating every tale.
1.292:
**Chorus**
He was said to have been killed by some wayfarers.
1.293:
**Oedipus**
I too have heard that. But no one sees the one who saw it.
1.294:
**Chorus**
If he knows what fear is, he will not hesitate to come forward when he
1.295: hears your curses, so dire are they.
1.296:
**Oedipus**
When a man does not shrink from a deed, he is not scared by a word.
1.297:
**Chorus**
But there is one to convict him. But here they bring at last the godlike prophet, the only man in whom truth lives.
*Teiresias enters, led by a boy.*
1.300:
**Oedipus**
Teiresias, whose soul grasps all things, both that which may be told and that which is unspeakable, the Olympian secrets and the affairs of the earth, you feel, though you cannot see, what a huge plague haunts our state. From which, great prophet, we find you to be our protector and only savior.
1.305: Now, Phoebus—if indeed you have not already heard the news—sent answer to our question that the only way to rid ourselves of this pest that afflicts us is to discover the slayers of Laius, and then to slay them or banish them from our land.
1.310: So do not begrudge us the voice of the birds or any other path of prophecy, but save yourself and your state, save me, save all that is defiled by the dead. We are in your hands, and man’s noblest task is to help others
1.315: to the best of his means and powers.
1.316:
**Teiresias**
Alas, how terrible it is to have wisdom when it does not benefit those who have it. I knew this well, but let it slip from my mind: otherwise I would not have come here.
1.319:
**Oedipus**
What now? How disheartened you have come!
1.320:
**Teiresias**
Let me go home. For you will bear your own burden to the end, and I will bear mine, if you consent.
1.322:
**Oedipus**
Your words are strange and unkind to the state which nurtured you, since you withhold this response.
1.324:
**Teiresias**
I see that you, for your part, speak inappropriately.
1.325: Therefore do not speak, so I will not suffer the same.
1.326:
**Oedipus**
For the love of the gods, do not turn away, if you have knowledge: all we suppliants implore you on our knees.
1.328:
**Teiresias**
For all of you are without knowledge. But never will I reveal my troubles—not to call them yours.
1.330:
**Oedipus**
What are you saying? Do you know the secret and refuse to tell it? Will you betray and destroy the state?
1.332:
**Teiresias**
I will grieve neither myself nor you. Why do you ask these things in vain? You will not learn the answers from me.
1.334:
**Oedipus**
Will you not, basest of the base—
1.335: you would anger a stone—speak out? can nothing touch you? Will you never make an end?
1.337:
**Teiresias**
You blame my anger, but do not perceive your own: no, you blame me.
1.339:
**Oedipus**
Who would not be angry hearing such words,
1.340: with which you now are slighting the city?
1.341:
**Teiresias**
The future will come of itself, though I shroud it in silence.
1.342:
**Oedipus**
Since it must come anyway, it is right that you tell it to me.
1.343:
**Teiresias**
I will speak no further: rage, if you wish, with the fiercest wrath your heart knows.
1.345:
**Oedipus**
In my anger I will not spare to speak all my thoughts. Know that you seem to me to have helped in plotting the deed, and to have done it, short of performing the actual murder with your own hands: if you had eyesight, I would have said that you had done even this by yourself.
1.350:
**Teiresias**
In truth? I order you to abide by you own decree, and from this day forth not to speak to these men or to me: you are the accursed defiler of this land.
1.354:
**Oedipus**
So brazen with your blustering taunt?
1.355: Where do you think to escape to?
1.356:
**Teiresias**
I have escaped. There is strength in my truth.
1.357:
**Oedipus**
Who taught you this? Not your skill, at any rate.
1.358:
**Teiresias**
You yourself. For you spurred me on to speak against my will.
1.359:
**Oedipus**
What did you say? Speak again, so I may learn it better.
1.360:
**Teiresias**
Did you not understand before, or are you talking to test me?
1.361:
**Oedipus**
I cannot say I understood fully. Tell me again.
1.362:
**Teiresias**
I say that you are the killer of the man whose slayer you seek.
1.363:
**Oedipus**
Now you will regret that you have said such dire words twice.
1.364:
**Teiresias**
Should I tell you more, that you might get more angry?
1.365:
**Oedipus**
Say as much as you want: it will be said in vain.
1.366:
**Teiresias**
I say that you have been living in unguessed shame with your closest kin, and do not see into what woe you have fallen.
1.368:
**Oedipus**
Do you think that you will always be able to speak like this without smarting for it?
1.369:
**Teiresias**
Yes, if indeed there is any strength in truth.
1.370:
**Oedipus**
But there is, except not for you. You do not have that strength, since you are maimed in your ears, in your wit, and in your eyes.
1.372:
**Teiresias**
And you are a poor wretch to utter taunts that every man here will soon hurl at you.
1.374:
**Oedipus**
Night, endless night has you in her keeping, so that you can never hurt me,
1.375: or any man that sees the light of the sun.
1.376:
**Teiresias**
No, it is not your fate to fall at my hands, since Apollo, to whom this matter is a concern, is sufficient.
1.378:
**Oedipus**
Are these Creon’s devices, or your own?
1.379:
**Teiresias**
Creon is no trouble for you: you are your own.
1.380:
**Oedipus**
O wealth, and empire, and skill surpassing skill in life’s keen rivalries, how great is the envy in your keeping, if for the sake of this office which the city has entrusted to me, a gift unsought,
1.385: Creon the trustworthy, Creon, my old friend, has crept upon me by stealth, yearning to overthrow me, and has suborned such a scheming juggler as this, a tricky quack, who has eyes only for profit, but is blind in his art!
1.390: Come, tell me, where have you proved yourself a seer? Why, when the watchful dog who wove dark song was here, did you say nothing to free the people? Yet the riddle, at least, was not for the first comer to read: there was need of a seer’s help,
1.395: and you were discovered not to have this art, either from birds, or known from some god. But rather I, Oedipus the ignorant, stopped her, having attained the answer through my wit alone, untaught by birds. It is I whom you are trying to oust, assuming that
1.400: you will have great influence in Creon’s court. But I think that you and the one who plotted these things will rue your zeal to purge the land: if you did not seem to be an old man, you would have learned to your cost how haughty you are.
1.404:
**Chorus**
To our way of thinking, these words, both his and yours, Oedipus,
1.405: have been said in anger. We have no need of this, but rather we must seek how we shall best discharge the mandates of the god.
1.408:
**Teiresias**
Though you are king, the right of reply must be considered the same for both: over that I have control.
1.410: For I do not live as your slave, but as Loxias’. I will not stand enrolled as Creon’s client. And I tell you, since you have taunted my blindness, that though you have sight, you do not see what a state of misery you are in, or where you dwell, or with whom.
1.415: Do you know who your parents are? You have been an unwitting enemy to your own kin, both in the Underworld and on the earth above, and the double lash of your mother’s and your father’s curse will one day drive you from this land in dreadful haste, with darkness upon those eyes of yours which now can see.
1.420: What place will be harbor to your cries, what part of all Cithaeron will not ring with them soon, when you have learned the meaning of the nuptials in which, within that house, you found a fatal haven, after a voyage so fair? And you have not guessed at a throng of other ills
1.425: which will bring you level with your true self and with your own children. Therefore heap your scorn upon Creon and upon my message: for no man will ever be crushed more miserably than you.
1.429:
**Oedipus**
Are these taunts to be endured from him?
1.430: Be gone, to your ruin; be gone this instant! Will you not turn your back and leave this house?
1.432:
**Teiresias**
I would not have come if you had not called me.
1.433:
**Oedipus**
I did not know you would speak foolishly, for otherwise it would have been a long time before I summoned you to my home.
1.435:
**Teiresias**
I was born like this—as you think, a fool, but in the opinion of the parents who bore you, quite sane.
1.437:
**Oedipus**
What parents? Wait. What man is my father?
1.438:
**Teiresias**
This day will reveal your birth and bring your ruin.
1.439:
**Oedipus**
What riddles, what dark words you always say.
1.440:
**Teiresias**
Are you not the best at unravelling mysteries?
1.441:
**Oedipus**
Reproach me in what you will find me to be great.
1.442:
**Teiresias**
Yet it was just that fortune that undid you.
1.443:
**Oedipus**
But if it saved this city I care not.
1.444:
**Teiresias**
I will take my leave. You, boy, lead me.
1.445:
**Oedipus**
Yes, let him take you: while here, you are a hindrance, a source of trouble. When you have gone, you will vex me no more.
1.447:
**Teiresias**
I will go when I have performed the errand for which I came, fearless of your frown: you can never destroy me. I tell you: the man whom you have been seeking this long while,
1.450: uttering threats and proclaiming a search into the murder of Laius, is here, ostensibly an alien sojourner, but soon to be found a native of Thebes; nor will he enjoy his fortune. A blind man, though now he sees,
1.455: a beggar, though now rich, he will make his way to a foreign land, feeling the ground before him with his staff. And he will be discovered to be at once brother and father of the children with whom he consorts; son and husband of the woman who bore him;
1.460: heir to his father’s bed, shedder of his father’s blood. So go in and evaluate this, and if you find that I am wrong, say then that I have no wit in prophecy.
1.463:
**Chorus**
Who is he of whom the divine voice from the Delphian rock has said
1.465: to have wrought with blood-red hands horrors that no tongue can tell? It is time that he ply in flight a foot stronger than the feet of storm-swift steeds.
1.470: The son of Zeus is springing upon him with fiery lightning, and with him come the dread unerring Fates.
1.473:
**Chorus**
Recently the message has flashed forth from snowy Parnassus
1.475: ordering all to search for the unknown man. He wanders under cover of the wild wood, among caves and rocks, fierce as a bull, wretched and forlorn on his joyless path, still seeking to separate himself from the doom revealed at the central shrine of the earth.
1.480: But that doom lives forever, forever flits around him.
1.483:
**Chorus**
The wise augur moves me, neither approving nor denying, with dread, with dread indeed.
1.485: I am at a loss what to say. I am flustered in my expectations, seeing neither the present nor the future clearly. Never in past days or in these have I heard how the house of Labdacus or the son of Polybus had any quarrel with one another that
1.490: I could bring as proof in assailing the public reputation of Oedipus, seeking to avenge the line of Labdacus
1.496:
**Chorus**
Zeus and Apollo indeed are keen of thought and know the affairs of the earth.
1.500: But there is no sure test of whether a mortal seer attains more knowledge than I do, though man may surpass man in wisdom. But until I see the word made good, I will never assent when men blame Oedipus. Before all eyes the winged maiden came against him once upon a time, and he was seen to be wise,
1.510: and bore the test in welcome service to the state. Never, therefore, will he be adjudged guilty of evil.
1.513:
**Creon**
Fellow citizens, having learned that Oedipus the king lays dire charges against me, I have come in indignation.
1.515: If he thinks that in the present troubles he has suffered from me, by word or by deed, anything harmful, truly I do not desire my full term of years, when I must bear such blame as this. The wrong of this rumor
1.520: touches me not in one point alone, but has the largest scope, if I am to be called a traitor in the city, a traitor by you and by my friends.
1.523:
**Chorus**
But perhaps this taunt came under the stress of anger, rather than from the purpose of his heart.
1.525:
**Creon**
Was the opinion given that my counsels had brought the seer to utter his falsehoods?
1.527:
**Chorus**
Such things were said—I do not know with what meaning.
1.529:
**Creon**
And was this charge laid against me with steady eyes and steady mind?
1.530:
**Chorus**
I do not know. I see not what my masters do. But here comes our lord from the house.
*Oedipus enters.*
1.532:
**Oedipus**
You, how did you get here? Are you so boldfaced that you have come to my house, you who are manifestly the murderer of its master,
1.535: the palpable thief of its crown? Come, tell me, in the name of the gods, was it cowardice or folly which you saw in me and which led you to plot this thing? Did you think that I would not notice this deed of yours creeping upon me by stealth, or that if I became aware of it I would not ward it off?
1.540: Is your attempt not foolish, to seek the throne without followers or friends—a prize which followers and wealth must win?
1.543:
**Creon**
Mark me now: hear a fair reply in answer to your words, and then judge for yourself on the basis of knowledge.
1.545:
**Oedipus**
You are apt in speech, but I have a poor wit for lessons, since I have found you a malignant foe.
1.547:
**Creon**
Now hear first how I will explain this very thing.
1.548:
**Oedipus**
One thing—that you are not false—do not bother to explain to me.
1.550: without sense is a virtue, you are not wise.
1.551:
**Oedipus**
If you think you can wrong a kinsman and escape the penalty, you are not sane.
1.553:
**Creon**
Justly said, I grant you: but tell me what the wrong is that you say you are suffering at my hands.
1.555:
**Oedipus**
Did you, or did you not, advise me to send for that reverend seer?
1.557:
**Creon**
Even now I am of the same mind.
1.558:
**Oedipus**
How long is it, then, since Laius...
1.559:
**Creon**
Did what? I do not understand.
1.560:
**Oedipus**
was swept out of sight by deadly violence?
1.561:
**Creon**
The count of years would run far into the past.
1.562:
**Oedipus**
Did this seer possess this skill in those days?
1.563:
**Creon**
He was wise as now, and held in equal honor.
1.564:
**Oedipus**
Did he make mention of me at that time?
1.565:
**Creon**
Never, certainly, when I was within hearing.
1.566:
**Oedipus**
Did you never investigate the murder?
1.567:
**Creon**
Due search we made, of course, though we learned nothing.
1.568:
**Oedipus**
And how was it that this sage did not tell this story then.
1.569:
**Creon**
I do not know: where I lack insight it is my custom to be silent.
1.570:
**Oedipus**
This much, at least, you know, and could declare with insight enough.
1.571:
**Creon**
What is that? If I know it, I will not deny it.
1.572:
**Oedipus**
That, if he had not conferred with you, he would not have named me as Laius’ slayer.
1.574:
**Creon**
If he says this, you know best: but I deem it just
1.575: to learn from you as much as you have from me now.
1.576:
**Oedipus**
Learn your fill. I will never be found guilty of the bloodshed.
1.577:
**Creon**
Say, then—have you married my sister?
1.579:
**Creon**
And you rule the land as she does, with equal sway.
1.580:
**Oedipus**
She obtains from me all that she wishes.
1.581:
**Creon**
And do I not rank as a third peer of you two?
1.582:
**Oedipus**
It is just in this that you are seen to be a false friend.
1.583:
**Creon**
Not so, if you would reason with your heart as I do with mine. Weigh this first—whether you think that anyone would
1.585: choose to rule amid terrors rather than in unruffled peace, granted that he is to have the same powers. Now I, for one, have by nature no yearning to rule as a king rather than to do kingly deeds, and neither does any man I know who has a sound mind.
1.590: For now I attain all everything from you without fear, but, if I were ruler myself, I would have to do much that went against my own pleasure. How, then, could royalty be sweeter to me to have than painless rule and influence? I am not yet so misguided
1.595: that I desire other honors than those which bring profit. Now, every man has a greeting for me; now, all that have a request of you crave to speak with me, since in me lies all their hope of success. Why then should I give up these things and take those others?
1.600: No mind will become false while it is wise. No, I am no lover of such a policy, and if another put it into action, I could never bear to go along with him. And, in proof of this, first go to Pytho, and ask whether I brought a true report of the oracle.
1.605: Then next, if you have found that I have planned anything in concert with the soothsayer, take and slay me, by the sentence not of one mouth, but of two—by my own no less than yours. But do not assume my guilt on unproven inference. It is not just to judge bad men good at random,
1.610: or good men bad. I think that casting off a true friend is for a man like casting away the life in his own bosom, which he most loves. You will surely learn about these affairs in time, since time alone reveals a just man.
1.615: But you can discern a bad man even in one day alone.
1.616:
**Chorus**
He has spoken well, my king, for one who is taking care not to fall: those who are quick in counsel are not sure.
1.618:
**Oedipus**
When the stealthy plotter is moving on me quickly, I, too, must be quick in my counterplot.
1.620: If I await him in repose, his ends will have been gained, and mine lost.
1.622:
**Creon**
What do you want then? To banish me from the land?
1.623:
**Oedipus**
Hardly. I desire your death, not your exile, so that I might show what a thing envy is.
1.625:
**Creon**
Are you resolved not to yield or believe?
1.626:
**Creon**
No, for I see you are not sane.
**Oedipus**
Sane, at least, in my own interest.
1.627:
**Creon**
But you should be so in mine also.
**Oedipus**
You are false.
1.628:
**Creon**
But if you understand nothing?
**Oedipus**
Still I must rule.
1.629:
**Creon**
Not if you rule badly.
**Oedipus**
Hear him, city of Thebes!
1.630:
**Creon**
The city is mine too, not yours alone.
1.631:
**Chorus**
Cease, lords. In good time I see Iocasta coming from the house, with whose help you should resolve your present feud.
*Iocasta enters.*
1.634:
**Iocasta**
Misguided men, why have you raised
1.635: such a foolish argument? Are you not ashamed, while the land is so sick, to stir up troubles of your own? Come, go into the house—and you, Creon, go to yours—and stop making so much of a petty grief.
1.640: wants to do one of two terrible things to me, either to thrust me from the land of my fathers or to arrest and slay me.
1.642:
**Oedipus**
Yes indeed, for I have caught him, lady, working evil against my person with his wicked craft.
1.645: but perish accursed, if I have done any of the things of which you charge me.
1.646:
**Iocasta**
In the name of the gods, believe it, Oedipus, first for the sake of this awful oath to the gods, then for my sake and for the sake of those who stand before you.
1.649:
**Chorus**
Consent, reflect, listen, my king, I beg you.
1.650:
**Oedipus**
What would you have me grant you?
1.651:
**Chorus**
Respect him who was in the past not foolish, and who now is strong in his oath.
1.653:
**Oedipus**
Do you understand what you crave?
1.655:
**Oedipus**
Tell me, then, what you mean.
1.656:
**Chorus**
That you should never use an unproved rumor to cast a dishonoring charge on the friend who has bound himself with a curse.
1.658:
**Oedipus**
Then be quite aware that when you seek this you are seeking death or exile from this land for me.
1.660:
**Chorus**
No, by the god that stands at the head of all the host of the gods, no, by the sun. Unblest, unbefriended, may I die the worst possible death, if I have this thought!
1.665: But my unhappy soul is worn by the withering of the land, as well as by the thought that our old sorrows should be crowned by new ones arising from the two of you.
1.669:
**Oedipus**
Then let him go, though I am surely doomed to be killed
1.670: or thrust dishonored from the land. Your words, not his, move me to compassion; but he, wherever he be, shall be hated.
1.673:
**Creon**
You are truly sullen in yielding, as you are vehement in the excesses of your wrath. But such natures are
1.675: justly most difficult for themselves to bear.
1.676:
**Oedipus**
Will you not be gone and leave me in peace?
**Creon**
I will go on my way. I have found you undiscerning, but in the view of these men I am just.
*He exits.*
1.678:
**Chorus**
Lady, why do you hesitate to take this man into the house?
1.680:
**Iocasta**
I will, when I have learned what has happened.
1.681:
**Chorus**
Blind suspicion, bred of talk, arose, and injustice inflicts wounds.
1.685:
**Chorus**
It is enough, I think, enough, when our land is already vexed, that the matter should rest where it stopped.
1.687:
**Oedipus**
Do you see to what you have come, for all your noble intent, in seeking to slacken and blunt my zeal?
1.689:
**Chorus**
King, I have said it more than once—
1.690: be sure that I would have proved myself a madman, bankrupt in sane counsel, if I forsook you—you, who gave a true course to my beloved country when it was
1.695: distraught with troubles, and who now are likely to prove our prospering guide.
1.698:
**Iocasta**
In the name of the gods, tell me, king, the reason that you have conceived this steadfast wrath.
1.700:
**Oedipus**
That I will do, for I honor you, lady, above these men. Creon is the cause, and the plots he has laid against me.
1.702:
**Iocasta**
Come, tell me how the argument began.
1.703:
**Oedipus**
He says that I stand guilty of Laius’ blood.
1.704:
**Iocasta**
On his own knowledge or on hearsay from another?
1.705:
**Oedipus**
He has made a rascal seer his mouth piece: as for himself, he keeps his lips wholly pure.
1.707:
**Iocasta**
Then absolve yourself of the things about which you are speaking. Listen to me, and take comfort in learning that nothing of mortal birth shares in the science of the seer.
1.710: I will give you a pithy proof of this. An oracle came to Laius once—I will not say from Phoebus himself, but from his ministers—saying that he would suffer his doom at the hands of the child to be born to him and me.
1.715: And Laius—as, at least, the rumor goes—was murdered one day by foreign robbers at a place where the three highways meet. And the child’s birth was not yet three days past, when Laius pinned his ankles together and had him thrown, by others’ hands, on a remote mountain.
1.720: So, in that case, Apollo did not bring it to pass that the child should become the slayer of his father, or that Laius should suffer that which he feared, death at the hands of his child: thus the messages of the seer’s art had mapped out the future. Pay them no regard. Whatever necessary event
1.725: the god seeks, he himself will easily bring to light.
1.726:
**Oedipus**
What restlessness of soul, lady, what tumult has come upon me since I heard you speak!
1.728:
**Iocasta**
What anxiety has startled you, that you say this?
1.729:
**Oedipus**
I thought that I heard this from you—that Laius
1.730: was slain where the three roads meet.
1.731:
**Icasta**
Yes, that was the report, and so it is still thought.
1.732:
**Oedipus**
And where is the place where this occurred?
1.733:
**Iocasta**
The land is called Phocis; the branching forks lead to the same spot from Delphi and from Daulia.
1.735:
**Oedipus**
And how much time has passed since these events took place?
1.736:
**Iocasta**
The news was announced to the town shortly before you first attained power over this land.
1.738:
**Oedipus**
O Zeus, what have you decreed for me?
1.739:
**Iocasta**
Why, Oedipus, does this matter weigh upon your heart?
1.740:
**Oedipus**
Do not ask me yet. Tell me rather what stature Laius had, and how ripe his manhood was.
1.742:
**Iocasta**
He was tall—the silver just lightly strewn among his hair—and his form was not greatly unlike your own.
1.744:
**Oedipus**
Unhappy that I am! I think that I have
1.745: laid myself under a terrible curse without realizing it.
1.746:
**Iocasta**
How do you mean? I tremble when I look at you, my lord.
1.747:
**Oedipus**
I have dread fears that the seer can see. But you will reveal the matter better if you tell me one thing more.
1.749:
**Iocasta**
Indeed, though I tremble, I will hear and answer all that you ask.
1.750:
**Oedipus**
Did he go with a small force, or like a chieftain, with many armed followers?
1.753:
**Iocasta**
Five they were in all—a herald among them—and there was one carriage which bore Laius.
1.755:
**Oedipus**
Alas! It is all clear now! Who gave you this information, lady?
1.756:
**Iocasta**
A servant, the only survivor who returned home.
1.757:
**Oedipus**
Is he by any chance in the house now?
1.758:
**Iocasta**
No. Soon after he returned and found you ruling in Laius’ stead,
1.760: he pled with me, with hand laid on mine, to send him to the fields, to the pastures of the flocks, that he might be far from the sight of this town. And I sent him; he was worthy, for a slave, to win even a larger favor than that.
1.765:
**Oedipus**
Would, then, that he return to us without delay!
1.766:
**Iocasta**
That is easy. But why do you enjoin this?
1.767:
**Oedipus**
I fear, lady, that my words have been rash, and therefore I wish to see him.
1.769:
**Iocasta**
He will come. But I think that
1.770: I too have a claim to learn what lies heavy on your heart, my king.
1.771:
**Oedipus**
It will not be kept from you, now that my forebodings have advanced so far. To whom more than to you would I speak in suffering such a fortune as this? My father was Polybus of Corinth,
1.775: my mother the Dorian Merope. I was considered the greatest of the folk in that town, until a chance event befell me, worthy, indeed, of wonder, though not of my overreaction regarding it. At a banquet, a man drunk with wine
1.780: cast it at me that I was not the true son of my father. And I, vexed, restrained myself for that day as best as I could, but on the next went to my mother and father and questioned them. They were angry at the one who had let this taunt fly.
1.785: So I had comfort about them, but the matter rankled in my heart, for such a rumor still spread widely. I went to Delphi without my parents’ knowledge, and Phoebus sent me forth disappointed of the knowledge for which I had come,
1.790: but in his response set forth other things, full of sorrow and terror and woe: that I was fated to defile my mother’s bed, that I would reveal to men a brood which they could not endure to behold, and that I would slay the father that sired me. When I heard this, I turned in flight from the land of Corinth,
1.795: from then on thinking of it only by its position under the stars, to some spot where I should never see fulfillment of the infamies foretold in my evil fate. And on my way I came to the land in which you say that this prince perished.
1.800: Now, lady, I will tell you the truth. When on my journey I was near those three roads, there I met a herald, and a man in a carriage drawn by colts, as you have described. The leader and the old man
1.805: himself tried to thrust me rudely from the path. Then, in anger, I struck the one pushing me aside, the driver, and the old man, when he saw this, watched for the moment I was passing, and from his carriage, brought his double goad straight down on my head.
1.810: Yet he was paid back with interest: with one swift blow from the staff in this hand he rolled right out of the carriage onto his back. I slew every one of them. But if this stranger had any tie of kinship to Laius,
1.815: who is now more wretched than this man before you? What mortal could be proved more hateful to the gods? No stranger, no citizen, is allowed to receive him at home, it is unlawful for anyone to accost him, and all must push him from their homes. And this—this curse—
1.820: was laid on me by no other mouth than my own. And I pollute the bed of the slain man with the hands by which he perished. Am I now vile? Oh, am I not utterly unclean, seeing that I must be banished, and in banishment neither see my own people,
1.825: nor set foot in my own land, or else be joined in wedlock to my mother, and slay my father Polybus, who sired and reared me? Then would he who judged these things to be sent down by some cruel divinity not be right about Oedipus?
1.830: Prevent, prevent, you pure and awful gods, me from ever seeing that day! No, may I be swept away from all men, before I see myself visited with that brand of doom.
1.834:
**Chorus**
To us, king, these things are fraught with fear. Yet have hope, until at least you have gained full knowledge
1.835: from the one who saw the deed.
1.836:
**Oedipus**
I have, in truth, this much hope alone: I await the man summoned from the pastures.
1.838:
**Iocasta**
And what do you want from him when he appears?
1.839:
**Oedipus**
I will tell you. If his story is found
1.840: to match withwith yours, I at least, will stand clear of disaster.
1.841:
**Iocasta**
And what special note did you hear from me?
1.842:
**Oedipus**
You said that he spoke of Laius as slain by robbers. If, then, he still speaks of several as before, I was not the slayer:
1.845: a solitary man could not be considered the same as that band. But if he names one lonely wayfarer, then beyond doubt this guilt rests upon me.
1.848:
**Iocasta**
Be assured that thus, at least, the tale was first told. He cannot revoke that,
1.850: for the city heard it, not I alone. But even if he should diverge somewhat from his former story, never, king, can he show that the murder of Laius, at least, is truly square with the prophecy, for Loxias plainly said that he was to die at the hand of my child.
1.855: How was it then that that poor innocent never slew him, but perished first? From now on then, as far as divination goes, I would not look to my right hand or my left.
1.859:
**Oedipus**
You are right. But nevertheless send someone to fetch the peasant,
1.860: and do not neglect this matter.
1.861:
**Iocasta**
I will send for him without delay. But let us go into the house: I will do nothing which does not please you.
*Exeunt Oedipus and Iocasta.*
1.863:
**Chorus**
May destiny still find me winning the praise of reverent purity in all words and
1.865: deeds sanctioned by those laws of sublime range, called into life through the high clear aether, whose father is Olympus alone. Their parent was no race of mortal men,
1.870: no, nor shall oblivion ever lay them to sleep: the god is mighty in them, and he does not grow old.
1.873:
**Chorus**
Insolence breeds the tyrant. Insolence, once vainly stuffed with wealth
1.875: that is not proper or good for it, when it has scaled the topmost ramparts, is hurled to a dire doom, where one’s feet cannot serve to good advantage. But I pray that the god never
1.880: quell such rivalry as benefits the state. I will always hold the god as our protector.
1.884:
**Chorus**
But if any man walks haughtily in deed or word,
1.885: with no fear of Justice, no reverence for the images of gods, may an evil doom seize him for his ill-starred pride, if he does not gain his advantage fairly,
1.890: or avoid unholy deeds, but seeks to lay profaning hands on sanctities. Where such things occur, what mortal shall boast any more that he can ward off the arrow of the gods from his life?
1.895: No. For if such deeds are held in honor, why should we join in the sacred dance?
1.897:
**Chorus**
No longer will I go reverently to the earth’s central and inviolate shrine, no more to Abae’s temple or to Olympia,
1.900: if these oracles do not fit the outcome, so that all mortals shall point at them with their fingers.
1.905: No, King—if this you are rightly called—Zeus all ruling, may it not escape you and your deathless power! The old prophecies concerning Laius are fading; already men give them no value, and nowhere is Apollo glorified with honors;
1.910: the worship of the gods is perishing.
1.911:
**Iocasta**
Princes of the land, I am planning to visit the shrines of the gods, with this wreathed branch and these gifts of incense in my hands. For Oedipus excites his soul excessively with all sorts of grief,
1.915: as he does not judge the new things from the old, like a man of sense, but is under the control of the speaker, if he speaks of frightful things. Since, then, I can do no good by counsel, to you, Lycean Apollo—for you are nearest—
1.920:
I have come as a suppliant with these symbols of prayer, that you may find us some escape from uncleanliness. For now we are all afraid, like those who see fear in the helmsman of their ship.
*Enter a messenger.*
1.924:
**Messenger**
Can you tell me, strangers, where
1.925: the house of King Oedipus is? Or better still, tell me where he himself is, if you know.
1.927:
**Chorus**
This is his dwelling, and he himself, stranger, is within. This lady here is the mother of his children.
1.929:
**Messenger**
Then may she be ever happy in a happy home,
1.930: since she is his blessed queen.
1.931:
**Iocasta**
Happiness to you also, stranger! Your fair greeting deserves this. But say what you have come to seek or to tell.
1.934:
**Messenger**
Good tidings, lady, for your house and your husband.
1.935:
**Iocasta**
What are they? From whom have you come?
1.936:
**Messenger**
From Corinth, and at the message I will give now you will doubtless rejoice, though you may perhaps grieve too.
1.938:
**Iocasta**
What is it? Why has it this double potency?
1.939:
**Messenger**
The people will make him king of the
1.940: Isthmian land, as it was said there.
1.941:
**Iocasta**
How then? Is the aged Polybus no longer in power?
1.942:
**Messenger**
No. For death holds him in the tomb.
1.943:
**Iocasta**
What do you mean? Is Polybus dead, old man?
1.944:
**Messenger**
If I do not speak the truth, I am content to die.
1.945:
**Iocasta**
Handmaid, away with all speed, and tell this to your master! Oracles of the gods, where do you stand now? It is this man that Oedipus long feared he would slay. And now this man has died in the course of destiny, not by his hand.
*Enter Oedipus.*
1.950:
**Oedipus**
Iocasta, dearest wife, why have you summoned me forth from these doors?
1.952:
**Iocasta**
Hear this man, and judge, as you listen, what the awful oracles have come to.
1.954:
**Oedipus**
Who is he and what news does he have for me?
1.955:
**Iocasta**
He comes from Corinth to tell you that your father Polybus lives no longer, but has perished.
1.957:
**Oedipus**
How, stranger? Let me have it from your own mouth.
1.958:
**Messenger**
If I must first make these tidings plain, know indeed that he is dead and gone.
1.961:
**Messenger**
A light tilt of the scale brings the aged to their rest.
1.962:
**Oedipus**
Ah, he died, it seems, of sickness?
1.963:
**Messenger**
Yes, and of the long years that he had lived.
1.964:
**Oedipus**
Alas, alas! Why indeed, my wife, should one look to the
1.965: hearth of the Pythian seer, or to the birds that scream above our heads, who declared that I was doomed to slay my father? But he is dead, and lies beneath the earth, and here I am, not having put my hand to any spear—unless, perhaps, he died out of longing for me:
1.970: thus, indeed, I would be the cause of his death. But as the oracles stand, at least, Polybus has swept them with him to his rest in Hades. They are worth nothing.
1.973:
**Iocasta**
Did I not long ago foretell this to you?
1.974:
**Oedipus**
You did, but I was mislead by my fear.
1.975:
**Iocasta**
Now no longer take any of those things to heart.
1.976:
**Oedipus**
But surely I must fear my mother’s bed.
1.977:
**Iocasta**
What should a mortal man fear, for whom the decrees of Fortune are supreme, and who has clear foresight of nothing? It is best to live at random, as one may.
1.980: But fear not that you will wed your mother. Many men before now have slept with their mothers in dreams. But he to whom these things are as though nothing bears his life most easily.
1.984:
**Oedipus**
All these words of yours would have been well said,
1.985: were my mother not alive. But as it is, since she lives, I must necessarily fear, though you do speak well.
1.987:
**Iocasta**
Your father’s death is a great sign for us to take cheer.
1.988:
**Oedipus**
Great, I know. But my fear is of her who lives.
1.989:
**Messenger**
And who is the woman about whom you fear?
1.990:
**Oedipus**
Merope, old man, the consort of Polybus.
1.991:
**Messenger**
And what is it in her that moves your fear?
1.992:
**Oedipus**
A divine oracle of dread import, stranger.
1.993:
**Messenger**
Proper, or improper, for another to know?
1.994:
**Oedipus**
Proper, surely. Loxias once said that I was
1.995: doomed to marry my own mother, and to shed with my own hands my father’s blood. For which reasons I long shirked my home in Corinth—with a happy outcome, to be sure, but still it is sweet to see the face of one’s parents.
1.999:
**Messenger**
Was it really for fear of this that you became an exile from that city?
1.1000:
**Oedipus**
And because I did not wish, old man, to be the murderer of my father.
1.1001:
**Messenger**
Why have I not relieved you of this second fear, my lord, since I came to give you pleasure?
1.1002:
**Oedipus**
And indeed you will have worthy thanks from me.
1.1004:
**Messenger**
And indeed I came specially for this, that
1.1005: I might profit from your returning home.
1.1007:
**Oedipus**
But by no means will I ever go near my parents again.
1.1008:
**Messenger**
My son, it is crystal clear that you do not know what you are doing.
1.1009:
**Oedipus**
How so, old man? In the name of the gods, tell me.
1.1010:
**Messenger**
If on account of this you are fleeing from returning home.
1.1011:
**Oedipus**
Fearing indeed lest Apollo’s prophecy come true in me.
1.1012:
**Messenger**
Lest you acquire some pollution from your parents?
1.1013:
**Oedipus**
This very thing, old man, this constantly frightens me.
1.1014:
**Messenger**
Do you know, then, that your fears are wholly in vain?
1.1015:
**Oedipus**
How so, if I was born of those parents?
1.1016:
**Messenger**
Because you had no blood in common with Polybus.
1.1017:
**Oedipus**
What are you saying? Was Polybus not my father?
1.1018:
**Messenger**
Just as much, and no more, than he who speaks to you.
1.1019:
**Oedipus**
And how can my father be equal to him who is as though nothing to me?
1.1020:
**Messenger**
But he did not father you, any more than I did.
1.1021:
**Oedipus**
How, then, did he call me his son?
1.1022:
**Messenger**
Long ago he received you as a gift from my hands.
1.1023:
**Oedipus**
And yet he loved me so dearly, who came from another’s hand?
1.1024:
**Messenger**
His former childlessness won him over.
1.1025:
**Oedipus**
And had you bought me or found me by chance, when you gave me to him?
1.1026:
**Messenger**
I found you in Cithaeron’s winding glens.
1.1027:
**Oedipus**
And why were you roaming those regions?
1.1028:
**Messenger**
