I was in charge of mountain flocks.
1.1029:
**Oedipus**
What, you were a shepherd—a vagrant hireling?
1.1030:
**Messenger**
But your savior, my son, in that hour.
1.1031:
**Oedipus**
And what was my pain when you took me in your arms?
1.1032:
**Messenger**
The ankles of your feet might bear witness.
1.1033:
**Oedipus**
Ah me, why do you speak of that old trouble?
1.1034:
**Messenger**
I freed you when you had your ankles pinned together.
1.1035:
**Oedipus**
It was a dread brand of shame that I took from my cradle.
1.1036:
**Messenger**
So much so that from that fortune you were called by that name which you still bear.
1.1037:
**Oedipus**
Oh, in the name of the gods, was the deed my mother’s or father’s? Speak!
1.1038:
**Messenger**
I know not. He who gave you to me knows better of that than I.
1.1039:
**Oedipus**
What, you got me from another? You did not find me yourself?
1.1040:
**Messenger**
No. Another shepherd gave you to me.
1.1041:
**Oedipus**
Who was he? Can you tell clearly?
1.1042:
**Messenger**
I think he was said to be one of the household of Laius.
1.1043:
**Oedipus**
The king who ruled this country long ago?
1.1044:
**Messenger**
The same. The man was a herdsman in his service.
1.1045:
**Oedipus**
Is he still alive, that I might see him?
1.1046:
**Messenger**
You natives of this country should know best.
1.1047:
**Oedipus**
Is there any of you here present that knows the herdsman of whom he speaks, having seen him either in the pastures or here in town? Answer!
1.1050: The hour has come for these things to be revealed finally.
1.1051:
**Chorus**
I think he speaks of no other than the peasant you already wanted to see. But our lady Iocasta might best tell you that.
1.1054:
**Oedipus**
Lady, do you know the one whom we summoned just now?
1.1055: Is it of him that this man speaks?
1.1056:
**Iocasta**
Why ask of whom he spoke? Regard it not; waste not a thought on what he said; it would be vain.
1.1058:
**Oedipus**
It must not happen that, with such clues in my grasp, I fail to bring my birth to light.
1.1060:
**Iocasta**
For the gods’ sake, if you have any care for your own life, do not continue this search! My anguish is enough.
1.1062:
**Oedipus**
Be of good courage. Even if I should be found the son of a servile mother—a slave by three descents—you will not be proven baseborn.
1.1064:
**Iocasta**
Hear me, I implore you: do not do this.
1.1065:
**Oedipus**
I will not hear of not discovering the whole truth.
1.1066:
**Iocasta**
Yet I wish you well—I counsel you for the best.
1.1067:
**Oedipus**
These best counsels, then, vex my patience.
1.1068:
**Iocasta**
Oh ill-fated man, may you never know who you are!
1.1069:
**Oedipus**
Go, some one, fetch me the herdsman.
1.1070: Leave this woman to glory in her princely stock.
1.1071:
**Iocasta**
Alas, alas, miserable man—that word alone can I say to you—and no other word ever again.
*She rushes into the palace.*
1.1073:
**Chorus**
Why has this woman gone, Oedipus, rushing off in wild grief? I fear
1.1075: a storm of sorrow will soon break forth from this silence.
1.1076:
**Oedipus**
Break forth what will! Be my race ever so lowly, I crave to learn it. That woman perhaps—for she is proud with more than a woman’s pride—feels ashamed of my lowly origin. But I, who hold myself son of Fortune
1.1080: that gives good, will not be dishonored. She is the mother from whom I spring, and the months, my kinsmen, have marked me sometimes lowly, sometimes great. Such being my heritage, never more can I prove
1.1085: false to it, or keep from searching out the secret of my birth.
1.1086:
**Chorus**
If I am a seer or wise of heart,
1.1090: Cithaeron, you will not fail—by heaven, you will not—to know at tomorrow’s full moon that Oedipus honors you as native to him, as his nurse, and his mother, and that you are celebrated in our dance and song,
1.1095: because you are well-pleasing to our prince. O Phoebus to whom we cry, may these things find favor in your sight!
1.1098:
**Chorus**
Who was it, my son, who of the race whose years are many, that bore you in wedlock with
1.1100: Pan, the mountain-roaming father? Or was it a bride of Loxias that bore you? For dear to him are all the upland pastures.
1.1105: Or perhaps it was Cyllene’s lord, or the Bacchants’ god, dweller on the hill-tops, that received you, a new-born joy, from one of the nymphs of Helicon, with whom he most often sports.
1.1110:
**Oedipus**
Elders, if it is right for me, who have never met the man, to guess, I think I see the herdsman we have been looking for for a lone time. In his venerable old age he tallies with this stranger’s years, and moreover I recognize those who bring him, I think, as servants of mine.
1.1115: But perhaps you have an advantage in knowledge over me, if you have seen the herdsman before.
1.1117:
**Chorus**
Yes, I know him, be sure. He was in the service of Laius—trusty as any shepherd.
*The herdsman is brought in.*
1.1119:
**Oedipus**
I ask you first, Corinthian stranger, if this is the man you mean.
1.1120:
**Messenger**
He is, the one you are looking at.
1.1121:
**Oedipus**
You, old man—look this way and answer all that I ask—were you once in the service of Laius?
1.1123:
**Servant**
I was—not a bought slave, but reared in his house.
1.1124:
**Oedipus**
Employed in what labor, or what way of life?
1.1125:
**Servant**
For the better part of my life I tended the flocks.
1.1126:
**Oedipus**
And what regions did you most frequently haunt?
1.1127:
**Servant**
Sometimes Cithaeron, sometimes the neighboring ground.
1.1128:
**Oedipus**
Are you aware of ever having seen this man in these parts?
1.1129:
**Servant**
Doing what? What man do you mean?
1.1130:
**Oedipus**
This man here. Have you ever met him before?
1.1131:
**Servant**
Not so that I could speak at once from memory.
1.1132:
**Messenger**
And no wonder, master. But I will bring clear recollection to his ignorance. I am sure he knows well of the time we dwelled in the region of Cithaeron
1.1135: for six month periods, from spring to Arcturus, he with two flocks, and I, his comrade, with one. And then for the winter I used to drive my flock to my own fold, and he took his to the fold of Laius.
1.1140: Did any of this happen as I tell it, or did it not?
1.1141:
**Servant**
You speak the truth, though it was long ago.
1.1142:
**Messenger**
Come, tell me now: do you remember having given me a boy in those days, to be reared as my own foster-son?
1.1144:
**Servant**
What now? Why do you ask the question?
1.1145:
**Messenger**
This man, my friend, is he who then was young.
1.1146:
**Servant**
Damn you! Be silent once and for all!
1.1147:
**Oedipus**
Do not rebuke him, old man. Your words need rebuking more than his.
1.1148:
**Servant**
And in what way, most noble master, do I offend?
1.1150:
**Oedipus**
In not telling of the boy about whom he asks.
1.1151:
**Servant**
He speaks without knowledge, but is busy to no purpose.
1.1152:
**Oedipus**
You will not speak with good grace, but will in pain.
1.1153:
**Servant**
No, in the name of the gods, do not mistreat an old man.
1.1154:
**Oedipus**
Someone, quick—tie his hands him this instant!
1.1155:
**Servant**
Alas, why? What do you want to learn?
1.1156:
**Oedipus**
Did you give this man the child about whom he asks?
1.1157:
**Servant**
I did. Would that I had perished that day!
1.1158:
**Oedipus**
Well, you will come to that, unless you tell the honest truth.
1.1159:
**Servant**
But if I speak I will be destroyed all the more.
1.1160:
**Oedipus**
This man is bent, I think, on more delays.
1.1161:
**Servant**
No, no! I said before that I gave it to him.
1.1162:
**Oedipus**
Where did you get it from? From your own house, or from another?
1.1163:
**Servant**
It was not my own: I received it from another.
1.1164:
**Oedipus**
From whom of the citizens here? From what home?
1.1165:
**Servant**
For the love of the gods, master, ask no more!
1.1166:
**Oedipus**
You are dead if I have to question you again.
1.1167:
**Servant**
It was a child, then, of the house of Laius.
1.1168:
**Oedipus**
A slave? Or one of his own clan?
1.1169:
**Servant**
Alas! I am on the brink of speaking the dreaded words.
1.1170:
**Oedipus**
And I of hearing: I must hear nevertheless.
1.1171:
**Servant**
You must know then, that it was said to be his own child. But your lady within could say best how these matters lie.
1.1173:
**Oedipus**
How? Did she give it to you?
**Servant**
Yes, my lord.
1.1174:
**Oedipus**
For what purpose?
**Servant**
That I should do away with it.
1.1175:
**Oedipus**
Her own child, the wretched woman?
**Servant**
Yes, from fear of the evil prophecies.
1.1176:
**Oedipus**
What were they?
**Servant**
The tale ran that he would slay his father.
1.1177:
**Oedipus**
Why, then, did you give him to this old man?
1.1178:
**Servant**
Out of pity, master, thinking that he would carry him to another land, from where he himself came. But he saved him for the direst woe.
1.1180: For if you are what this man says, be certain that you were born ill-fated.
1.1182:
**Oedipus**
Oh, oh! All brought to pass, all true. Light, may I now look on you for the last time—I who have been found to be accursed in birth,
1.1185:
accursed in wedlock, accursed in the shedding of blood.
*He rushes into the palace.*
1.1186:
**Chorus**
Alas, generations of mortals, how mere a shadow I count your life! Where, where is the mortal who
1.1190: attains a happiness which is more than apparent and doomed to fall away to nothing? Your fate warns me—yours, unhappy Oedipus—to call no
1.1196:
**Chorus**
For he, O Zeus, shot his shaft with peerless skill, and won the prize of an all-prosperous fortune, having slain the maiden with crooked talons, who sang darkly.
1.1200: He arose for our land like a tower against death. And from that time, Oedipus, you have been called our king, and have been honored supremely, holding power in great Thebes.
1.1204:
**Chorus**
But now whose story is more grievous in men’s ears?
1.1205: Who is a more wretched slave to fierce plagues and troubles, with all his life reversed? Alas, renowned Oedipus! The same bounteous harbor was sufficient for you, both as child and as father, to make your nuptial couch in. Oh, how can the soil
1.1210: in which your father sowed, unhappy man, have endured you in silence for so long?
1.1212:
**Chorus**
Time the all-seeing has found you out, against your will: he judges the monstrous marriage in which
1.1215: parent and child have long been one. Alas, child of Laius, would that I had never seen you. I wail as one who pours a dirge from his lips.
1.1220:
It was you who gave me new life, to speak directly, and through you darkness has fallen upon my eyes.
*A second messenger enters from the house.*
1.1223:
**Second Messenger**
You who are most honored in this land, what deeds you will hear, what deeds you will behold, what burden of sorrow will be yours,
1.1225: if, true to your race, you still care for the house of Labdacus. For I think that neither the Ister nor the Phasis could wash this house clean, so many are the ills that it shrouds, or will soon bring to light, ills wrought not unwittingly, but on purpose.
1.1230: And those griefs smart the most which are seen to be of our own choice.
1.1232:
**Chorus**
Indeed the troubles which we knew before are far from being easy to bear. Besides them, what do you have to announce?
1.1234:
**Second Messenger**
This is the shortest tale to tell and hear:
1.1235: our royal lady Iocasta is dead.
1.1236:
**Chorus**
Alas, wretched lady! From what cause?
1.1237:
**Second Messenger**
By her own hand. You will not suffer the worst part of the painful event, since you do not behold the events. Nevertheless, so far as my memory serves,
1.1240: you will learn that unhappy woman’s fate. When, frantic, she passed within the vestibule, she rushed straight towards her marriage couch, clutching her hair with the fingers of both hands. Once within the chamber,
1.1245: she dashed the doors together behind her, then called on the name of Laius, long since a corpse, thinking of that son, born long ago, by whose hand the father was slain, leaving the mother to breed accursed offspring with his own child. And she bewailed the marriage in which, wretched woman, she had given birth to a twofold brood,
1.1250: husband by husband, children by her child. And how she perished is more than I know. For with a shriek Oedipus burst in, and did not allow us to watch her woe until the end: on him, as he rushed around, our eyes were set.
1.1255: To and fro he went, asking us to give him a sword, asking where he could find the wife who was no wife, but a mother whose womb had borne both him and his children. And in his frenzy a power greater than mortal man was his guide, for it was none of us mortals who were near.
1.1260: With a dread cry, as though someone beckoned him on, he sprang at the double doors, forced the bending bolts from the sockets, and rushed into the room. There we beheld the woman hanging by the neck in a twisted noose of swinging cords.
1.1265: And when he saw her, with a dread deep cry he released the halter by which she hung. And when the hapless woman was stretched out on the ground, then the sequel was horrible to see: for he tore from her raiment the golden brooches with which she had decorated herself,
1.1270: and lifting them struck his own eye-balls, uttering words like these: No longer will you behold such horrors as I was suffering and performing! Long enough have you looked on those whom you ought never to have seen, having failed in the knowledge of those whom I yearned to know—henceforth you shall be dark!
1.1275: With such a dire refrain, he struck his eyes with raised hand not once but often. At each blow the bloody eye-balls bedewed his beard, and sent forth not sluggish drops of gore, but all at once a dark shower of blood came down like hail.
1.1280: From the deeds of the two of them such ills have broken forth, not on one alone, but with mingled woe for man and wife. The old happiness of their ancestral fortune was once happiness indeed. But now today lamentation, ruin, death, shame,
1.1285: and every earthly ill that anyone could name are all theirs.
1.1286:
**Chorus**
And does the sufferer have any respite from pain now?
1.1287:
**Second Messenger**
He cries for some one to unbar the gates and show to all the Cadmeans his father’s slayer, his mother’s—the words must not pass my lips—
1.1290: in order to banish himself from the land and not to put the house under his own curse by waiting here. And yet he lacks strength, and one to guide his steps, for the anguish is more than he can bear. He will soon show this to you: look, the bars of the gates are withdrawn,
1.1295: and soon you will behold a sight which even he who abhors it must pity.
1.1297:
**Chorus**
O dread fate for men to see, O most dreadful of all that I have set my eyes on! Unhappy one, what madness has come upon you?
1.1300: Who is the unearthly foe who, with a leap of more than mortal range has made your ill-starred life his prey? Alas, alas, you hapless man! I cannot even look on you, though there is much I desire to ask, much I desire to learn,
1.1305: much that draws my wistful gaze: with such a shuddering do you fill me!
1.1308:
**Oedipus**
Woe is me! Alas, alas, wretched that I am! Where, where am I carried in my misery?
1.1310: How is my voice swept abroad on the wings of the air? Oh, my fate, how far you have sprung!
1.1312:
**Chorus**
To a dread place, dire in men’s ears, dire in their sight.
1.1313:
**Oedipus**
Oh horror of darkness that enfolds me, unspeakable visitant,
1.1315: resistless, sped by a wind too favorable! Oh, me! and once again, Oh, me! How my soul is pierced by the stab of these goads and by the memory of sorrows!
1.1319:
**Chorus**
No wonder that amidst these woes
1.1320: you mourn and bear a double pain.
1.1321:
**Oedipus**
Ah, friend, you still are steadfast in your care for me, and still have patience to tend to the blind man! Ah, me!
1.1325: Your presence is not hidden from me—no, blind though I am, nevertheless I know your voice full well.
1.1327:
**Chorus**
Man of dread deeds, how could you quench your vision in this way? What divinity urged you on?
1.1329:
**Oedipus**
It was Apollo, friends, Apollo who brought these troubles
1.1330: to pass, these terrible, terrible troubles. But the hand that struck my eyes was none other than my own, wretched that I am!
1.1335: Why should I see, when sight showed me nothing sweet?
1.1336:
**Chorus**
These things were just as you say.
1.1337:
**Oedipus**
What, my friends, can I behold anymore, what can I love, what greeting can touch my ear with joy? Hurry, friends,
1.1340: lead me from the land, lead me from here, the utterly lost,
1.1345: the thrice-accursed, the mortal most hateful to the gods!
1.1347:
**Chorus**
Wretched alike for your fortune and for your understanding of it, would that I had never known you!
1.1349:
**Oedipus**
Perish the man, whoever he was, who freed me in the past years from the cruel shackle on my feet—a thankless deed! Had I died then,
1.1355: I would not have been so sore a grief to my friends and to my own soul.
1.1356:
**Chorus**
I too would have had it thus.
1.1357:
**Oedipus**
In this way I would not have come to shed my father’s blood, or been known among men as the husband of the woman from whom I was born.
1.1360: Now I am forsaken by the gods, son of a defiled mother, successor to the bed of the man who gave me my own wretched being:
1.1365: if there is a woe surpassing all woes, it has become Oedipus’ lot.
1.1367:
**Chorus**
I cannot agree that you have counseled well: you would have been better dead than living and blind.
1.1369:
**Oedipus**
Do not tell me that things have not been best done in this way:
1.1370: give me counsel no more. If I had sight, I know not with what eyes I could even have looked on my father, when I came to the house of Hades, or on my miserable mother, since against both I have sinned such sins as hanging myself could not punish.
1.1375: But do you think that the sight of children, born as mine were, was lovely for me to look upon? No, no, never lovely to my eyes! No, neither was this town with its towering walls, nor the sacred statues of the gods, since I, thrice wretched that I am—
1.1380: I, noblest of the sons of Thebes—have doomed myself to know them no more by commanding that all should reject the impious one, the one whom the gods have revealed as unholy, a member of Laius’ own race! After bearing such a stain upon myself,
1.1385: was I to look with steady eyes on this folk? No indeed: were there a way to choke the source of hearing, I would not have hesitated to make a fast prison of this wretched frame, so that I should have known neither sight nor sound.
1.1390: It is sweet for our thought to dwell beyond the sphere of grief. Alas, Cithaeron, why did you provide a shelter for me? When I was given to you, why did you not slay me straightway, that I might never reveal my origin to men. Ah, Polybus, ah, Corinth, and you that were called the ancient house of my father,
1.1395: how fair-seeming was I, your nurseling, and what evils were festering underneath! Now I am found to be evil and of evil birth. Oh you three roads, and you secret glen, you, thicket, and narrow way where three paths met—
1.1400: you who drank my father’s blood from my own hands—do you remember, perhaps, what deeds I have performed in your sight, and then what fresh deeds I went on to do when I came here? Oh marriage rites, you gave me birth, and when you had brought me forth,
1.1405: you again bore children to your child, you created an incestuous kinship of fathers, brothers, sons, brides, wives, and mothers—all the foulest deeds that are wrought among men! But it is improper to mention what it is improper to do—
1.1410: hurry, for the love of the gods, hide me somewhere beyond the land, or slay me, or cast me into the sea, where you will never behold me any longer! Approach—deign to lay your hands on a wretched man—listen and fear not: my plague can rest
1.1416:
**Chorus**
But here is Creon in good time to plan and perform that which you request. He alone is left to guard the land in your place.
1.1419:
**Oedipus**
Ah, me, how will I address him?
1.1420:
What claim to credence can be shown on my part? For in the past I proved to be wholly false to him.
*Enter Creon.*
1.1422:
**Creon**
I have not come to mock or reproach you with any any past fault.
*To the Attendants.*
1.1424: But you, if you no longer respect the children of men,
1.1425: revere at least the all-nurturing flame of our lord the Sun, and don’t show so openly such a pollution as this, one which neither earth, nor holy rain, nor the light itself can welcome. Take him into the house as quickly as you can: it best accords with pity that
1.1430: kinfolk alone should see and hear a kinsman’s woes.
1.1432:
**Oedipus**
For the gods’ love—since you have done a gentle violence to my prediction and come in a spirit so noble to me, a man most vile—grant me a favor: I will speak for your own good, not mine.
1.1435:
**Creon**
And what do you wish so eagerly to get from me?
1.1436:
**Oedipus**
Cast me out of this land with all speed, to a place where no mortal shall be found to greet me.
1.1438:
**Creon**
This I could have done, to be sure, except I craved first to learn from the god all my duty.
1.1440:
**Oedipus**
But his pronouncement has been set forth in full—to let me perish, the parricide, unholy one that I am.
1.1442:
**Creon**
Thus it was said. But since we have come to such a pass, it is better to learn clearly what should be done.
1.1444:
**Oedipus**
Will you, then, seek a response on behalf of such a wretch as I?
1.1445:
**Creon**
Yes, for even you yourself will now surely put faith in the god.
1.1446:
**Oedipus**
Yes. And on you I lay this charge, to you I make this entreaty: give to the woman within such burial as you wish—you will properly render the last rites to your own. But never let this city of my father be condemned
1.1450: to have me dwelling within, as long as I live. No, allow me to live in the hills, where Cithaeron, famed as mine, sits, which my mother and father, while they lived, fixed as my appointed tomb, so that I may die according to the decree of those who sought to slay me.
1.1455: And yet I know this much, that neither sickness nor anything else can destroy me; for I would never have been snatched from death, except in order to suffer some strange doom. But let my fate go where it will. Regarding my children, Creon, I beg you to take no care of my sons:
1.1460: they are men, so that they will never lack the means to live wherever they should be. My two girls, poor hapless ones—who never knew my table spread separately, or lacked their father’s presence, but always had a share of all that
1.1465: reached my hands—I implore you to take care of them. And, if you can, allow me to touch them with my hands, and to indulge my grief. Grant it, prince, grant it, noble heart. Ah, if I could but once touch them with my hands, I would think that I had them
1.1470:
just as when I had sight.
*Creon’s Attendants lead in the children, Antigone and Ismene.*
1.1471: What is this? Oh, gods, can it be my loved ones that I hear sobbing, can Creon have taken pity on me and sent my children, my darlings?
1.1476:
**Creon**
You are. I have brought this about, for I knew the joy which you have long had from them—the joy you now have.
1.1478:
**Oedipus**
Bless you, and for this errand may the god prove a kinder guardian to you than he has to me.
1.1480: My children, where are you? Come, here, here to the hands of the one whose mother was your own, the hands that have made your father’s once bright eyes to be such orbs as these—his, who seeing nothing, knowing nothing,
1.1485: became your father by her from whom he was born! For you also do I weep, though I cannot see you, when I think of the bitter life that men will make you live in days to come. To what company of the citizens will you go, to what festival,
1.1490: from which you will not return home in tears, not sharing in the holiday? But when you reach a ripe age for marriage, who shall he be, who shall be the man, my daughters, to risk taking upon himself the reproaches
1.1495: that will certainly be baneful to my offspring and yours? What misery is lacking? Your father killed his own father, and bore you from the source of his own being!
1.1500: Such are the taunts that will be cast at you. And who then will wed you? The man does not live, no, it cannot be, my children, but you will wither in barren maidenhood. Son of Menoeceus, hear me: since you are the only father left to them—we, their parents, are both gone—
1.1505: do not allow them to wander poor and unwed, for they are your own kin, nor abase them to the level of my woes. Pity them, seeing them deprived of everything but you at such an age.
1.1510: Promise, noble man, and touch them with your hand. To you, children, I would have given much counsel, if your minds were mature. But now pray that you may live where occasion allows, and that the life which is your lot may be happier than your father’s.
1.1515:
**Creon**
Your grief has had a sufficient scope: move on into the house.
1.1516:
**Oedipus**
I must obey, though I do it in no way gladly.
**Creon**
Yes, for it is in season that all things are good.
1.1517:
**Oedipus**
Do you know on what terms I will go?
**Creon**
You will tell me, and then I will know when I have heard them.
1.1518:
**Oedipus**
See that you send me to dwell outside this land.
**Creon**
You ask for what the god must give.
1.1519:
**Oedipus**
But to the gods I have become most hateful.
**Creon**
Then you will quickly get your wish.
1.1520:
**Oedipus**
So you consent?
**Creon**
It is not my way to say idly what I do not mean.
1.1521:
**Oedipus**
Then it is time to lead me away.
**Creon**
Come, then, but let your children go.
1.1522:
**Oedipus**
No, do not take them from me!
1.1523:
**Creon**
Do not wish to be master in all things: the mastery which you did attain has not followed you through life.
1.1524:
**Chorus**
Residents of our native Thebes, behold, this is Oedipus,
1.1525: who knew the renowned riddle, and was a most mighty man. What citizen did not gaze on his fortune with envy? See into what a stormy sea of troubles he has come! Therefore, while our eyes wait to see the final destined day, we must call no mortal happy until
1.1530: he has crossed life’s border free from pain.

1.1:
**Paedagogus**
Son of him who once commanded our forces at Troy, son of Agamemnon!—now you may survey all that your heart has desired for so long. There is the ancient Argos of your yearning,
1.5: that consecrated land from which the gad-fly drove the daughter of Inachus; there, Orestes, is the Lycean market place, named from the wolf-slaying god; there on the left is Hera’s famous temple; and in this place to which we have come, know that you see Mycenae, the rich in gold,
1.10: and here the house of Pelops’ heirs, so often stained with bloodshed. Long ago from here, away from the murder of your father, I carried you for her whose blood is yours, your sister, and saved you and reared you up to manhood to be the avenger of your murdered father.
1.15: Now, therefore, Orestes, and you, best of allies, Pylades, our plan of action must be quickly laid; for look, already the sun’s bright ray is stirring the birds’ songs into clarity, and the kindly darkness of the stars is spent.
1.20: Before, then, anyone comes out from the house, we must make our plans, since we are at the point where it is no longer opportune to hesitate, but it is the moment for action.
1.23:
**Orestes**
True friend and follower, how well you prove your loyalty to our house!
1.25: Just as a thoroughbred mount, even if advanced in years, does not lose courage in danger, but pricks up his ears, so you speed us forward and follow in the first ranks. I will tell you, then, what I have determined.
1.30: Listen closely to my words and correct me, if I miss the mark in any way.When I went to the Pythian oracle to learn how I might avenge my father on his murderers,
1.35: Phoebus gave me the commandment which you will now hear: that alone, and by stealth, without the aid of arms or large numbers, I should carry off my right hand’s just slaughters. Accordingly, since I received this divine declaration, you must go into that house there
1.40: when opportunity gives you entrance, and learn all that is happening, so that you may report to us out of sure knowledge. Your age and the lapse of time will prevent them from recognizing you; they will never suspect who you are with that silvered hair. Let your story be that you are a Phocian stranger
1.45: sent by Phanoteus, since he is the greatest of their allies. Tell them, and affirm it with your oath, that Orestes has perished by a fatal chance, hurled at the Pythian games
1.50: from his speeding chariot. Let that be the substance of your message. Meanwhile, we will first crown my father’s tomb as the god ordered with libations and the luxuriant tribute of a severed lock; then we will return here, bearing in our hands an urn of hammered bronze
1.55: —now hidden, as you no doubt know, in the brushwood—so that we may gladden them with the false tidings that this body of mine exists no more, but has been consumed with fire and reduced to ashes. How does it hurt me, when by feigned death
1.60: I find true life and win renown? No word is ill-omened, I trust, if it yields gain. For often before now I have seen clever men die in false report; then, when they return home, they are held in greater honor.
1.65: And so for myself I trust that as a result of this rumor I, too, shall live, shining down like a star upon my enemies.But you, O my fatherland and native gods of my soil, receive me with good fortune in this journey, and you also, house of my ancestors,
1.70: since I come by divine mandate to cleanse you as justice demands. Do not dismiss me from this land in dishonor, but grant that I may rule over my possessions and restore my house!I have said enough. Go now, old one, and take care to watch over your task.
1.75:
The two of us will depart; for so opportunity bids, chief ruler of every enterprise for men.
*Within.*
1.78:
**Paedagogus**
Listen, my son; from the doors of the house, I think, came the sound of some serving girl moaning inside.
1.80:
**Orestes**
Can it be my joyless Electra? Shall we remain here and listen to her cries?
1.82:
**Paedagogus**
No, no; before all else, let us strive to obey the commands of Loxias and from them make a fair beginning by pouring libations to your father. For such actions bring
1.85:
victory within our grasp and give us mastery in all our doings.
*Exeunt Paedagogus on the spectators left, Orestes and Pylades on the right.*
*Enter Electra, from the house.*
1.86:
**Electra**
O you pure sunlight, and you air, light’s equal partner over earth, how often have you heard the chords of my laments
1.90: and the thudding blows against this bloodied breast at the time of gloomy night’s leaving off! My accursed bed in that house of suffering there knows well already how I observe my night-long rites—how often I bewail my miserable
1.95: father, whom bloody Ares did not welcome with deadly gifts in a foreign land, but my mother and her bedfellow Aegisthus split his head with murderous axe, just as woodmen chop an oak.
1.100: And for this crime no pitying cry bursts from any lips but mine, when you, Father, have died a death so cruel and so deserving of pity!
1.103: But never will I end from cries and bitter lamentation,
1.105: while I look on the stars’ glistening flashes or on this light of day. No, like the nightingale, slayer of her offspring, I will wail without ceasing, and cry aloud to all here at the doors of my father.
1.110: O House of Hades and Persephone! O Hermes of the shades! O potent Curse, and you fearsome daughters of the gods, the Erinyes, who take note when a life is unjustly taken, when a marriage-bed is thievishly dishonored,
1.115: come, help me, bring vengeance for the murder of my father and send me my brother. I no longer have the strength to hold up alone against
1.120: the load of grief that crushes me.
1.121:
**Chorus**
Ah, Electra, child of a most wretched mother, why are you always wasting away in this unsated mourning for Agamemnon, who long ago was godlessly
1.125: ensnared in your false mother’s wiles and betrayed by her corrupt hand? May the one who did that perish, if I may speak such a curse without breaking the gods’ laws.
1.130: you have come to relieve me in my troubles. I know and feel it: it does not escape me. Still I cannot leave this task undone, nor abandon this mourning for my poor father. Ah, friends whose love responds to mine in every mood,
1.135: allow me to rave as I am, oh, please, I beg you!
1.137:
**Chorus**
But never by weeping nor by prayer will you resurrect your father from the pool of Hades which receives all men.
1.140: No, by grieving without end and beyond due limits you will find cureless misery and your own ruin; in these actions there is no deliverance from evils. Tell us, why do you pursue such suffering?
1.145:
**Electra**
Foolish is the child who forgets a parent’s piteous death. No, closer to my heart is the mourner who eternally wails, Itys, Itys, that bird mad with grief, the messenger of Zeus.
1.150: Ah, all-suffering Niobe, you I count divine, since you weep forever in your rocky tomb!
1.154:
**Chorus**
Not to you alone of mortals, my daughter, has sorrow come,
1.155: though you face it with less restraint than those girls inside, Chrysothemis and Iphianassa, whose parents and blood you share. They still live, as he, too, lives, sorrowing in his secluded youth,
1.160: yet happy in that this famous realm of the Mycenaeans shall one day receive him as a noble lord, if with the blessing of Zeus’s escort he, Orestes, returns to this land.
1.164:
**Electra**
Yes, I await him with unwearied longing,
1.165: as I walk my sad path from day to day childless and unwed, bathed in tears, bearing that endless doom of evils. But he forgets all that he has suffered and learned.
1.170: What message comes to me that is not proven false? He constantly desires to be with us, but though he desires it, he does not choose to appear.
1.174:
**Chorus**
Courage, my daughter, courage; Zeus in the sky
1.175: is still mighty, and he sees and rules all. Leave your oversharp anger to him; be neither excessively hostile to those you hate, nor forgetful of them, since Time is a god who brings ease.
1.180: Neither the son of Agamemnon, who dwells by Crisa’s cattle-feeding shore nor the god who reigns beside Acheron is unmindful of you.
1.185:
**Electra**
But the best part of life has passed away leaving me in hopelessness, and I have no strength left. I waste away without children and have no loving husband to champion me, but like some despised foreign slave,
1.190: I serve in the halls of my father, wrapped in shabby garments and standing to eat scanty meals.
1.193:
**Chorus**
Mournful was the voice heard at his return, and mournful the voice amidst your father’s reclining banquet
1.195: when the straight, swift blow of the bronze-jawed axe was sped against him. Deceit was the plotter, Lust the slayer, two dread parents of a dreadful
1.200: phantom, whether it was god or mortal that did this deed.
1.201:
**Electra**
O that hated day, hated beyond all that have come to me; O that night, the terrible grief of that unutterable feast, the shameless death-strokes
1.205: my father saw from their twin hands, hands which took my life captive by treachery, which cast me to ruin! May the great god of Olympus
1.210: create for them sufferings in penalty, and may they never have enjoyment of their splendor since they have committed such crimes!
1.213:
**Chorus**
Be advised to say no more; do you not see by what actions
1.215: under the present circumstances you plunge so shamefully into self-made miseries? You have far excelled in achieving misfortune, ever breeding wars in your hardhearted soul. But such strife
1.220: should not be pushed into a conflict with the powerful.
1.221:
**Electra**
I have been forced to it, forced by a terrible compulsion. I know my own passion; it does not escape me; but, under such terrible compulsion, I will not restrain these disastrous cries of frenzy,
1.225: so long as life is in me. Who indeed, my noble friends, who that keeps what is appropriate in mind, would think any word of comfort right for my ears? Let me be, let me be, my comforters!
1.230: For these ills will be reckoned with those which have no cure; I will never know a respite from my pains, or the sum of this wailing.
1.233:
**Chorus**
It is nevertheless with goodwill, like a true-hearted mother,
1.235: that I dissuade you from begetting misery upon miseries.
1.236:
**Electra**
But what limit has nature begot for my affliction? Tell me, how can it be right to neglect the dead? Has such a seed been sown in any mortal? May I never have such men’s esteem;
1.240: never, when I am close to prosperity, may I dwell in ease, hindering the wings of shrill lamentation so as to deprive my begetter of his honors!For if the dead is to lie a wretch, merely dust and nothingness,
1.245: while his slayers do not pay back to him blood for blood in penalty,
1.250: then shame and reverence will vanish from all humanity.
1.251:
**Chorus**
I came, my child, mindful of your interests no less than my own. But if what I say is wrong, let your way prevail; for united we will follow you.
1.254:
**Electra**
I am ashamed, my friends, if you judge me
1.255: too intolerant with my many laments; but, since rough compulsion forces me to act this way, forgive me. How indeed could any woman of noble nature not act, when she sees her father’s sufferings as I see them day and night continually,
1.260: and flourishing rather than fading? First, everything to do with the mother who bore me has become most hateful towards me; next, in my own home I live with my father’s murderers; they rule over me and from them
1.265: equally I either have or do without.And then think what manner of days I pass, when I see Aegisthus sitting on my father’s throne; when I look on him wearing the very robes which my father wore and
1.270: pouring libations at the hearth where he killed him; and when I see the chief outrage of them all, the murderer in my father’s bed at my wretched mother’s side, if I must call her mother, even though she shares her bed with that man.
1.275: So hardened is she that she joins with this polluter, fearing no Erinys. No, as if laughing at her deeds, having found the day on which in the past she treacherously killed my father,
1.280: she celebrates it with dance and song, and in monthly rites she sacrifices sheep to the gods who worked her deliverance.
1.282: But I, as I joylessly witness it, cry out, waste away in the house and bewail the unholy feast named after my father,
1.285: in solitary weeping. For I cannot even grieve to the full extent which would please my heart, since this lady, who is in fact no lady, loudly reproaches me with such shameless taunts as these: Wicked and hateful girl, have you alone lost your father,and is no one else in the world grieving? May your death be harsh, and may the gods below never free you from your current mourning. Just so she abuses me, except when she gets word that Orestes is coming. Then, infuriated,
1.295: she comes up to me and cries;—Have you not brought this upon me? Is this not your doing, since you stole Orestes from my hands and secretly sent him away? Yes—but rest assured that you will be justly punished. Like this she barks, and in agreement
1.300: her glorious bridegroom by her side urges her on—that total impotent, that utter plague who fights his battles with the help of women. But my heart is broken by my suffering as I constantly wait for Orestes to come and end these troubles.
1.305: For the perpetual imminence of his actions has eradicated every hope that I could conceive. In such a state of affairs, then, friends, there is no room for self-restraint or for reverence. Rather, in these dire straits there is much need to pursue a dire course.
1.310:
**Chorus**
Tell me, is Aegisthus nearby as you speak these words to us, or has he left the house?
1.312:
**Electra**
He is gone, to be sure. Do not think that I would have come to the doors, if he were nearby. He happens now to be in the country.
1.315: more boldly, if this is so?
1.316:
**Electra**
He is not here, so question me. What is it you want?
1.317:
**Chorus**
I ask you, then, what report can you give of your brother? Will he come soon, or is he delaying? I wish to know.
1.319:
**Electra**
He says he will come, but although he promises he never does what he says.
1.320:
**Chorus**
True, a man will hesitate on the verge of a great undertaking.
1.321:
**Electra**
And yet I saved him with no hesitation.
1.322:
**Chorus**
Take heart: he is noble enough to stand by his friends.
1.323:
**Electra**
I believe it; otherwise I would not have remained alive so long.
1.324:
**Chorus**
Say no more now, since I see your sister
1.325:
coming from the house, Chrysothemis, offspring of the same father and mother. In her hands are sepulchral offerings, such as are customary for those in the world below.
*Enter Chrysothemis, from the house.*
1.328:
**Chrysothemis**
What is this speech of yours, sister, which you have come forth yet again to speak at the public doors?
1.330: Will you not learn with any lapse of time to end your vain indulgence in futile anger? Yet this much I know—that I myself am saddened by our present circumstances; indeed so much so that, could I find the strength, I would bare my feelings towards them.
1.335: But now, in these evil times I think it best to navigate with shortened sail so that I may not seem to be on the attack, when I am unable to cause harm. I wish that your own conduct were the same! Nevertheless, right is on the side which you favor, not on that which I advise. But if I am to live the life of the freeborn,
1.340: those in power must be obeyed in all things.
1.341:
**Electra**
It is strange, indeed, that you, the daughter of our father from whom you grew, should forget him and instead show concern for your mother! All your admonitions to me have been taught by her; you speak no word of your own.
1.345: So now take your choice: be imprudent, or be prudent, but forgetful of your friends. You have just said that if could you find the strength, you would show your hatred of them; yet, when I am doing my utmost to avenge our father,
1.350: you do not work with me, but seek to deflect your sister from her deed.Does this not add cowardice to our miseries? Therefore instruct me, or rather learn from me what gain there might be for me if I ended my lamentation. Am I not now alive? Miserably so, I know, but well enough for me.
1.355: And I hurt them, and thereby affix an honorable tribute to the dead, in case those in that world can enjoy it and feel gratitude. But you, who tell me of your hatred, hate in word alone, while by your behavior you unite with the murderers of our father. I, however, would never yield to them, not even if
1.360: one of them were to bring to me the gifts in which you now glory. Let yours be the richly-spread table and superabundant lifestyle. As for me, let my sustenance be only that I do not wound my own conscience—I do not covet such privilege as yours and
1.365: neither would you, if you had self-control. But now, when you could be called the child of the noblest father among men, be called instead your mother’s daughter, for in this way your corruptness will be evident to the greatest number as you betray your dead father and your true friends.
1.369:
**Chorus**
Away with anger, for the gods’ sake! There is
1.370: advantage for both of you in what is urged, if you, Electra, would learn to implement her advice, and she, again, yours.
1.372:
**Chrysothemis**
For my part, friends, I am not at all unaccustomed to her insults, nor would I have mentioned this, if I had not heard that the greatest disaster is now rushing down on her,
1.375: one which will restrain her from her long mourning.
1.376:
**Electra**
Come then, name this terror! If you can tell me of anything worse than my present condition, I would resist no more.
1.378:
**Chrysothemis**
I will tell you all that I know. If you will not cease from your mourning, they intend
1.380: to send you where you will never look upon the sun’s brilliance, but passing your life in a covered chamber beyond this land’s borders you will make hymns of your calamity. Think on this, and do not blame me later, when you suffer. Now is the time to think wisely.
1.385:
**Electra**
Have they in fact decided to do this to me?
1.386:
**Chrysothemis**
They certainly have, as soon as Aegisthus comes home.
1.387:
**Electra**
Then for this, may he arrive quickly!
1.388:
**Chrysothemis**
Troubled girl, what curse are you laying on yourself?
1.389:
**Electra**
That he may come, if he plans to do any of what you said.
1.390:
**Chrysothemis**
So that you may suffer? In what way? Where are your wits?
1.391:
**Electra**
So that I may fly as far as possible from you all.
1.392:
**Chrysothemis**
Have you no care for the life you lead now?
1.393:
**Electra**
oh, yes, my life is so wondrously fine.
1.394:
**Chrysothemis**
It would be, if only you learned good sense.
1.395:
**Electra**
Do not teach me to betray my friends.
1.396:
**Chrysothemis**
I do not, but to bend before the strong.
1.397:
**Electra**
Keep your flattery to yourself; it is not in my character.
1.398:
**Chrysothemis**
Regardless, it brings no honor to fall through senselessness.
1.399:
**Electra**
I will fall, if need be, while honoring my father.
1.400:
**Chrysothemis**
But our father, I know, pardons me for this.
1.401:
**Electra**
It is for cowards to commend such sentiments.
1.402:
**Chrysothemis**
So you will not be persuaded to agree with me?
1.403:
**Electra**
No, indeed; may I not yet be so devoid of intelligence.
1.404:
**Chrysothemis**
Then I will move on to where I was sent.
1.405:
**Electra**
And where is it that you go? For whom do you take these offerings to be burned?
1.406:
**Chrysothemis**
Mother sends me with funeral libations for our father.
1.407:
**Electra**
What are you saying? For her deadliest enemy?
1.408:
**Chrysothemis**
Whom she herself killed, no doubt you wanted to say this as well.
1.409:
**Electra**
What friend persuaded her? Whose idea was it?
1.410:
**Chrysothemis**
The cause, I think, was fear induced by some vision in the night.
1.411:
**Electra**
My father’s Gods! Stand with me now at last!
1.412:
**Chrysothemis**
Do you find something heartening in this terror?
1.413:
**Electra**
If you would tell me the vision, then I could answer.
1.414:
**Chrysothemis**
I know no more than a small part of the story.
1.415:
**Electra**
Tell me that, anyway; a small tale has often before now tripped men up, or set them upright.
1.417:
**Chrysothemis**
It is said that she saw the father of you and of me restored to the sunlight and to her company once more. Then he took the scepter—
1.420: once his own, but now carried by Aegisthus—and planted it at the hearth. From it branched upward a flourishing limb, by which the whole land of the Mycenaeans was overshadowed. Such was the tale that I heard told by one who was present
1.425: when she revealed her dream to the Sun-god. More than this I do not know, except that she sent me by reason of this fear of hers. Now, I beg you by our ancestral gods, obey me, and do not fall in your senselessness!
1.430: If you reject me now, it is in misery that you will next seek me out.
1.431:
**Electra**
Dear sister, let none of these offerings in your hands touch the tomb. For neither divine law nor piety allows you to dedicate funeral gifts or bring libations to our father from his hateful wife.
1.435: No! To the winds with them! Or cover them in a deep, dusty hole, where not one of them will ever come near our father’s resting place. Rather let these treasures be preserved for her below when she dies. Were she not by nature the most audacious
1.440: of all women, she would never at all have tried to pour these ill-willed offerings to the man she killed. Consider whether you believe that the dead in his tomb will welcome this tribute with affection towards her, by whose hand he died dishonored and was mutilated
1.445: like an enemy? She, who, as if to wash herself clean, wiped off the bloodstains on his head? Surely you do not believe that your bringing these things will absolve her of the murder?It is not possible. No, be rid of them. Give him instead a lock of your hair’s ends, cut from your own head,
1.450: and from wretched me, too, give these gifts, poor as they are, though all I have. Take this hair, not glossy with unguents, and this girdle, decked with no rich ornament. Then fall down and pray that he himself may come in kindness to us from the world below, a helper against our enemies;
1.455: and that young Orestes may live to set his foot upon our enemies in superior might, so that hereafter we may crown our father’s tomb with wealthier hands than those with which we honor him now.I think, yes, I think that he too had some part
1.460: in sending her these appalling dreams. Still, sister, do yourself this service and help me, and him, too, that most beloved of all men, who rests in Hades’ domain, our shared father.
1.464:
**Chorus**
The girl’s advice is pious; you,
1.465: dear friend, will do what she says, if you are wise.
1.466:
**Chrysothemis**
I will. In regard to a just deed, it is unreasonable for two people to argue, but reasonable to jump to action. But, by the gods, my friends, when I attempt this task, let me have your silence,
1.470:
since if my mother hears of it, I believe that this attempt which I will dare shall in the end cause me bitterness.
*Exit Chrysothemis on the spectators’ right.*
1.472:
**Chorus**
If I am not a deranged prophet and one who lacks wise judgments,
1.475: Justice, the sender of the omen, will come, winning the just victory of her hands’ might. She will come in pursuit before long, my child. Courage is mine,
1.480: since I heard just now of this sweet-blowing dream. Never does the lord of the Hellenes, your producer forget,
1.485: nor does the axe of long ago forget, striking with bronze on its jaws, which in most shameless disgrace annihilated him.
1.488:
**Chorus**
She, too, will come, she of many hands and many feet who lurks in her terrible ambush,
1.490: the bronze-shod Erinys. For an unwed, unbetrothed passion for a marriage polluted by murder seized the pair, though divine law forbade it to them.
1.495: Therefore I am confident that the portent—a wonder which I will never blame—will draw near to the criminals and conspirators. To be sure, mortal prophecy
1.500: from fearful dreams or divine signs exists no more, if this vision of the night does not find due fulfillment.
1.504:
**Chorus**
O chariot-race of Pelops long ago, source of many a sorrow,
1.505: what disaster you have brought upon this land! For ever since Myrtilus sank to rest beneath the waves,
1.510: hurled to utter destruction from his golden chariot in disgraceful outrage, from that time to this, outrage and its many sorrows
1.515:
were never yet gone from this house.
*Enter Clytaemnestra, with attendants, from the house.*
1.516:
**Clytaemnestra**
You run loose again, it seems, since Aegisthus is not here, who used always to keep you at least from coming out to the gates and shaming your family. But now, since he is absent, you pay
1.520: me no mind. And yet you have said of me often and to many listeners that I am a rash and unjust tyrant, who violently abuse you and yours. But it is not I who do violence; I only return the insults that I so often hear from you.
1.525: Your father—this and nothing else is your constant pretext—was slain by me. Yes, by me. I know it well. I make no denial. Justice took hold of him, not I alone—Justice, whom you ought to have supported, if you had been in your right mind.
1.530: For this father of yours whom you constantly bewail alone of all the Greeks had the heart to sacrifice your own blood, your sister, to the gods—he, who, when sowing his seed, felt none of the pains I did when I gave birth.Come, tell me now, why, or to please whom,
1.535: did he sacrifice her? To please the Argives, you will say? No, they had no right to kill my daughter. Or, if indeed it was for the sake of his brother Menelaus that he killed my child, was he not to pay me the penalty for that? Did Menelaus not have two children,
1.540: who should in fairness have died instead of my daughter, since the father and mother from whom they were sprung had caused that voyage? Did Hades have some greater desire to feast on my offspring than on hers? Or had all love of the children of my womb been
1.545: abandoned by their accursed father, while love for the children of Menelaus filled him? Were these not the marks of a thoughtless and malicious parent? I think so, even if I differ from your judgment. So, too, would the dead girl speak, if she could find a voice. For myself, then, I view the past without
1.550: dismay; but if you think my attitude criminal, see that your own judgment is just before you blame your neighbor.
1.552:
**Electra**
This time, at least, you cannot say that I first gave you cause for upset and thereby provoked such words from you. But, if you will permit me,
1.555: I would gladly declare the truth, on behalf of my dead father and my sister alike.
1.556:
**Clytaemnestra**
Certainly I permit you; and if you always addressed me in such a tone, you would not be difficult to listen to.
1.558:
**Electra**
Then I will speak. You admit that you killed my father. What statement could be more shameful still than that,
1.560: whether you did it justly or not? But I will demonstrate to you that you did not justly kill him. No, the persuasion of that wicked man with whom you now sleep dragged you to it.Ask the huntress Artemis what wrong she punished when she stayed the frequent winds at Aulis;
1.565: or I will tell you, since we may not learn from her. My father, as I have heard, was once hunting in the grove of the goddess, when his footfall flushed a dappled and antlered stag; he shot it, and chanced to make a certain boast concerning its slaughter.
1.570: Angered by this, Leto’s daughter detained the Greeks so that in requital for the beast’s life my father should sacrifice his own daughter. So it was that she was sacrificed, since the fleet had no other release, neither homeward nor to Troy.
1.575: For that reason, under fierce constraint and with much resistance, at last he sacrificed her—but it was not for the sake of Menelaus.But suppose—for I will make your own plea—suppose that the motive of his deed was to benefit his brother. Should you have killed him because of that? Under what sort of law?
1.580: See that by laying down such a law for men, you do not lay down trouble and remorse for yourself. For, if we are to take blood for blood, you surely would be the first to die, if you were to meet with justice.But consider whether this pretext is any excuse at all.
1.585: For tell me, if you please, what crime it is that you requite by doing the most shameless deeds of all: sharing your bed with that blood-guilty one, with whom you first destroyed my father and now bear his children
1.590: while you have cast out the earlier born, the pious offspring of a pious marriage? How can I commend these deeds? Or will you claim that this, too, is recompense for your daughter? No, it is a shameful plea, if you so plead, for there is nothing noble in marrying an enemy for a daughter’s sake.
1.595: But no, I can hardly even admonish you, when your every cry is that I slander my mother. I think, rather, that you are no less a mistress to me than a mother; so lowly is the life that I live,
1.600: ever beset with miseries come from you and your consort. And your other child, the exile who scarcely escaped your hand, poor Orestes, wastes away his unhappy life. You have often accused me of rearing him to punish your crime,
1.605: and I would have done so, if I could, you may be sure. As far as he is concerned, you can denounce me to all as disloyal, if you like, or loud-mouthed, or impudent. For if my nature is familiar with such wrongdoings, I hardly bring disgrace upon your nature.
1.610:
**Chorus**
I see her breathing fury; but whether justice is with her, her concern for this I see no longer.
1.612:
**Clytaemnestra**
And what manner of concern should I use against her, who has abused her mother like this at her mature age? Do you not think
1.615: that she would go forward to any deed without shame?
1.616:
**Electra**
Now be assured that I do feel shame for it, though I seem not to you. I know that my behavior is unsuited to my age and inappropriate. But then the enmity I get from you and your
1.620: behavior compel me with harsh necessity to do this; for reprehensible deeds are learned from reprehensible examples.
1.622:
**Clytaemnestra**
You shameless creature! Truly I and my speech and my deeds give you too much to talk about.
1.624:
**Electra**
The words are yours, not mine; for yours
1.625: are the deeds, and they find their own expression.
1.626:
**Clytaemnestra**
Now by our mistress Artemis, you shall not escape the consequences of this audacity once Aegisthus returns.
1.628:
**Electra**
You see? You are driven to rage and, even though you grant me free speech, you have no patience to listen.
1.630:
**Clytaemnestra**
Will you not allow me to sacrifice without ominous shouting, when I have permitted you to say anything and everything you wished?
1.632:
**Electra**
I allow it; I exhort you to it: sacrifice! But do not blame my voice, for I would not say another word.
1.634:
**Clytaemnestra**
Raise then, my attendant, the offerings
1.635: of many fruits, so that I may uplift my prayers for release from my present fears to this image of our King. Please, O Phoebus our defender, may you now listen to my prayer, though it is muffled; for I do not make my plea among friends, nor does it suit me to unfold it all
1.640: to the light while she stands near me, lest by her malice and a cry of her clamorous tongue she sow reckless rumors through the whole city. Nevertheless, hear me thus, since in this way I will speak. That vision which I saw last night
1.645: in ambiguous dreams—if its appearance was to my good, grant, Lycean king, that it be fulfilled; but if to my harm, then hurl it back upon those who would harm me. And if any are plotting to eject me by treachery from my present prosperity, do not permit them.
1.650: Rather grant that living forever unharmed as I am I may govern the house of the sons of Atreus and their throne, sharing prosperous days with the friends who share them now, and with those of my children who feel no enmity or bitterness towards me.
1.655:
O Lycean Apollo, hear these prayers with favor, and grant them to us all just as we ask! As for all my other prayers, though I am silent, I judge that you, a god, must know them, since it is appropriate that Zeus’s children see all.
*Enter the Paedagogus from the left.*
1.660:
**Paedagogus**
Foreign ladies, how might I know for certain if this be the palace of the king Aegisthus?
1.662:
**Chorus**
This is the palace, stranger; you yourself have guessed correctly.
1.663:
**Paedagogus**
And am I on target when I surmise that this lady is his wife? She is indeed regal to look upon.
1.665:
**Chorus**
Exactly right; this is she before you.
1.666:
**Paedagogus**
Greetings, royal lady! I bring happy news to you and to Aegisthus from a friend.
1.668:
**Clytaemnestra**
I welcome your greeting; but I would like first to know who may have sent you.
1.670:
**Paedagogus**
Phanoteus the Phocian provided me the weighty task.
1.671:
**Clytaemnestra**
And what is it, sir? Tell me. Coming from a friend you will bring, I know, a kindly message.
1.673:
**Paedagogus**
Orestes is dead, to put it briefly.
1.674:
**Electra**
Oh, miserable me! My ruin comes today!
1.675:
**Clytaemnestra**
What, friend? What did you say? Do not listen to her!
1.676:
**Paedagogus**
I said, and say again, Orestes is dead.
1.677:
**Electra**
This is my wretched end! I am no more!
1.678:
**Clytaemnestra**
*To Electra.*
You, go about your business! But you, sir, tell me exactly in what manner he was destroyed.
1.680:
**Paedagogus**
I was sent for that purpose, and will tell you all. Having gone to the shrine which is Greece’s common glory in order to compete for Delphi’s prizes and having heard the herald’s loud summons to the foot-race, the first contest,
1.685: he entered the lists, a brilliant form, a wonder in the eyes of all there. When he had finished the race at the point where it began, he went out with the glorious honor of victory. To say the most with the least words, I do not know the man whose deeds and triumphs have matched his.
1.690: But this one thing you must know: in all the contests that the judges announced, he carried away the prize, and men deemed him happy as often as the herald proclaimed him an Argive, by name Orestes, son of
1.695: Agamemnon, who once marshalled Greece’s famous expedition.So far Orestes fared as I described. But when a god sends harm, not even the strong man can escape. For on another day, when with the rising sun there was held the race of the swift-footed horses,
1.700: he entered it along with many charioteers. One was an Achaean, one from Sparta; two masters of yoked cars were Libyans; Orestes, driving Thessalian mares, came fifth among them; the sixth was from Aetolia,
1.705: with chestnut colts; a Magnesian was the seventh; the eighth, with white horses, was of Aenian stock; the ninth hailed from Athens, built of gods; there was a Boeotian too, making the tenth chariot. They took their stations where the appointed umpires
1.710: placed them by lot and ranged the cars. Then at the sound of the bronze trumpet, they started. All shouted to their horses, and shook the reins in their hands; the whole course was filled with the clatter of rattling chariots; and the dust flew upward.
1.715: All of them in a confused throng kept plying their goads unsparingly, so that one of them might pass the wheel-hubs and the snorting steeds of his rivals; for both at their backs and at their rolling wheels the breath of the horses foamed and smattered.
1.720: Orestes, driving close to the near edge of the turning-post, almost grazed it with his wheel each time and, giving rein to the trace-horse on the right, he checked the horse on the inner side. To this point, all the chariots still stood upright. But then the Aenian’s
1.725: hard-mouthed colts carried him out of control as they passed out of the turn from the sixth into the seventh lap and dashed their foreheads against the rig of the Barcaean. Next, as a result of this one mishap, the cars kept smashing and colliding with each other, and the whole
1.730: race-ground of Crisa swelled with shipwrecked chariots.
1.731: Seeing this, the clever charioteer from Athens drew aside and paused, allowing the equestrian flood to pass in mid-crest. Orestes was driving last, keeping his horses
1.735: behind, as his trust was in the race’s end. But when he sees that the Athenian is alone left in, he sends a shrill cry ringing through the ears of his swift colts, and gives chase. Bringing yoke level with yoke the two of them raced, first one man, then the other,
1.740: showing his head in front of the other’s chariot. Up to now the ill-fated Orestes had driven upright safely through every circuit, upright in his upright car. But then he slackened his left rein while the horse was turning and unwittingly struck the edge of the pillar,
1.745: breaking the axle-box in two. He spilled forward over the chariot-rail and was caught in the trim reins, and as he fell to the ground, his colts were scattered into the middle of the course.But when the crowd saw that he had fallen
1.750: from the chariot, a cry of pity went up for the young man who had done such deeds and was allotted such bad fortune—now dashed against the earth, now tossed with his feet to the sky until the charioteers with difficulty reigned in the gallop of his horses and
1.755: freed him, so covered with blood that no friend who saw it would have known the pitiful corpse. Immediately they burned him on a pyre, and chosen men of Phocis now bring the sad dust of that mighty form in a small urn of bronze,
1.760: so that he may find due burial in his fatherland.Such is my story—it is grievous even to hear, but for us witnesses who looked on, it was the greatest of sorrows that these eyes have seen.
1.764:
**Chorus**
Oh, sorrow! It seems now that all the stock of our ancient masters
1.765: has been leveled clean down to the roots.
1.766:
**Clytaemnestra**
O Zeus, how shall I name this news—fortunate? Or terrible, but beneficial? It is a bitter thing, when by my own misery I preserve my life.
1.769:
**Paedagogus**
Why are you so despondent, lady, at my news?
1.770:
**Clytaemnestra**
There is a terrible power in motherhood; a mother may be wronged, but she can feel no hate for those whom she bore.
1.772:
**Paedagogus**
Then it seems that we have come in vain.
1.773:
**Clytaemnestra**
No, not in vain; how can you say in vain when you have brought me sure proofs of his death?
1.775: He sprang from my own life, yet deserting my breast and my nurture he became a fugitive, completely alien from me. And me, once he left this land, he saw no more; but, charging me with the murder of his father, he made terrible threats,
1.780: so that neither by night nor by day could sweet sleep cover me, but the imminent moment made me live always as if I were about to die. Now, however, since today I am rid of terror of him and of this girl—that greater plague
1.785: who shared my home while consuming undiluted my life-blood—now, I think, for all her threats, I shall pass my days in peace.
1.788:
**Electra**
Ah, what misery! Now, indeed, Orestes, I must mourn your misfortune, since even dead as you are
1.790: you are abused by this woman, your mother! Is it not just fine?
1.791:
**Clytaemnestra**
You certainly are not, but he is fine as he is.
1.792:
**Electra**
Listen to her, Nemesis of the recently departed!
1.793:
**Clytaemnestra**
She has heard who should be heard, and has ordained well.
1.794:
**Electra**
Abuse us! Fortune is with you today.
1.795:
**Clytaemnestra**
You and Orestes will not stop me, then, will you?
1.796:
**Electra**
It is we who are stopped; we cannot stop you.
1.797:
**Clytaemnestra**
Your coming, sir, deserves large recompense, if you have stopped her clamorous tongue.
1.799:
**Paedagogus**
Then I would take my leave, if all is well.
1.800:
**Clytaemnestra**
Not so; your welcome would then be unworthy of me, and of my ally who sent you. No, come in. Leave her out here to shout out loud her misfortunes and those of her friends.
*Clytaemnestra and the Paedagogus enter the house.*
1.804:
**Electra**
What do you think? Does it seem to you that she, poor woman, wept and wailed terribly,
1.805: like a grieving, anguished woman, over her son thus destroyed? No, she left us with a laugh! Ah, miserable me! Dearest Orestes, how your death has destroyed me! For your passing has torn from my heart
1.810: the only hopes which still were mine: that you would live to return some day as the avenger of our father, and also of me in my misery. But now, where shall I turn? I am alone, cheated of you, as of my father. Hereafter I must be a slave again
1.815: among those I most hate, my father’s murderers. Am I not in a fine way? But at least in the time remaining me I will never enter the house to dwell with them. No, lying down at these gates, without a friend, I shall wither away my days.
1.820: Therefore, if anyone in the house be angry, let him kill me. It is a favor, if I die, but a pain, if I live. I desire life no more.
1.823:
**Chorus**
Where are the thunderbolts of Zeus, or where the
1.825: shining Sun, if they look upon these things and quietly cover them over?
1.828:
**Chorus**
My child, why do you weep?
1.830:
**Chorus**
Give no cry of bad omen!
**Electra**
You will break my heart!
1.832:
**Electra**
If you suggest that I keep hope for those who have surely passed to Hades,
1.835: you will trample even harder upon me as I waste away.
1.836:
**Chorus**
No, for I know that the prince Amphiaraus was ensnared by a woman’s chain of gold and swallowed up. And now beneath the earth—
1.841:
**Chorus**
—He reigns supreme with the wits of the living.
1.843:
**Chorus**
ah, me, indeed! For the murderess—
1.846:
**Electra**
I know it; I know it. For a champion arose to avenge the grieving dead. But for me no champion remains: he who yet remained has been snatched clean away.
1.849:
**Chorus**
Unhappy are you, unhappy your destiny!
1.850:
**Electra**
How well I know that, all too well, with my life swept through all the months by abundant terrors and horrors!
1.853:
**Chorus**
We have witnessed the events for which you mourn.
1.855:
**Electra**
Cease, then, to divert me from it, since no longer—
1.857:
**Electra**
—Since I no longer have hope in my brother, the seed of our shared noble line, to aid me.
1.860:
**Chorus**
Nature ordains death as the destiny of all mortals.
1.861:
**Electra**
What, a death like the one which that ill-fated one died beneath a race of swift hooves, entangled in the cutting, dragging reins?
1.865:
**Electra**
Yes, so it is, when in foreign soil, without being tended by my hands—
1.868:
**Electra**
—he has been buried not receiving from me either burial
1.870:
or lamentation.
*Enter Chrysothemis, from the right.*
1.871:
**Chrysothemis**
I am pursued by joy, dear sister, and I disregard seemliness in order to come with speed. I bring joyful news to relieve your former troubles and grief.
1.875:
**Electra**
And from where could you find help for my sufferings, when no cure for them can be imagined?
1.877:
**Chrysothemis**
Orestes is with us—know this from my lips—plainly visible, just as you see me now.
1.879:
**Electra**
What, are you insane, poor girl?
1.880: Do you laugh at my sorrows and your own?
1.881:
**Chrysothemis**
No, by our father’s hearth, I do not speak in mockery. I tell you that he truly is with us.
1.883:
**Electra**
Ah, miserable girl! And from whom on earth have you heard this tale, which you believe so lightly?
1.885:
**Chrysothemis**
I have it on my own knowledge, no one else’s; I have seen clear proofs.
1.887:
**Electra**
What have you seen, poor girl, to warrant your belief? What did you see, that you are warmed by this unquenchable fire?
1.889:
**Chrysothemis**
Now, for the gods’ love, listen, so that you may know
1.890: the rest from me before deciding whether I am sane or foolish.
1.891:
**Electra**
Speak on, then, if you find pleasure in speaking.
1.892:
**Chrysothemis**
Well, I will tell you all that I have seen. When I came to Father’s ancestral tomb, I saw that streams of milk had recently flowed from the top of the mound
1.895: and that his sepulchre was encircled with garlands of all flowers that grow. I was astonished at the sight, and peered about lest somehow someone should approach close to me. But when I perceived that all the place was in stillness,
1.900: I crept nearer to the tomb, and on the mound’s edge I saw a lock of hair, freshly severed.And the very moment I see it—ah me!—a familiar image rushes into my mind, and I feel that I am looking at a token of him whom I most love, Orestes.
1.905: Then I lift it in my hands and make no sound of bad omen, but the tears of joy straightaway fill my eyes. Even now I know well, just as I knew then, that this fair tribute has come from no one but him. Whom else does that tomb concern, save me and you?
1.910: And I did not make those offerings, I know, nor did you. How could you, when you cannot leave this house even to worship the gods without later regretting it? Nor, again, does our mother’s heart incline to do such deeds, nor could she have done so without our knowledge.
1.915: No, these offerings are from Orestes! Come, dear sister, have courage! Not always does the same fortune, it is true, attend the same individuals. Ours was once to be despised, but today, perhaps, will seal the promise of much good.
1.920:
**Electra**
Oh, what foolishness! How I have been pitying you!
1.921:
**Chrysothemis**
What, is my news unpleasing to you?
1.922:
**Electra**
You do not know where on earth or into what dreams you wander.
1.923:
**Chrysothemis**
How could I not know what I have plainly seen?
1.924:
**Electra**
He is dead, poor girl, and your
1.925: salvation by him is gone. Do not look to him.
1.926:
**Chrysothemis**
Ah, miserable me! From whom have you heard this?
1.927:
**Electra**
From the man who was present when he perished.
1.928:
**Chrysothemis**
And where is he? Amazement steals over my mind.
1.929:
**Electra**
He is inside, a welcome guest, not unpleasing to our mother.
1.930:
**Chrysothemis**
Ah, misery! Who, then, can have made those ample offerings to my father’s tomb?
1.932:
**Electra**
Most likely, I think, someone placed those gifts in memory of the dead Orestes.
1.934:
**Chrysothemis**
Oh, my misfortune! And I was hurrying here
1.935: with such joyous nows, ignorant after all of our downfall. But now that I have arrived, I find fresh sorrows added to the old!
1.938:
**Electra**
So it stands with you. Yet if you will be persuaded by me, you will lighten the load of our present trouble.
1.940:
**Chrysothemis**
How can I ever raise the dead back to life?
1.941:
**Electra**
That is not what I meant; I was not born so foolish.
1.942:
**Chrysothemis**
What do you urge, then, of those things that I am capable of doing?
1.943:
**Electra**
That you be brave in executing what I recommend.
1.944:
**Chrysothemis**
If any good can be done, I will not refuse.
1.946:
**Chrysothemis**
I know it, and I will share your burden with all my power.
1.947:
**Electra**
Hear, then, in what way I have decided to take action. As for the support of friends, you yourself doubtless know that we have none. Hades has taken our friends away,
1.950: and we two are left alone. I, so long as I heard that my brother still lived and prospered, had hopes that he would yet come to avenge the murder of our father. But now that he is no more, I look next to you
1.955: and ask that you not flinch from aiding me, your sister, to slay our father’s murderer, Aegisthus. There—I can have no secrets from you anymore.How long will you wait in indifference? What hope is left standing, to which your eyes can turn? Now you are right to complain
1.960: that you are robbed of possession of your father’s estate; now you may mourn that you have advanced this far in years without wedded love or bridal song. And do not cling to hopes that you will ever meet with such joys. The man, Aegisthus, is not so unthinking
1.965: as ever to permit that offspring should shoot up from you or from me either to be a certain bane for himself. But if you will follow my plans, first you will win praise for piety from our dead father below, and from our brother, too;
1.970: next, you shall be called hereafter free, just as you were born, and shall find a worthy marriage. For noble natures draw the gaze of all.Then do you not see what fair fame you will procure for yourself and for me, by obeying me?
1.975: What citizen or stranger when he sees us will not greet us with praises such as these: Behold these two sisters, my friends! They saved their father’s house, and at a time when their foes were firmly established, they took their lives in their hands and administered bloodshed! Worthy of love is this pair, worthy of reverence from all. At festivals, and wherever the citizenry is assembled, let these two be honored by all men for their manly courage. Thus will every one speak of us,
1.985: so that in life and in death our glory shall not fail.Come, dear sister, be persuaded! Toil with our father, share the burden of your brother, put an end to my troubles and an end to yours, keeping in mind that a shameful life brings shame upon the noble-born.
1.990:
**Chorus**
In a crisis such as this, forethought is an ally both to those who speak and those who listen.
1.992:
**Chrysothemis**
Yes, I agree. And before she spoke, my friends, if she were blessed with a sound mind, she would have remembered caution, even as she does not now.
1.995: Where can you have turned your eyes, that you arm yourself with such rashness and call me to serve beneath you? Do you not see? Your nature is a woman’s, not a man’s, and the strength of your hand is less than that of your adversaries. And their fortune prospers day by day,
1.1000: while ours ebbs and comes to nothing. Who, then, plotting to subdue such a man, would escape destruction unharmed? See to it that, badly as we fare now, we do not acquire greater evil, if any one hears this talk of yours.
1.1005: It brings us no relief or benefit, if after winning fair fame we die an ignominious death. For death is not the most odious thing; it is rather craving death, but lacking the means to die. No, I plead with you, before we are utterly, totally destroyed
1.1010: and before we leave our house desolate, restrain your rage! I will take care that your words remain secret and harmless for you. You in turn must get hold of good sense at long last and yield to the powerful since you have no strength.
1.1015:
**Chorus**
Listen to her. There is no better gain for mortals to win than foresight and a prudent mind.
1.1017:
**Electra**
You have said nothing unexpected. Well I knew that you would reject what I proposed. But the deed must be done with my own hand, by me and me alone.
1.1020: I certainly will not leave it unaccomplished.
1.1021:
**Chrysothemis**
Ah! If only you had had such resolve on the day of our father’s death! Then you would have accomplished everything!
1.1023:
**Electra**
My nature was the same then, but my mind was less ripe.
1.1024:
**Chrysothemis**
Strive to keep your mind that way through all your life.
1.1025:
**Electra**
You make these admonitions like one who will not assist me.
1.1026:
**Chrysothemis**
I will not, for he who sets hand to the deed is likely also to suffer disaster.
1.1027:
**Electra**
I admire you for your prudence. For your cowardice I hate you.
1.1028:
**Chrysothemis**
I will listen no less calmly when you praise me.
1.1029:
**Electra**
Never fear to suffer that from me, at least.
1.1030:
**Chrysothemis**
There is time enough in the future to decide that.
1.1031:
**Electra**
Leave! You have no power to help.
1.1032:
**Chrysothemis**
No, I have it, but you lack the ability to listen and learn.
1.1033:
**Electra**
Go, reveal everything to your mother!
1.1034:
**Chrysothemis**
But, again, I do not hate you with so great a hate.
1.1035:
**Electra**
Yet know at least to what dishonor you drive me.
1.1036:
**Chrysothemis**
Dishonor, no! It is forethought for you.
1.1037:
**Electra**
Am I bound, then, to follow your rule of right?
1.1038:
**Chrysothemis**
Yes, for when you are sensible, then at that time you shall lead the both of us.
1.1039:
**Electra**
How terrible it is that one who speaks so well should be so wrong!
1.1040:
**Chrysothemis**
You have well described the fault to which you devotedly cling.
1.1041:
**Electra**
What? Do you think that my words are not the words of Justice?
1.1042:
**Chrysothemis**
But sometimes even Justice herself causes harm.
1.1043:
**Electra**
I do not care to live where that attitude is lawful.
1.1044:
**Chrysothemis**
Well, if you must do this, you will commend me yet.
1.1045:
**Electra**
