1.1425: and then, chosen out as foremost among the warriors in prowess, with my bow you shall sever Paris, the author of these evils, from life. You shall sack Troy and shall receive from the army the spoils of supreme valor to carry home
1.1430: to the heights of your native Oeta for the delight of your father Poeas. And whatever spoils you receive from that army, from them carry to my pyre a thank-offering for my bow. And these counsels hold for you also, son of Achilles,
1.1435: for you have not the might to subdue the Trojan realm without him, nor he without you. Rather, like twin lions with the same quarry, each of you must guard the other’s life. For the healing of your sickness, I will send Asclepius to Troy, since it is doomed to fall a second time
1.1440: before my arrows. But of this be mindful, when you plunder the land—that you show reverence towards the gods. Do this because Father Zeus regards all else as of less account, and because Piety does not die along with mortals. Whether they are alive or dead, their piety does not perish.
1.1445:
**Philoctetes**
Ah, friend whose voice I have longed to hear, whose shape I see at long last, I will not disobey your commands!
1.1450: for the occasion and the fair wind there at your stern urge you forward.
1.1452:
**Philoctetes**
Come, then, let me hail this land as I depart. Farewell, chamber that shared my watches. Farewell,
1.1455: nymphs of stream and meadow, and you, strong pounding of the sea-lashed cape, where often in the cavern’s inmost recess my head was wetted by the south wind’s blasts, and where many times the Hermaean mount sent an echo
1.1460: to my sad groans in the gale of my sorrow! But now, clear springs and Lycian fount, I am leaving you, leaving you at last, though such a hope had never buoyed me! Farewell, sea-wrapped Lemnos,
1.1465: and send me off with sailing fair to my heart’s content, send me to the destination appointed me by mighty Fate and the will of my friends, and by the all-taming god who has brought these things to pass.
1.1469:
**Chorus**
Now let us all leave together,
1.1470: once we have prayed to the nymphs of the sea to come be the guides of our safe return.

1.1:
**Oedipus**
Child of a blind old man, Antigone, to what region have we come, or to what city of men? Who will entertain the wandering Oedipus today with scanty gifts?
1.5: Little do I crave, and obtain still less than that little, and with that I am content. For patience is the lesson of suffering, and of the long years upon me, and lastly of a noble mind. My child, if you see any resting-place,
1.10: either on profane ground or by groves of the gods, stop me and set me down, so that we may inquire where we are. We have come to learn as foreigners from the townsmen, and to bring to completion whatever we hear.
1.14:
**Antigone**
Father, toil-worn Oedipus, the towers that
1.15: ring the city, to judge by sight, are far off; and this place is sacred, to judge from its appearance: laurel, olive, and vine grow thick-set; and a feathered crowd of nightingales makes music within. So sit here on this unshaped stone;
1.20: you have travelled a long way for an old man.
1.21:
**Oedipus**
Seat me, then, and watch over the blind.
1.22:
**Antigone**
If time can teach, I need not learn that.
1.23:
**Oedipus**
Can you tell me, now, where we have arrived?
1.24:
**Antigone**
Athens I know, but not this place.
1.25:
**Oedipus**
Yes, so much every traveller told us.
1.26:
**Antigone**
Well, shall I go and learn what the spot is called?
1.27:
**Oedipus**
Yes, child, if indeed it is inhabited.
1.28:
**Antigone**
It surely is inhabited. But I think there is no need—I see a man nearby.
1.30:
**Oedipus**
Setting off and coming toward us?
1.31:
**Antigone**
He is at our side already. Speak whatever seems timely to you, for the man is here.
1.33:
**Oedipus**
Stranger, hearing from this maiden, who has sight both for herself and for me,
1.35:
that you have arrived as a scout of good fortune for the solving of our doubts—
*Enter a stranger, a man of Colonus.*
1.36:
**Stranger**
Now, before you question me at length, leave this seat. You occupy ground which is unholy to tread upon.
1.38:
**Oedipus**
And what is this ground? To which of the gods is it sacred?
1.39:
**Stranger**
Ground inviolable, on which no one may dwell. The dread
1.40: goddesses hold it, the daughters of Earth and Darkness.
1.41:
**Oedipus**
Who are they? Whose awful name might I hear and invoke in prayer?
1.42:
**Stranger**
The all-seeing Eumenides the people here would call them: but other names please elsewhere.
1.44:
**Oedipus**
Then graciously may they receive their suppliant!
1.45: Nevermore will I depart from my seat in this land.
1.46:
**Stranger**
What does this mean?
**Oedipus**
The watchword of my fate.
1.47:
**Stranger**
I dare not remove you without warrant from the city, until I report what I am doing.
1.48:
**Oedipus**
Now by the gods, stranger, do not deny me, hapless wanderer as you see,
1.50: the honor of the knowledge for which I beg you.
1.51:
**Stranger**
Tell me, and you will not be without honor from me.
1.52:
**Oedipus**
What, then, is the place that we have entered?
1.53:
**Stranger**
All that I myself know, you will hear and learn. This whole place is sacred;
1.55: august Poseidon holds it, and in it lives the fire-bearing god, the Titan Prometheus. But as for the spot on which you tread, it is called the bronze threshold of this land, the support of Athens. And the neighboring fields claim Colonus, the horse-rider, for their ancient ruler;
1.60: and all the people bear his name in common as their own. Such, you see, stranger, are these haunts. They receive their honor not through story, but rather through our living with them.
1.64:
**Oedipus**
Are there indeed dwellers in this region?
1.65:
**Stranger**
Yes indeed, the namesakes of that god there.
1.66:
**Oedipus**
Have they a king? Or does speaking rest with the masses?
1.67:
**Stranger**
These parts are ruled by the king in the city.
1.68:
**Oedipus**
And who is he that is sovereign in counsel and in might?
1.69:
**Stranger**
Theseus he is called, son of Aegeus who was before him.
1.70:
**Oedipus**
Could a messenger go to him from among you?
1.71:
**Stranger**
With what aim? To speak, or to prepare his coming?
1.72:
**Oedipus**
So that by a small service he may find a great gain.
1.73:
**Stranger**
And what help can come from one who cannot see?
1.74:
**Oedipus**
In all that I speak there will be vision.
1.75:
**Stranger**
Take care now, stranger, that you come to no harm; for you are noble, if I may judge by your looks, leaving your ill-fortune aside. Stay here, where I found you, until I go and tell these things to the people of this district—not in the city.
1.80:
They will decide for you whether you should stay or go back.
*Stranger exits.*
1.81:
**Oedipus**
My child, has the stranger left us?
1.82:
**Antigone**
He is gone, and so you can speak what you wish, father, fully at ease, knowing that I alone am near.
1.84:
**Oedipus**
Ladies of dread aspect, since your seat is
1.85: the first in this land at which I have bent my knee, show yourselves not ungracious to Phoebus or to myself; who, when he proclaimed that doom of many woes, spoke to me of this rest after long years: on reaching my goal in a land where I should find a seat of the Awful Goddesses
1.90: and a shelter for foreigners, there I should close my weary life, with profit, through my having fixed my abode there, for those who received me, but ruin for those who sent me forth, who drove me away. And he went on to warn me that signs of these things would come,
1.95: in earthquake, or in thunder, or in the lightning of Zeus. Now I perceive that in this journey some trusty omen from you has surely led me home to this grove; never otherwise could I have met with you, first of all, in my wanderings—I, in my sobriety, with you who touch no wine,
1.100: —or taken this august seat not shaped by men. Then, goddesses, according to the word of Apollo, give me at last some way to accomplish and close my course—unless, perhaps, I seem too lowly,
1.105: enslaved as I am evermore to woes the sorest on the earth. Hear, sweet daughters of primeval Darkness! Hear, you that are called the city of great Pallas, Athens, given most honor of all cities! Pity this poor ghost of the man Oedipus!
1.110: For in truth it is the former living body no more.
1.111:
**Antigone**
Hush! Here come some aged men to spy out your resting-place.
1.113:
**Oedipus**
I will be mute. But hide me in the grove, apart from the road, till I learn
1.115:
how these men will speak. For in learning is the safeguard of our course.
*They exit.*
*The Chorus of elders of Colonus enters the orchestra.*
1.118:
**Chorus**
Look! Who was he, then? Where is he staying? Where has he rushed from this place,
1.120: man most insatiate of all who live? Scan the ground, look well, press the search everywhere. A wanderer that old man must have been,
1.125: a wanderer, not a dweller in the land; otherwise he never would have advanced into this untrodden grove of the maidens with whom none may strive.
1.130: Their name we tremble to speak; we pass them by with eyes turned away, moving our lips, without sound or word, in still devotion. But now it is said that one has come who reveres them not at all;
1.135:
and him I cannot yet discern, though I look round all the holy place, nor do I know where to find his lodging.
*Oedipus steps forward with Antigone.*
1.138:
**Oedipus**
Behold the man you seek! In sound is my sight, as the saying goes.
1.140:
**Chorus**
Oh! Oh! Fearful he is to see, and fearful to hear!
1.142:
**Oedipus**
Do not regard me, I beg you, as a lawless man.
1.143:
**Chorus**
Zeus defend us! Who may this old man be?
1.144:
**Oedipus**
Not so wholly of the best fate
1.145: that you would call him fortunate, guardians of this land! It is plain; otherwise I would not be creeping, as you see, by the eyes of others, and buoying my strength upon weakness.
1.148:
**Chorus**
Alas! Were you sightless even from birth?
1.150: Evil have been your days, and many, it appears. But at least if I can help it, you shall not add this curse to your lot. You go too far—too far!
1.155: That your rash steps may intrude on the field of this voiceless, grassy glade, where the waters of the mixing bowl blend their stream with the flow of honied offerings, beware, unhappiest of strangers.
1.160: Retire! Withdraw! Let a wide space part us. Do you hear, toil-worn wanderer? If you have anything to say in converse with us,
1.165: leave forbidden ground, and speak where it is lawful for all; but, till then, refrain.
1.170:
**Oedipus**
Daughter, to what counsel shall we incline?
1.171:
**Antigone**
My father, we must behave just as the townspeople do, listening and giving way where it is necessary.
1.173:
**Oedipus**
Then give me your hand.
**Antigone**
I lay it in yours.
1.174:
**Oedipus**
Strangers, let me not suffer wrong
1.175: when I have trusted in you, and have passed from my refuge!
1.176:
**Chorus**
Never, old man, never will anyone remove you from your resting-place here against your will.
*Oedipus begins to move forward.*
1.180:
**Oedipus**
Further?
**Chorus**
Lead him onward, maiden, for you hear us and obey.
1.181:
**Antigone**
Come, follow this way with your dark steps, father, as I lead you.
1.185: poor man, have the courage to detest what the city steadfastly holds as not dear, and to reverence what it holds dear!
1.188:
**Oedipus**
Lead me, then, child, to a spot where I may speak and listen within piety’s domain,
1.190: and let us not wage war with necessity.
1.192:
**Chorus**
There! Do not incline your steps beyond that ledge of bedrock.
1.195:
**Oedipus**
Shall I sit down?
**Chorus**
Yes, move sideways, and crouch low on the edge of the rock.
1.198:
**Antigone**
Father, this is my task: calmly to—
1.200:
**Antigone**
—fit step to step, and lean your aged frame upon my dear arm.
1.202:
**Oedipus**
Alas for my sad destruction!
*Antigone seats him on the rock.*
1.203:
**Chorus**
Ah, poor man, since now you are at ease, speak! What is your lineage among mortals? With what name are you led on your weary path?
1.205: What fatherland can you tell us of?
1.207:
**Oedipus**
Strangers, I am without a city, but do not—
1.208:
**Chorus**
What is this that you forbid, old man?
1.210:
**Oedipus**
do not, do not ask me who I am! Do not seek or probe further!
1.214:
**Oedipus**
My child—ah, me!—what shall I say?
1.215:
**Chorus**
What is your lineage, stranger? Speak! And who is your father?
1.216:
**Oedipus**
Woe is me! What will become of me, my child?
1.217:
**Antigone**
Speak, for you are driven to the verge.
1.218:
**Oedipus**
Then speak I will. I have no way to hide it.
1.219:
**Chorus**
You two make a long delay. Come, hasten!
1.220:
**Oedipus**
Do you know of a son of Laius?
**Chorus**
Oh!
1.221:
**Oedipus**
—And the race of the Labdacidae?
**Chorus**
O Zeus!
1.222:
**Oedipus**
—and the pitiful Oedipus?
**Chorus**
You are he?
1.223:
**Oedipus**
Have no fear of any words that I speak—
1.224:
**Chorus**
Ah, no, no!
**Oedipus**
Unhappy that I am!
**Chorus**
Oh, oh!
1.225:
**Oedipus**
Daughter, what is about to happen?
1.226:
**Chorus**
Out with you! Go forth from the land!
1.227:
**Oedipus**
And your promise—to what fulfillment will you bring it?
1.228:
**Chorus**
No man is visited by the punishment of fate if he requites deeds which were first done to himself.
1.230: Deceit on the one part matches deceits on the other, and gives pain instead of pleasure for reward. And you—back with you! Out from your seat!
1.235: Away from my land with all speed, that you may not fasten some heavier burden on my city!
1.237:
**Antigone**
Reverent strangers, since you have not endured my aged father—knowing, as you do,
1.240: the rumor of his unintended deeds—pity at least my poor self, I implore you, who supplicate you for my father alone. I beg you with eyes that can still look
1.245: on your own, like one sprung from your own blood, that this sufferer may meet with reverent treatment. On you, as on a god, we depend in our misery. But come, grant the favor for which we hardly dare hope!
1.250: I implore you by everything that you hold dear at home: by child, by wife, or treasure, or god! Look well and you will not find the mortal who, if a god should lead him on, could escape.
1.254:
**Chorus**
Feel sure, daughter of Oedipus, that we pity you and him alike
1.255: for your misfortune; but dreading the punishment of the gods, we could not say anything beyond what we have now said to you.
1.259:
**Oedipus**
What help comes, then, of repute or fair fame, if it ends in idle breath;
1.260: seeing that Athens, as men say, is god-fearing beyond all, and alone has the power to shelter the outraged stranger, and alone the power to help him? And where are these things for me, when, after making me rise up from this rocky seat, you then drive me from the land, afraid of my name alone?
1.265: Not, surely, afraid of my person or of my acts; since my acts, at least, have been in suffering rather than doing—if I must mention the tale of my mother and my father, because of which you fear me. That know I full well.
1.270: And yet how was I innately evil? I, who was merely requiting a wrong, so that, had I been acting with knowledge, even then I could not be accounted evil. But, as it was, all unknowing I went where I went—while they who wronged me knowingly sought my ruin.
1.275: Therefore, strangers, I beseech you by the gods: just as you made me leave my seat, so protect me, and do not, while you render honor to the gods, consider those gods to be fools. But rather consider that they look on the god-fearing man
1.280: and on the godless, and that never yet has an impious man found escape. With the help of those gods, do not becloud the prosperity of Athens by paying service to unholy deeds. As you have received the suppliant under your pledge,
1.285: rescue me and guard me to the end; nor dishonor me when you look on this face unlovely to behold, for I have come to you as one sacred and pious, bearing comfort for this people. But when the master has come,
1.290: whoever is your leader, then you will hear and know all; meanwhile show yourselves in no way evil.
1.292:
**Chorus**
The thoughts you urge, old man, must move awe; they have been set forth in grave words.
1.295: But I am content that the rulers of our country should judge in this case.
1.296:
**Oedipus**
And where, strangers, is the lord of this realm?
1.297:
**Chorus**
He is at the city of his fathers in our land. The messenger who sent us here has gone to fetch him.
1.299:
**Oedipus**
Do you think that he will have any regard or care for the blind man,
1.300: so as to come here himself?
1.301:
**Chorus**
Yes, surely, as soon as he learns of your name.
1.302:
**Oedipus**
Who is there to bring him that word?
1.303:
**Chorus**
The way is long, and many words from travellers often wander about. When he hears them, he will soon be with us, never fear.
1.305: For your name, old man, has been loudly trumpeted through all lands, so that even if he is taking his ease, and slow to move, when he hears of you he will swiftly arrive.
1.308:
**Oedipus**
Well, may he come with good fortune both for his own city and for me! What noble man is not his own friend?
1.310:
**Antigone**
O Zeus! What shall I say? What shall I think, my father?
1.311:
**Oedipus**
What is it, Antigone, my child?
**Antigone**
I see a woman coming towards us, mounted on a colt of Etna; she wears a Thessalian bonnet to screen her face from the sun.
1.315: What shall I say? Is it she, or is it not? Does my judgment err? Yes—no—I cannot tell—ah, me! It is no other, yes! She greets me with bright glances
1.320: as she draws near, and makes a signal. Here is Ismene, clearly, and no other before me.
1.322:
**Oedipus**
What is that you say, my child?
**Antigone**
That I see your daughter, my sister. By her voice right away you can know her.
1.324:
**Ismene**
Father and sister, names most sweet to me! How hard it was to find you!
1.325: And how hard now to look upon you for my tears!
1.327:
**Oedipus**
My child, have you come?
**Ismene**
Father, your fate is sad to see!
1.328:
**Oedipus**
Are you with us, my child?
**Ismene**
Not without toil, indeed, for myself.
1.329:
**Oedipus**
Touch me, my daughter!
**Ismene**
I give a hand to each at once.
1.330:
**Oedipus**
Ah my children, my sisters!
**Ismene**
Alas, twice-wretched life!
1.331:
**Oedipus**
Her life and mine?
**Ismene**
And mine, wretched me, makes a third.
1.332:
**Oedipus**
Child, why have you come?
**Ismene**
Through concern for you, father.
1.333:
**Oedipus**
Through longing to see me?
**Ismene**
Yes, and to bring you news by my own mouth, with the only faithful servant that I had.
1.335:
**Oedipus**
And where are the young men, your brothers, in our need?
1.336:
**Ismene**
They are where they are; their circumstances now are terrible.
1.337:
**Oedipus**
True image of the ways of Egypt that they show in their spirit and their life! For there the men sit weaving in the house,
1.340: but the wives go forth to win the daily bread. And in your case, my daughters, those to whom these toils belonged keep the house at home like maidens, while you two, in their place, bear your poor father’s woes.
1.345: The one, from the time when her youth was past and she came into her strength, has always been this old man’s guide in weary wanderings, often roaming, hungry and barefoot, through the wild woods, often battered by rains and scorching sun.
1.350: And the comforts of home, poor girl, she holds in the second place, so long as her father should have her care. And you, my child, in former days came forth, bringing your father, unknown to the Cadmeans, all the oracles that had been given concerning Oedipus.
1.355: You became a faithful guardian on my behalf, when I was being driven from the land. Now, in turn, what new tidings have you brought your father, Ismene? On what mission have you set forth from home? For you do not come empty-handed, I know well,
1.360: or without some cause of fear for me.
1.361:
**Ismene**
The sufferings that I bore, father, in seeking where you dwelt, I will pass by; I would not renew the pain in the recital.
1.365: But the evils that now beset your ill-fated sons—it is of these that I have come to tell. At first it was their decision that the throne should be left to Creon, and the city spared pollution, when they thought calmly about the ancient blight on our race,
1.370: and how it has clung to your unfortunate house. But now, moved by some god and by sinful heart, an evil strife has seized them—thrice-deluded!—to grasp at rule and the power of a tyrant. And the younger son has stripped the elder, Polyneices, of the throne,
1.375: and has driven him from his fatherland. But he, as the widespread rumor says among us, has gone to the valley of Argos as an exile, and is taking to himself a new marriage connection, and warriors for his friends, intending that Argos soon get hold of the Cadmean land,
1.380: or send its praises to the sky. These are not empty words, my father, but terrible deeds; and where the gods will have pity on your grief, I cannot tell.
1.385:
**Oedipus**
What, had you come to hope that the gods would ever have concern enough for me to give me rescue?
1.387:
**Ismene**
Yes, that is my hope, father, from the present oracles.
1.388:
**Oedipus**
What are they? What has been prophesied, my child?
1.389:
**Ismene**
That you will be desired some day, in life and death, by the men of that land,
1.391:
**Oedipus**
And who could profit from such a one as I?
1.392:
**Ismene**
Their power, it is said, proves to be in your hands.
1.393:
**Oedipus**
When I no longer exist, then I am a man?
1.394:
**Ismene**
Yes, for the gods now raise you up; but before they worked your ruin.
1.395:
**Oedipus**
It is a paltry thing to raise up age, when youth was ruined.
1.396:
**Ismene**
Well, know at least that Creon will come to you on this account—and soon, not late.
1.398:
**Oedipus**
With what purpose, daughter? Interpret that to me.
1.399:
**Ismene**
To plant you near the Cadmean land, so that they may have you in their power,
1.400: while you may not set foot within their borders.
1.401:
**Oedipus**
And how can I profit them while I rest beyond their gates?
1.402:
**Ismene**
Your tomb contains a curse for them, if it should suffer misfortune.
1.403:
**Oedipus**
I need no god to help my wits so far.
1.404:
**Ismene**
For this reason, therefore, they wish to get you as their neighbor;
1.405: but in a place where they will have you at their mercy.
1.406:
**Oedipus**
Will they really cover me in Theban dust?
1.407:
**Ismene**
No, the guilt of related blood forbids you, father.
1.408:
**Oedipus**
Then never will they become my masters.
1.409:
**Ismene**
Someday then this will be a grief for the Cadmeans.
1.410:
**Oedipus**
In what conjunction of events, my child?
1.411:
**Ismene**
Under the power of your anger, when they stand at your tomb.
1.412:
**Oedipus**
And who has told you this, my child?
1.413:
**Ismene**
Sacred envoys, from the Delphian hearth.
1.414:
**Oedipus**
And has Phoebus indeed spoken this concerning me?
1.415:
**Ismene**
So say the men who have come back to Thebes.
1.416:
**Oedipus**
Has either of my sons heard this?
1.417:
**Ismene**
Yes, both have heard it, and know it well.
1.418:
**Oedipus**
And then those most evil of sons, aware of this, preferred the kingship to the wish of recalling me?
1.420:
**Ismene**
It grieves me to hear this, but I must bear it.
1.421:
**Oedipus**
Then may the gods not quench their fated strife, and may it fall to me to decide this war on which they are now setting their hands, raising spear against spear!
1.425: For then neither would he who now holds the scepter and the throne survive, nor would the exile ever return; seeing that when I, their father, was being thrust without honor from my country, they did not stop or defend me. No, they saw me sent forth homeless,
1.430: and heard the crier proclaim my sentence of exile. Perhaps you will say that that was my own wish then, and that the city fittingly granted me that gift. Not so! For on that first day, when my heart seethed,
1.435: and my sweetest wish was for death—indeed, death by stoning—no one was found to help me in that desire. But after a time, when all my anguish was now softened, and when I began to feel that my heart had been excessive in punishing those past errors,
1.440: then it was that the city set about to drive me by force from the land, after all that time. And my sons, when they had the strength to bring help—sons to their own father—they would not do it. For lack of one little word from them, I was left to wander, an outcast and a beggar forever.
1.445: Instead, it is from these, maidens as they are, insofar as nature enables them, that I obtain my daily food, and a shelter in the land, and the aid of family. Their brothers have bartered their father for the throne, the scepter of power, and the rule of the realm.
1.450: No, never will they win Oedipus for an ally, nor will good ever come to them from this reign at Thebes; that I know, when I hear this maiden’s oracles and reflect on the old prophecies stored in my own mind, which Phoebus has fulfilled for me at last.
1.455: Therefore let them send Creon to seek me—or whoever else is mighty in Thebes. For if you, strangers, with the help of the dread goddesses who reign among your district, are willing to defend me, you will obtain a great savior for this city,
1.461:
**Chorus**
You are worthy of compassion, Oedipus, both you and these maidens. And since to this plea you append your power to save our land, I wish to advise you for your advantage.
1.465:
**Oedipus**
Dearest friends, be my patrons, and I will bring everything to completion.
1.466:
**Chorus**
Then make atonement to these divinities, to whom you have come first, and on whose ground you have trespassed.
1.468:
**Oedipus**
With what rites? Instruct me, strangers.
1.470: spring bring sacred drink-offerings, borne in ritually pure hands.
1.471:
**Oedipus**
And when I have gotten this unmixed draught?
1.472:
**Chorus**
There are bowls, the work of a skilled craftsman; crown their edges and the handles at either side.
1.474:
**Oedipus**
With olive branches, or woollen cloths, or in what way?
1.475:
**Chorus**
Take the freshly-shorn wool of a ewe-lamb.
1.476:
**Oedipus**
Good; and then to what last rite shall I proceed?
1.477:
**Chorus**
Pour the drink-offerings, with your face to the dawn.
1.478:
**Oedipus**
Shall I pour them with these vessels of which you speak?
1.479:
**Chorus**
Yes, in three streams; but the last vessel—
1.480:
**Oedipus**
With what shall I fill this, before I set it down? Teach me this also.
1.481:
**Chorus**
With water and honey; but add no wine.
1.482:
**Oedipus**
And when the ground under the dark shade has drunk these?
1.483:
**Chorus**
Three times lay on it nine branches of olive with both your hands, and meanwhile make this prayer.
1.485:
**Oedipus**
I wish to hear this prayer; it is the most important part.
1.486:
**Chorus**
We call them Eumenides, so that with well-wishing power they may receive the suppliant as his saviors. Let this be your prayer, or of whoever prays for you. Speak inaudibly, and do not lift up your voice; then depart, without looking behind.
1.490: If you should do this, I would be bold enough to come to your aid; but otherwise, stranger, I would fear for you.
1.493:
**Oedipus**
Daughters, do you hear these strangers who dwell nearby?
1.494:
**Antigone**
We have listened. Tell us what to do.
1.495:
**Oedipus**
I cannot make the trip; for I am disabled by lack of strength and lack of sight, twin evils. But let one of you two go and do these things. For I think that one soul suffices to pay this debt for ten thousand, if it comes with good will.
1.500: Act, then, with speed. But do not abandon me, for my body would not have the strength to move, without help or a guiding hand.
1.503:
**Ismene**
Then I will go to perform the rite; but where I am to find the place—this I wish to learn.
1.505:
**Chorus**
On the further side of this grove, stranger. And if you have need of anything, there is a guardian of the place. He will direct you.
1.507:
**Ismene**
Off to my task. But you, Antigone, watch our father here. In the case of parents, if we toil, we must not keep a memory of it.
*Ismene exits.*
1.510:
**Chorus**
Terrible it is, stranger, to arouse the old woe that has for so long been laid to rest: and yet I yearn to hear—
1.513:
**Chorus**
—Of that grief-filled anguish, cureless, with which you have wrestled.
1.515:
**Oedipus**
By your hospitality, do not uncover the shame that I have suffered!
1.517:
**Chorus**
Seeing that the tale is wide-spread and in no way weakens, I wish, friend, to hear it straight.
1.519:
**Oedipus**
Ah me!
**Chorus**
Grant the favor, I beg!
**Oedipus**
Alas, alas!
1.520:
**Chorus**
Grant my wish, as I have granted yours to the full.
1.521:
**Oedipus**
I have suffered the greatest misery, strangers—suffered it through unintended deeds—may the god know it! No part was of my own choice.
1.525:
**Oedipus**
In an evil marriage, the city bound me, unknowing, to ruin.
1.527:
**Chorus**
Is it true, as I hear, that you made your mother the partner of your bed, to its infamy?
1.529:
**Oedipus**
Ah, me! These words, strangers, are like death to my ears. And those two maidens of mine—
1.530:
**Chorus**
What will you say?
**Oedipus**
—Two daughters—two curses—
1.532:
**Oedipus**
—of mine, sprung from the travail of the womb that bore me too.
1.534:
**Chorus**
These, then, are at once your daughters, and—
1.536:
**Chorus**
Oh!
**Oedipus**
Indeed, woes untold sweep back upon my soul!
1.537:
**Chorus**
You have suffered—
**Oedipus**
I have suffered woes grievous to bear.
1.538:
**Chorus**
You have performed—
**Oedipus**
I have not performed!
1.539:
**Chorus**
How?
**Oedipus**
A gift was given to me—O, wretched that I am, if only I had never won from the city that gift for my services!
1.542:
**Chorus**
Cursed man! What of this? Did you commit the murder—
1.543:
**Oedipus**
What now? What would you learn?
1.544:
**Chorus**
—Of your father?
**Oedipus**
Oh! oh! a second stab—wound on wound!
1.545:
**Chorus**
You killed—
**Oedipus**
I killed—yet I have a plea—
1.546:
**Chorus**
What can you plead?
**Oedipus**
—A plea of justice.
**Chorus**
What?
**Oedipus**
I will tell you: I killed in ignorance and perished utterly. Pure before the law, without knowledge of my act, I have come to this!
1.549:
**Chorus**
Look, there comes our lord, Theseus son of Aegeus,
1.550:
at the sound of your voice, to do that for which he was summoned.
*Enter Theseus.*
1.551:
**Theseus**
Through hearing from many in the past about the bloody marring of your sight, I recognized it was you, son of Laius; and now on coming here, through sight I am more fully certain.
1.555: For your clothing and that heart-rending face alike assure me that it is you. And in all compassion I ask you, ill-fated Oedipus, with what petition to the city and to me have you taken your place here, you and the poor maiden at your side. Declare it. Dire indeed must be the fortune which you tell,
1.560: for me to stand aloof from it; since I know that I myself also was reared in exile, just as you, and that in foreign lands I wrestled with perils to my life, like no other man.
1.565: Never, then, would I turn aside from a stranger, such as you are now, or refuse to help in his deliverance. For I know well that I am a man, and that my portion of tomorrow is no greater than yours.
1.569:
**Oedipus**
Theseus, in a few words your nobleness has come to such a point
1.570: that I need make only a brief reply. You have said who I am, from what father I am sprung, and from what land I have come; and so nothing else remains for me but to speak my wish, and the tale is told.
1.575:
**Theseus**
Then inform me of this very thing, so that I may learn it.
1.576:
**Oedipus**
I come to offer you my care-worn body as a gift—not one fine to look on, but the gains from it are better than beauty.
1.579:
**Theseus**
And what gain do you claim to have brought?
1.580:
**Oedipus**
Later you may learn it—but not yet.
1.581:
**Theseus**
At what time, then, will the benefit become clear?
1.582:
**Oedipus**
When I am dead, and you have given me burial.
1.583:
**Theseus**
You crave life’s last service; but for all between you have no memory, or no care.
1.585:
**Oedipus**
Indeed, for by that service I gather in all the rest.
1.586:
**Theseus**
Well then, this favor you crave from me is brief indeed.
1.587:
**Oedipus**
Yet take care; the struggle here is no light one. No, indeed.
1.588:
**Theseus**
Do you mean in respect to your sons, or to me?
1.589:
**Oedipus**
They will compel you to convey me there to Thebes.
1.590:
**Theseus**
But if you are willing, then exile is not becoming.
1.591:
**Oedipus**
No, when I was willing, they refused.
1.592:
**Theseus**
Foolish man, anger amidst woes is not suitable.
1.593:
**Oedipus**
When you have heard my story, admonish; till then, forbear.
1.594:
**Theseus**
Speak. I must not pronounce without knowledge.
1.595:
**Oedipus**
I have suffered, Theseus, terrible woes upon woes.
1.596:
**Theseus**
Will you speak of the ancient trouble of your race?
1.597:
**Oedipus**
No, indeed; all Greeks speak of that.
1.598:
**Theseus**
How, then, do you suffer beyond what is mortal?
1.599:
**Oedipus**
The circumstance is this: from my country I have been driven by my own sons;
1.600: and I may not return, since I am guilty of a father’s blood.
1.602:
**Theseus**
Why would they have you brought back, if you must dwell apart?
1.603:
**Oedipus**
The word of the god will compel them.
1.604:
**Theseus**
What suffering do they fear from the oracles?
1.605:
**Oedipus**
That they must be struck down in this land.
1.606:
**Theseus**
And how should bitterness come between them and me?
1.607:
**Oedipus**
Dearest son of Aegeus, to the gods alone old age and death never come, but everything else sinks into chaos from time which overpowers all.
1.610: Earth’s strength decays, and so too the strength of the body; trust dies; distrust is born; and the same spirit is never steadfast among friends, or between city and city. For some now, for others tomorrow, sweet feelings turn to bitter, and then once more to being dear.
1.615: And if now the sun shines brightly between Thebes and you, yet time in his course gives birth to days and nights untold, in which from a small cause they will
1.620: scatter with the spear today’s pledges of concord. Then one day my slumbering and buried corpse, cold in death, will drink their warm blood, if Zeus is still Zeus, and Phoebus, the son of Zeus, speaks clear. But, since I would not break silence concerning words that must not spoken, allow me to cease where I began.
1.625: Only keep your own pledge good, and never will you say that in vain you welcomed Oedipus to dwell in this land—if indeed the gods do not deceive me.
1.629:
**Chorus**
Lord, from the first this man has shown a
1.630: will to bring these words, or similar ones, to completion for our land.
1.631:
**Theseus**
Who, then, would reject the goodwill of such a one? To whom, first, the hearth of a spear-friend is always available on our side, by reciprocal right; then too he has come as a suppliant to our gods,
1.635: paying no small recompense to this land and to me. In reverence for these claims, I will never spurn his favor, and I will establish a dwelling for him as a citizen in the land. And if it is the pleasure of the stranger to remain here, I will command you to
1.640: protect him; or, if it pleases him, to come with me. This choice or that, Oedipus, you may take; your desire will be mine.
1.642:
**Oedipus**
O Zeus, may you be good to men such as these!
1.643:
**Theseus**
What is your wish, then? Will you come to my house?
1.644:
**Oedipus**
Yes, I would, if it were right. But this is the place—
1.645:
**Theseus**
What will you do here? Speak, for I will not hinder you.
1.646:
**Oedipus**
—Where I will conquer those who cast me out.
1.647:
**Theseus**
The promised gift of your presence would be great.
1.648:
**Oedipus**
It shall be, if you keep your pledge with me.
1.649:
**Theseus**
Have courage concerning me; never will I betray you.
1.650:
**Oedipus**
I will not bind you with an oath as if an evil man.
1.651:
**Theseus**
Well, you would win nothing more than by my word.
1.652:
**Oedipus**
What will you do, then?
**Theseus**
What is it that you fear?
1.653:
**Oedipus**
Men will come—
**Theseus**
But these men here will see to that.
1.654:
**Oedipus**
Beware that if you leave me—
**Theseus**
Do not instruct me in my duties.
1.655:
**Oedipus**
Fear constrains me—
**Theseus**
My heart feels no fear.
1.656:
**Oedipus**
You do not know the threats—
**Theseus**
I know that none will lead you from here against my will. Often threats have blustered in men’s hearts with words loud and vain; but when the mind comes to itself once more,
1.660: the threats have vanished. For those men, too, perhaps—yes, even if in boldness they have spoken dreadful things of bringing you back, the voyage here will prove long and hard to sail. Now I exhort you, apart from any decision of mine, to take heart,
1.665: if indeed Phoebus has been your escort here. Even if I am not present, still my name, I know, will shield you from harm.
1.668:
**Chorus**
Stranger, in this land of fine horses you have come to earth’s fairest home, the shining Colonus.
1.670: Here the nightingale, a constant guest, trills her clear note under the trees of green glades, dwelling amid the wine-dark ivy
1.675: and the god’s inviolate foliage, rich in berries and fruit, unvisited by sun, unvexed by the wind of any storm. Here the reveller Dionysus ever walks the ground,
1.680: companion of the nymphs that nursed him.
1.681:
**Chorus**
And, fed on heavenly dew, the narcissus blooms day by day with its fair clusters; it is the ancient crown of the Great Goddesses.
1.685: And the crocus blooms with a golden gleam. Nor do the ever-flowing springs diminish, from which the waters of Cephisus wander, and each day with pure
1.690: current it moves over the plains of the land’s swelling bosom, bringing fertility. Nor have the dancing Muses shunned this place, nor Aphrodite of the golden rein.
1.694:
**Chorus**
And there is a thing such as I have not heard of on Asian ground,
1.695: nor as ever yet born in the great Dorian isle of Pelops: a plant unconquered, self-renewing, causing terror to destroying enemies.
1.700: It greatly flourishes in this land—the gray-leafed olive, nurturer of children. Youth cannot harm it by the ravages of his hand, nor can any who lives with old age. For the sleepless eye
1.705: of Zeus Morios watches over it, and gray-eyed Athena.
1.707:
**Chorus**
And I have more praise for this city our mother,
1.710: the gift of a great divinity, a glory most great: the might of horses, the might of colts, and the might of the sea. For you, son of Cronus, lord Poseidon, have set her on the throne of this pride,
1.715: by establishing first in our roads the bit that cures the rage of horses. And the shapely oar, well-fitted for the sea, in flying past the land leaps to follow the hundred-footed Nereids.
1.720:
**Antigone**
Land that is praised above all lands, now it is your task to make those bright praises seen in deeds!
1.722:
**Oedipus**
What strange new thing has happened, my daughter?
**Antigone**
Creon there draws near us, and not without followers, father.
1.724:
**Oedipus**
Ah, dearest old men, now give me
1.725: the final proof of my salvation!
1.726:
**Chorus**
Courage! It will be yours. For even if I am aged, this country’s strength has not grown old.
*Enter Creon, with attendants.*
1.728:
**Creon**
Gentlemen, noble dwellers in this land, I see from your eyes that a sudden fear has troubled you at my coming;
1.730: but do not shrink back from me, and let no evil word escape you. I am here with no thought of force; I am old, and I know that the city to which I have come is mighty, if any in Hellas has might.
1.735: No, I have been sent, aged as I am, to plead with this man to return with me to the land of Cadmus. I am not one man’s envoy, but have a mandate from all our people; since it belonged to me, by family, beyond all other Thebans to mourn his woes.
1.740: Unhappy Oedipus, hear us, and come home! Justly are you summoned by all the Cadmeans, and most of all by me, since I—unless I am the worst of all men born—feel most sorrow for your woes, old man,
1.745: when I see you, unhappy as you are, a stranger and a wanderer evermore, roaming in beggary, with one handmaid for your support. Ah, me, I had not thought that she could fall to such a depth of misery as that to which she has fallen—
1.750: this poor girl!—as she tends forever your dark life amid poverty; in ripe youth, but unwed: a prize for the first passerby to seize. Is it not a cruel reproach—alas!—that I have cast at you, and me, and all our race?
1.755: But indeed an open shame cannot be hidden. Oedipus, in the name of your ancestral gods, listen to me! Hide it, and consent to return to the city and the house of your ancestors, after bidding a kind farewell to this city. Athens is worthy; yet your own city has the first claim on your reverence,
1.760: since it was Thebes that nurtured you long ago.
1.761:
**Oedipus**
You who will dare anything, who from any just plea would derive a crafty trick, why do you make this attempt on me, and seek once more to snare me in your trap where I would feel most grief?
1.765: Long ago, when I labored under the sickness of my self-made evils, and I yearned to be cast out of the land, you refused to grant the favor. But when my fierce anger had spent its force, and seclusion in the house was sweet to me,
1.770: it was then that you thrust me from the house and cast me from the land. And this common race that you mention—that was not at all dear to you then. Now, in turn, when you see that I have a kindly welcome from this city and all its race, you try to pluck me away, wrapping your cruel thoughts in soft words.
1.775: And yet what pleasure do you find in this, in treating me as dear against my will? As if a man should refuse you a gift, bring you no aid, when you continually begged for it; but after your heart was sated with your desires, he should grant it then, when the favor could bring no joy
1.780: —would you not find your delight in this empty? Yet such is the nature of your own offers to me: noble in appearance, but in substance base. And I will declare it to these men too, to show you up as base. You have come to get me,
1.785: not to bring me home, but to plant me near your borders, so that your city might escape uninjured by evils from this land. That fate is not for you, but this one: the brooding of my vengeful spirit on your land forever; and for my sons, this heirloom:
1.790: just so much soil in my realm in which to die. Am I not wiser than you in the fortunes of Thebes? Yes, far wiser, by as much as the sources of my knowledge are truer: Phoebus I mean, and his father, Zeus himself. But you have come here with fraud on your lips, yes,
1.795: and with a tongue keener than the edge of a sword; yet by their use you may well reap more sorrow than salvation. Still, since I know that I cannot persuade you of this, go! Allow us to live on here; for even in this plight our life would not be bad, if we should be content with it.
1.800:
**Creon**
Which of us, do you think, suffers more in this exchange—I by your action, or you by your own?
1.802:
**Oedipus**
For me, it is enough if your pleading fails both with me and with these men nearby.
1.804:
**Creon**
Unhappy man, will you let everyone see that even in your years you have gained no sense?
1.805: Must you live on to disgrace your old age?
1.806:
**Oedipus**
You have a clever tongue, but I know no just man who can produce from every side a pretty speech.
1.808:
**Creon**
Words may be many, and yet not to the point.
1.809:
**Oedipus**
As if yours, indeed, were few, but on the mark.
1.810:
**Creon**
They cannot be, not for one whose mind is such as yours.
1.811:
**Oedipus**
Begone! I will say it for these men too. And do not besiege me with a jealous watch where I am destined to remain.
1.813:
**Creon**
I call these men, and not you, to witness the tenor of your words to your friends. And if I ever catch you—
1.815:
**Oedipus**
And who could catch me against the will of these allies?
1.816:
**Creon**
I promise you, soon you will be pained even without that.
1.817:
**Oedipus**
Where is the deed which backs that threatening word?
1.818:
**Creon**
One of your two daughters I have myself just seized and sent away. The other I will drag off immediately.
1.820:
**Oedipus**
Oh, no!
**Creon**
You will soon find more to weep about.
1.821:
**Oedipus**
You have my child?
**Creon**
And I will have this one in no long time.
1.822:
**Oedipus**
Oh! Strangers, what will you do? Will you betray me? Will you not drive the godless man from this land?
1.825: Your present deed is not just, nor the deed which you have done.
1.826:
**Creon**
*To his attendants.*
It is time for you to drag this girl off against her will, if she will not go freely.
1.828:
**Antigone**
Wretched that I am! Where can I flee? Where find help from gods or men?
1.830:
**Creon**
I will not touch this man, but her who is mine.
1.831:
**Oedipus**
Lords of the land!
**Chorus**
Stranger, you are acting unjustly.
1.832:
**Creon**
Justly.
**Chorus**
How?
**Creon**
I take my own.
*He lays his hand on Antigone.*
1.834:
**Chorus**
What are you doing, stranger? Release her!
1.835: Your strength and ours will soon come to the test.
1.836:
**Creon**
Stand back!
**Chorus**
Not while this is your purpose.
1.837:
**Creon**
There will be war with Thebes for you, if you harm me.
1.838:
**Oedipus**
Did I not say so?
**Chorus**
Unhand the girl at once!
1.839:
**Creon**
Do not make commands where you are not the master.
1.840:
**Chorus**
Let go, I tell you!
**Creon**
*To his guards, who seize Antigone.*
And I tell you: be off!
1.841:
**Chorus**
Help, men of Colonus, bring help! The city, our city, is attacked by force! Come to our aid!
1.844:
**Antigone**
I am being dragged away in misery. Strangers, strangers!
1.845:
**Oedipus**
My child, where are you?
**Antigone**
I am led off by force.
1.846:
**Oedipus**
Give me your hand, my child!
**Antigone**
I am helpless.
1.847:
**Creon**
Away with you!
**Oedipus**
I am wretched, wretched!
*The guards exit with Antigone.*
1.848:
**Creon**
So those two staffs will never again support your path.
1.850: But since you wish to overcome your country and your friends, whose will I, though tyrant as well, am here discharging, then I wish you victory. For in time, I am sure, you will come to recognize all this, that now too as in time past, it is you who have done yourself no good, by indulging your anger despite your friends.
1.855: This has always been your ruin.
1.856:
**Chorus**
Stop there, stranger!
**Creon**
Hands off, I say!
1.857:
**Chorus**
I will not let go, unless you give back the maidens.
1.858:
**Creon**
Then you will soon give the city a more valuable prize, for I will lay hands on more than those two girls.
1.860:
**Chorus**
What! What do you intend?
**Creon**
This man here will be my captive.
1.861:
**Chorus**
A valiant threat!
**Creon**
Straightaway it will be done.
1.862:
**Chorus**
Indeed, unless the ruler of this realm prevents you.
1.863:
**Oedipus**
Voice of shamelessness! Will you really lay hands on me?
1.864:
**Creon**
Shut up, I say!
**Oedipus**
No! May the powers of this place grant me to utter this further curse! Most evil of men, when these eyes were dark, you wrenched from me the helpless one who was my eyesight and made off with her by force. Therefore to you and to your race may the Sun, the god who sees all things,
1.870: grant in time an old age such as mine!
1.871:
**Creon**
Do you see this, people of the land?
1.872:
**Oedipus**

The Tracking Satyrs is a substantial fragment of a satyr play by Sophocles, discovered at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt in 1907. We have some 400 lines of a play that was probably about 800 lines long. The plot is the same as that of the: Apollo’s cows have been stolen, and the culprit turns out to be his newborn brother Hermes. This translation is adapted from. Walker established his own text for the fragment, filling in many of the gap reason="lost"s. I have occasionally adopted his supplements, but have basically translated the text of the first publication of the play, Apollo, son of Zeus and god of prophecy Silenus, father of the satyrs Cyllene, a nymph Hermes, newborn son of Zeus Chorus of satyrs
